en: The Lotus Sutra, Fascicle One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty, by Imperial Decree.
1. The Prologue, Chapter One. Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of twelve thousand bhikṣus. All were arhats whose outflows were exhausted, who were free from further afflictions, who had attained their own benefit, who had destroyed all fetters of existence, and whose minds had attained mastery.
Their names were:

Ājñātakauṇḍinya, Mahākāśyapa, Uruvilvākāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, Nadīkāśyapa, Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākātyāyana, Aniruddha, Kapphiṇa, Gavāmpati, Revata, Piṇḍola-bhāradvāja, Bakula, Mahākauṣṭhila, Nanda, Sundarananda, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Subhūti, Ānanda, and Rāhula—these and other such great arhats renowned to all.
Furthermore, there were two thousand monks, both those still in training and those beyond training.
The bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī was present with her retinue of six thousand,
as was the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā, mother of Rāhula, together with her own retinue.
There were eighty thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all of whom were non-retrogressive regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
all had attained dhāraṇīs;
they possessed the eloquence of joyful exposition and turned the irreversible wheel of Dharma.
They have made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, planted many roots of virtue in the presence of those Buddhas, and are constantly praised by them;
they cultivate their bodies with loving-kindness, skillfully enter the Buddha’s wisdom,
penetrate great insight, and reach the other shore.
His fame was heard throughout immeasurable worlds, and he was able to deliver countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings.
His names were:

Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, Bodhisattva Nityodyukta, Bodhisattva Anikṣiptadhura, Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, Bodhisattva Śūradatta, Bodhisattva Ratnacandra, Bodhisattva Candraprabha, Bodhisattva Pūrṇacandra, Bodhisattva Mahābala, Bodhisattva Aparimitabala, Bodhisattva Trailokyavikrama, Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, Bodhisattva Maitreya, Bodhisattva Ratnākara, and Bodhisattva Nāyaka. Together with these eighty thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, [the Buddha dwelt].
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra was present together with his retinue of twenty thousand devaputras.

Also present were the devaputra Candraprabha, the devaputra Samantagandha, the devaputra Ratnaprabha, and the Four Great Heavenly Kings, each accompanied by their own retinues of ten thousand devaputras.
The Devaputra Īśvara and the Devaputra Maheśvara were present together with their retinue of thirty thousand devaputras.
The Brahmā King, Lord of the Sahā World—Mahābrahmā Śikhin, Mahābrahmā Prabhāsa, and others—were present together with their retinue of twelve thousand devaputras.

There were eight dragon kings—Nanda the Dragon King, Upananda the Dragon King, Sāgara the Dragon King, Vāsuki the Dragon King, Takṣaka the Dragon King, Anavatapta the Dragon King, Mānasa the Dragon King, and Utpala the Dragon King—each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
There were four kinnara kings—Dharmakinnara-rāja, Sudharmakinnara-rāja, Mahādharmakinnara-rāja, and Dharmadhārakinnara-rāja—each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of followers.
There were four gandharva kings—Gandharvarāja Rati, Gandharvarāja Ratigvara, Gandharvarāja Surati, and Gandharvarāja Surativara—each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of followers.
There were four asura kings—Asura King Bāli, Asura King Kharaskandha, Asura King Vemacitrin, and Asura King Rāhu—each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.

There were four garuḍa kings—the Garuḍa King Mahātejas, the Garuḍa King Mahākāya, the Garuḍa King Mahāpūrṇa, and the Garuḍa King Manojña—each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of attendants.
King Ajātaśatru, the son of Vaidehī, together with several hundreds of thousands of retinues,
each bowed at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly, who were making offerings, paying homage, showing respect, and offering praise.

For the sake of the bodhisattvas, he preached a Mahāyāna sūtra titled *The Immeasurable Meanings*, a teaching for the instruction of bodhisattvas, which is protected by the mindfulness of the Buddhas.
Having spoken this sūtra, the Buddha sat cross-legged and entered the samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meanings, remaining with body and mind unmoving.
At that time, the heavens rained down māndārava flowers, mahāmāndārava flowers, mañjūṣaka flowers, and mahāmañjūṣaka flowers, scattering them over the Buddha and the great assembly.
Throughout all Buddha-worlds, the earth shook in six ways.

At that time, within the assembly—consisting of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, as well as minor kings and universal monarchs—all these great multitudes experienced what they had never before encountered; with joy, they joined their palms and gazed upon the Buddha with single-minded devotion.

At that time, the Buddha emitted a ray of light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, which illuminated eighteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction, pervading them all without exception, reaching downward as far as the Avīci Hell and upward as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
Within this world, one sees all the sentient beings of the six realms in those lands, as well as the present Buddhas of those lands, and hears the sutras and teachings spoken by those Buddhas.
He also saw those bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who had attained the Way through various practices;
he further saw the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the bodhisattva path with various causes and conditions, various convictions and understandings, and various appearances.
Furthermore, he saw various Buddhas entering parinirvāṇa.
He also saw that after those Buddhas had entered parinirvāṇa, stupas made of the seven precious substances were erected for their relics.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva had this thought:
"Now the World-Honored One has manifested this sign of supernatural transformation; by what causes and conditions does such an auspicious omen exist?
Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has entered into samādhi—this is an inconceivable manifestation of a rare and marvelous event."
"To whom should I ask?
Who would be able to answer?
He then had this further thought:
"This Mañjuśrī, the son of the Dharma King, has already drawn near to and made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas of the past; he must surely have seen this rare and wondrous sign."
"I shall now ask him.
At that time, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, as well as the devas, nāgas, and spirits, all had this thought:
"This is the sign of the Buddha’s light and supernormal power; whom should we now ask?"

At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, wishing to resolve his own doubts and also observing the minds of the fourfold assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—as well as the multitude of devas, nāgas, spirits, and others, asked Mañjuśrī:

“By what causes and conditions has this auspicious sign of supernatural power appeared, emitting a great radiance that illuminates eighteen thousand lands in the eastern direction, so that all the adornments of those Buddha-fields are clearly seen?”
Thereupon, Maitreya Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, asked in verse:
"Mañjuśrī! For what reason does the Guide’s white tuft between his eyebrows emit such a great light that it shines everywhere?"
Mandārava and Mañjūṣaka flowers rain down; sandalwood-scented winds delight the hearts of all.
By these causes and conditions, the earth is everywhere adorned and purified, and this world trembles in six ways.
At that time, the fourfold assembly was filled with joy; their bodies and minds were refreshed, having attained what they had never experienced before.
The eighteen thousand lands all became the color of gold, reaching even down to the Avīci Hell.
Reaching upward to the Peak of Existence,
one sees therein all the destinies of birth and death, the causal conditions of wholesome and unwholesome karma, and the beautiful or ugly retributions received.
Furthermore, I behold the Buddhas, the holy lords and lions, expounding the sūtras, which are subtle and supreme.
They emit gentle sounds to instruct countless billions of bodhisattvas;
their Brahma-voices are profound and wondrous, causing all who hear them to rejoice.
In each world, they preach the True Dharma through various causes and conditions;
by means of immeasurable parables, they illuminate the Buddha-dharma and awaken sentient beings.
If there are those who encounter suffering and weary of old age, illness, and death, I preach *nirvāṇa* for them so that they may reach the end of all suffering.
If there are those with merit who have made offerings to the Buddha and aspire to seek the supreme Dharma,
I preach the path of the *pratyekabuddha* for them.
If there are sons of the Buddha who cultivate various practices and seek unsurpassed wisdom, for them I preach the path of purity. Mañjuśrī!
Abiding here, I have seen and heard such things as these, as well as thousands of millions of other matters;
though they are so numerous, I shall now briefly describe them.
I behold in that land bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, seeking the Buddha-way through various causes and conditions.
Some practice giving, offering gold, silver, coral, pearls, mani-jewels, *śaṅkha-śilā*, agate, diamonds, and all manner of rare treasures; they give away their slaves, servants, and vehicles.
With jeweled ornaments and palanquins, they joyfully practice giving;
dedicating this toward the Buddha-way, they vow to obtain this vehicle, supreme within the three realms and praised by all Buddhas.
There may be bodhisattvas who give away precious chariots drawn by four horses, adorned with railings and flowered canopies;
yet they further see bodhisattvas who give their own flesh, hands, and feet, as well as their wives and children, seeking the unsurpassed path.
Furthermore, I see bodhisattvas who joyfully give away their heads, eyes, bodies, and limbs, seeking the wisdom of the Buddha. Mañjuśrī!
Having asked about the Unsurpassed Way, he immediately abandoned his pleasant lands, palaces, ministers, and concubines;
he shaved off his hair and beard and donned the dharma robes.
In some instances, one sees a bodhisattva who has become a bhikṣu, dwelling alone in quietude and delighting in reciting the sūtras.
Furthermore, one sees a bodhisattva who, with courageous diligence, enters deep mountains to contemplate the Buddha-way.
Furthermore, I see those who have transcended desire, dwelling perpetually in seclusion, deeply cultivating meditative concentration, and attaining the five supernormal powers.
I also see Bodhisattvas, settled in dhyāna with palms joined, praising the Kings of Dharma with tens of millions of verses.
Again I see bodhisattvas, whose wisdom is profound and whose resolve is firm; they are able to question the Buddhas and, having heard [the teachings], receive and uphold them all.
Furthermore, I see sons of the Buddha, complete in concentration and wisdom, who use immeasurable parables to preach the Dharma for the sake of the multitudes.
He delights in preaching the Dharma to transform all bodhisattvas, shatters the hosts of Māra, and beats the drum of the Dharma. Furthermore,
he sees bodhisattvas who remain in tranquil silence, and though devas and nāgas pay them homage,
they do not consider this a cause for joy.
Furthermore, I see Bodhisattvas dwelling in the forests emitting light, rescuing those in the hells from suffering and causing them to enter the Buddha-way.
I also see these sons of the Buddha who never sleep, walking in meditation within the groves, diligently seeking the Buddha-way.
Furthermore, seeing those endowed with precepts, their majestic deportment flawless and pure as a precious jewel,
seeking the path of the Buddha;
even when arrogant people revile them with foul language or strike them with blows, they are able to endure it all.
Seeking the path of the Buddha,
together with their deluded retinues, they draw near to the wise;
with single-mindedness they eliminate distraction and withdraw their thoughts in mountain forests for hundreds of millions of years, seeking the path of the Buddha.
Or they see Bodhisattvas giving various delicacies, foods, and drinks, as well as a hundred kinds of medicinal decoctions,
to the Buddha and the Sangha;
or giving famous robes and superior garments worth ten million, or even priceless garments, to the Buddha and the Sangha.
Tens of millions of kinds of precious sandalwood mansions and various exquisite couches were given to the Buddha and the Saṃgha.
Pure gardens and groves, with flourishing flowers and fruits, and flowing springs and bathing pools were given to the Buddha and the Saṃgha.
Through such various and subtle acts of giving, they joyfully practice without weariness, seeking the unsurpassed path.
Some Bodhisattvas preach the Dharma of quiescent extinction, providing diverse instructions to countless sentient beings.
Or one sees a bodhisattva contemplating the nature of all phenomena, which possess no dual characteristics and are like empty space.
Furthermore, one sees a son of the Buddha whose mind is free from attachment, seeking the unsurpassed path through this wondrous wisdom.
Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, make offerings to the śarīras.
They also see sons of the Buddha constructing various stūpas and temples, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The boundaries of the land were magnificently adorned; the jeweled stupa was lofty and sublime, five thousand yojanas in height, and exactly two thousand yojanas in both length and breadth.
Each stupa and temple has a thousand banners and streamers; pearl-latticed canopies hang above, and precious bells chime in harmony.
Gods, dragons, spirits, humans, and non-humans constantly offer incense, flowers, and music as worship.
Mañjuśrī! To make offerings to the śarīra, they adorned the stūpas and temples;
the realm naturally became extraordinary and wondrously beautiful, like the king of celestial trees with its flowers in full bloom.
The Buddha emits a single ray of light, and I, along with this assembly, behold these lands in all their various wonders and excellences.
Through the spiritual power and rare wisdom of the Buddhas, they emit a single pure light that illuminates immeasurable lands.
"We have seen this and attained what we have never experienced before.
O Son of the Buddha, Mañjuśrī!
We pray that you will resolve the doubts of the assembly."
The fourfold assembly looks up with joy, gazing upon you, O Benevolent One, and me.
For what reason, World-Honored One, do you emit this radiance?
Son of the Buddha, please answer at this time; resolve our doubts and bring us joy.
For what benefit does he radiate this light?
Is it because the Buddha, seated at the site of enlightenment, wishes to proclaim the wondrous Dharma he has attained?
Is it that you shall receive a prophecy?
To reveal the various Buddha-lands, adorned and purified with myriad jewels, and to cause one to behold the Buddhas—
this is no small matter.
“Mañjuśrī, you should know that the fourfold assembly, along with the nāgas and spirits, are gazing upon you, O Benevolent One; what will you preach for them?
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva and the other great beings:
“O sons of good family!

As I reflect upon it, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, now wishes to proclaim the Great Dharma, to rain down the great rain of Dharma, to blow the great conch of Dharma, to beat the great drum of Dharma, and to expound the great meaning of Dharma.
"O sons of good family!
In the past, I have witnessed this omen among the Buddhas of former times: after emitting such light, they immediately preached the Great Dharma.

Therefore, you should know that the present Buddha’s manifestation of light is likewise so; he wishes to cause all sentient beings to hear and know the Dharma that is difficult for all the world to believe, and thus he manifests this omen."
“O sons of good family!

In the past, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Candrasūryapradīpa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. He expounded the True Dharma, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; its meaning is profound and far-reaching, its phrasing is exquisite, it is pure and unadulterated, and it is fully endowed with the characteristics of the pure and holy Brahma-conduct.”

For those seeking the vehicle of the śrāvaka, he teaches the Dharma appropriate to the Four Noble Truths, so that they may transcend birth, old age, sickness, and death, and ultimately attain nirvāṇa;
for those seeking the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha, he teaches the Dharma appropriate to the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination;
and for all bodhisattvas, he teaches the Dharma appropriate to the six pāramitās, enabling them to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and achieve the knowledge of all modes.

"Next, there was another Buddha also named Candrasūryapradīpa; next, there was yet another Buddha also named Candrasūryapradīpa. In this manner, twenty thousand Buddhas all shared the same name, titled Candrasūryapradīpa, and also shared the same clan name, Bharadvāja."
Maitreya, you should know that from the first Buddha to the last, they all share the same name, Sūryacandrapradīpa, and are fully endowed with the ten titles.
The Dharma they teach is virtuous in its beginning, middle, and end.
The last of those Buddhas, before he had left the household life, had eight princes:

the first was named Meaningful Intent (Yiyi), the second Good Intent (Shanyi), the third Immeasurable Intent (Wuliangyi), the fourth Jewel Intent (Baoyi), the fifth Increasing Intent (Zengyi), the sixth Doubt-Dispelling Intent (Chuyiyi), the seventh Resonant Intent (Xiangyi), and the eighth Dharma Intent (Fayi).
These eight princes possessed majestic power and sovereignty, each governing a four-continent world-system.

When these princes heard that their father had renounced the world and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they all relinquished their royal thrones and likewise followed him into the homeless life. They resolved upon the Mahāyāna path, constantly cultivated pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), and all became Dharma-preachers; they had already planted various roots of goodness under ten million buddhas.
At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa preached a Mahāyāna sūtra titled *Anantārtha*, a teaching for bodhisattvas, which is protected by the Buddhas.
Having finished preaching this sūtra, he sat cross-legged in the midst of the great assembly and entered the *Anantārthavyūha-samādhi*, remaining with body and mind unmoving.
At that time, the heavens rained down mandārava flowers, mahāmandārava flowers, mañjūṣaka flowers, and mahāmañjūṣaka flowers, scattering them over the Buddha and the great assembly.
Throughout all Buddha-worlds, the earth shook in six ways.

At that time, within the assembly—consisting of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, as well as various minor kings and universal monarchs—all these great multitudes experienced what they had never before encountered; with joy, they joined their palms and gazed one-pointedly upon the Buddha.

At that time, the Tathāgata emitted a ray of light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, which illuminated eighteen thousand Buddha-lands in the eastern direction, pervading them all without exception, just as these various Buddha-lands are seen now.
Maitreya, you should know that at that time, within the assembly, there were twenty billion bodhisattvas who desired to hear the Dharma.

When these bodhisattvas saw this light universally illuminating the buddha-field, they experienced what they had never known before and wished to understand the causes and conditions for the appearance of this light.
At that time there was a bodhisattva named Wonderful Light who had eight hundred disciples.

Then, the Buddha Sun Moon Lamp Bright arose from samādhi and, through the bodhisattva Wonderful Light, preached a Mahāyāna sūtra titled *The Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma*, a teaching for bodhisattvas protected by the Buddhas, remaining seated without rising for sixty minor kalpas.

The listeners in the assembly were also seated in one place; for sixty minor kalpas they remained unmoving in body and mind as they listened to what the Buddha preached, yet it seemed to them like the duration of a single meal.
At that time, not a single person among the multitude felt weariness of either body or mind.
After the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa had preached this sutra for sixty intermediate kalpas, he spoke these words amidst the assembly of Brahmās, Māras, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, gods, humans, and asuras:
"This very day, at midnight, the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa without remainder."
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Guṇakośa, whom the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa immediately bestowed with a prediction of enlightenment.
He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"This Bodhisattva Guṇakośa shall next become a Buddha, known by the name Viśuddhakāya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
After the Buddha had bestowed this prediction, he entered nirvana without remainder during the middle watch of the night.
Following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light upheld the Lotus Sutra and expounded it for others for a full eighty minor kalpas.
The eight sons of the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa all took Mārajit as their teacher; Mārajit instructed and transformed them, causing them to become firm in their resolve for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

After these princes had made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, they all attained the Way of the Buddha; the last among them to achieve Buddhahood was named Dīpaṃkara.

Among his eight hundred disciples, there was one named Seeking Fame (Yashaskāma). He was greedily attached to gain and offerings; although he recited many sutras, he did not master them and forgot much of what he had learned, which was why he was called Seeking Fame.

Because this person has also planted various roots of goodness as causal conditions, they shall encounter immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, making offerings to them, honoring them, respecting them, and praising them.
Maitreya, you should know this: at that time, was the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light anyone else?
It was my own self.
As for the Bodhisattva Seeking Fame, he was you yourself.
Now, seeing this auspicious omen, which is no different from that of old, I reflect thus:
"Today the Tathāgata shall preach a Mahāyāna sūtra titled 'The Lotus of the Wonderful Dharma,' the teaching for bodhisattvas, which is protected by the Buddhas."
At that time, Mañjuśrī, wishing to reiterate this meaning within the great assembly,
spoke these verses: "I recall a past life, In immeasurable and countless kalpas,
There was a Buddha, Honored among Men, Named Candrasūryapradīpa."
The World-Honored One expounds the Dharma,
delivering immeasurable sentient beings and countless billions of bodhisattvas, causing them to enter the Buddha’s wisdom.
Before the Buddha left the household life, eight princes were born to him.
Seeing the Great Sage renounce the world, they also followed him to practice the pure life.
At that time, the Buddha preached the Mahāyāna;
the sūtra was named "The Immeasurable Meanings," which he extensively analyzed and explained for the great assembly.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra,
he sat cross-legged upon the Dharma-seat in samādhi, named the Station of Immeasurable Meanings.
Heavenly *māndārava* flowers rained down, and celestial drums resounded spontaneously.
The devas, nāgas, and spirits made offerings to the Honored One among Men.
All the Buddha-lands immediately shook with great tremors;
the Buddha emitted light from between his eyebrows, manifesting various rare and wondrous events.
This light shines upon the eastern direction, reaching eighteen thousand Buddha-lands,
revealing to all sentient beings the places where they undergo the retribution of birth and death through their karma.
Some see these various Buddha-lands adorned with a multitude of precious jewels.
The colors of lapis lazuli and crystal arise from the light of the Buddha’s radiance. Furthermore,
one beholds the various devas and humans, the hosts of nāgas, spirits, and yakṣas,
as well as the gandharvas and kiṃnaras, each making offerings to that Buddha.
Furthermore, I see all the Tathāgatas, who have spontaneously attained the Buddha-way;
their bodies are like mountains of gold, sublime and most wondrously beautiful.
Like a pure crystal vessel, within which a true golden image appears.
The World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly, expounds the profound meaning of the Dharma.
In each and every Buddha-land, there are countless hosts of śrāvakas;
illuminated by the Buddha’s light, they all behold those great assemblies.
There are some bhikṣus who, dwelling amidst mountains and forests,
diligently uphold the pure precepts as if guarding a bright pearl.
Furthermore, one sees various bodhisattvas practicing generosity, patience, and so forth.
Their number is like the sands of the Ganges, all due to the illumination of the Buddha’s light.
Furthermore, one sees various bodhisattvas deeply entering various meditative concentrations;
their bodies and minds are tranquil and unmoving as they seek the unsurpassed path.
Furthermore, I see various bodhisattvas, Who know the mark of the quiescence of all phenomena;
Each, within their own land, Preaches the Dharma seeking the Buddha-way.
At that time, the fourfold assembly Beheld the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa.
Manifesting great supernormal powers, their hearts were all filled with joy,
and each asked one another:
"What is the cause and condition for this?"
The Honored One, revered by devas and humans, having just arisen from samādhi, praised Bodhisattva Wonderful Light:
"You are that to whom all turn for refuge and trust; you are able to uphold the treasury of the Dharma."
"The Dharma I have taught, you alone are able to realize and know.
Having thus praised him and gladdened Subhāṣitaghoṣa,
the World-Honored One preached this Lotus Sūtra for a full sixty intermediate kalpas."
Without rising from this seat,
the Dharma Master Wondrous Light was able to receive and uphold entirely the sublime and wondrous Dharma that was preached.
After the Buddha had spoken this Lotus Sūtra and caused the assembly to rejoice, he [continued]:
Immediately on that very day, he addressed the assembly of devas and humans:
"The meaning of the true mark of all dharmas has already been explained for you;
this very night at midnight, I shall enter parinirvāṇa."
You must practice with single-minded diligence and remain free from negligence;
for Buddhas are extremely difficult to encounter, appearing but once in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
You, the sons of the World-Honored One, having heard that the Buddha has entered nirvana, [should act accordingly].
Each harbors grief and distress, wondering, "How can the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa be so swift?
The Holy Lord, King of Dharma, comforts the immeasurable multitudes:
"When I enter parinirvāṇa, you should not grieve or fear."
This Bodhisattva Guṇagañja has already attained thorough penetration into the outflow-free true mark (*anāsrava-lakṣaṇa*).
He shall next become a Buddha named Viśuddhakāya, who will likewise deliver immeasurable multitudes.
This night the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, like a fire extinguished when the fuel is spent;
his relics were distributed, and immeasurable stūpas were erected.
Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, their number like the sands of the Ganges, [honored them].
He redoubled his diligent effort to seek the unsurpassed path.
This Dharma Master Wondrous Light upheld the treasury of the Buddha’s teachings and,
throughout eighty minor kalpas, widely proclaimed the Lotus Sūtra.
These eight princes, converted by Prabhāsa,
have become firm in the unsurpassed path and shall behold countless Buddhas.
Having made offerings to all these Buddhas, they will practice the Great Way in accordance with it.
They attained Buddhahood one after another, receiving their predictions in succession.
Finally, the God among Gods appeared, known as Dīpaṃkara Buddha;
the teacher of all seers, he delivered and liberated immeasurable multitudes.
This Dharma Master Wonderful Light had at that time a disciple whose mind was constantly filled with indolence;
he was greedily attached to fame and profit,
never tiring in his pursuit of them, and frequented the homes of the noble families.
They abandon what they have studied and recited, falling into forgetfulness and failing to master it.
For these reasons, they are called "those who seek fame.
Yet they also perform various wholesome deeds and succeed in seeing countless Buddhas.
Having made offerings to all Buddhas, practicing in accordance with the Great Way and fulfilling the six pāramitās, he now beholds the Lion of the Śākyas.
Hereafter he shall become a Buddha, named Maitreya.
He extensively delivered all sentient beings, their number being immeasurable.
After that Buddha passed into extinction, you were the one who was indolent;
as for the Dharma Master Wondrous Light, he is my very self now.
I beheld the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, whose original radiance was such as this;
by this I know that the present Buddha intends to preach the Lotus Sūtra.
The present signs are like those original omens; these are the skillful means of all Buddhas.
Now the Buddha emits a radiance, To assist in bringing forth the meaning of the true mark.
All you people should now know: With palms joined and single-minded, wait!
The Buddha shall rain down the rain of Dharma, To satisfy those who seek the Way.
"For all those seeking the three vehicles, if there are any who harbor doubts or regrets, the Buddha shall eliminate them for them, so that they may be exhausted without remainder.
Chapter Two: The Expedient Means *The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Two: The Expedient Means At that time, the World-Honored One arose serenely from his samādhi and addressed Śāriputra:

“The wisdom of the Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable; the gateway to that wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter, such that it cannot be known by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.”

Why is this? The Buddha has personally attended upon countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas and fully practiced the immeasurable Dharma-paths of all those Buddhas. With courageous and diligent effort, his fame is heard everywhere; he has accomplished profound and unprecedented dharmas, and the underlying intent of what he teaches according to what is appropriate is difficult to understand.

Śāriputra! Since my attainment of Buddhahood, I have extensively expounded the verbal teachings through various causes and conditions and various parables, employing countless skillful means to guide sentient beings and cause them to leave behind all attachments.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has already fully perfected the pāramitās of skillful means, knowledge, and vision. Śāriputra!

The Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are vast and profound, immeasurable and unimpeded; his powers, fearlessnesses, meditative concentrations, liberations, and samādhis penetrate the boundless depths, accomplishing all unprecedented dharmas.
Śāriputra! The Tathāgata is able to make various distinctions and skillfully expound all dharmas; his words are gentle and supple, gladdening the hearts of the multitude. Śāriputra!
To speak briefly, the Buddha has fully accomplished immeasurable, boundless, and unprecedented dharmas.
"Stop, Śāriputra! There is no need to say more."
Why is this? Because the Buddha has accomplished a foremost, rare, and difficult-to-understand Dharma.

Only a Buddha and a Buddha can exhaustively fathom the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena—that is to say, that all phenomena have such characteristics, such natures, such essences, such powers, such functions, such causes, such conditions, such fruits, such retributions, and are equal in their beginning, middle, and end.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Hero of the World is immeasurable; Neither the devas nor the people of the world, Nor any class of sentient beings, Is able to know the Buddha."
The Buddha’s powers and fearlessnesses, his liberations and various samādhis,
as well as all other Buddha-qualities— none can measure them.
Having followed countless Buddhas from the beginning, he has fully practiced all paths.
The most profound and subtle Dharma is difficult to see and difficult to comprehend.
Having practiced these various paths for immeasurable billions of kalpas and attained the fruit at the site of enlightenment, I have fully known and seen them all.
Such great fruits of retribution, with their various natures, characteristics, and meanings—only I and the Buddhas of the ten directions can know these matters.
This Dharma cannot be shown; its words and signs are quiescent.
Among all other classes of sentient beings, none are able to understand it,
except for the assembly of Bodhisattvas whose power of faith is firm.
These disciples of the Buddhas have, in the past, made offerings to the various Buddhas.
All outflows are exhausted, dwelling in their final bodies;
such persons as these cannot be overcome by any power.
Even if the entire world were filled with those like Śāriputra, [they would still be unable to do so].
Exhausting all thought to measure it together, one cannot fathom the Buddha’s wisdom.
Even if those who fill the ten directions were all like Śāriputra,
and the other disciples likewise filled the lands of the ten directions—
Even if they were to exhaust their thoughts and deliberate together,
they still could not know it. Pratyekabuddhas of sharp wisdom, free from outflows, in their final bodies—
should they fill the worlds of the ten directions, their number being like that of the bamboo groves, [they would still not know].
If these beings were to unite their minds for immeasurable billions of kalpas,
desiring to contemplate the Buddha’s true wisdom, they would not be able to know even a small fraction of it.
Even a bodhisattva who has newly resolved to attain enlightenment, though having made offerings to countless buddhas, [remains unable to fathom it].
Thoroughly comprehending all meanings and purposes, and being further able to skillfully expound the Dharma—
like rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds, filling the lands of the ten directions—
with a single mind and wondrous wisdom, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
All together they deliberated, yet could not know the Buddha’s wisdom.
Even the non-retrogressive bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
though seeking it with a single mind, likewise could not know it.
Again he addressed Śāriputra:
"The profound and subtle Dharma, which I have now fully attained—
only I know its characteristics, and so it is with the Buddhas of the ten directions."
Śāriputra, you should know that the words of all Buddhas do not differ.
Regarding the Dharma taught by the Buddha, you should give rise to great power of faith.
After a long time, the World-Honored One will surely speak the truth.
He addressed the assembly of śrāvakas, as well as those seeking the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas:
"It is I who have caused you to be liberated from the bonds of suffering and enabled you to attain nirvāṇa."
"By the power of skillful means, the Buddha reveals the teachings of the three vehicles;
for sentient beings are attached everywhere, he leads them so that they may attain liberation.

At that time, within the great assembly, there were various śrāvakas and arhats whose outflows were exhausted, such as Ājñātakauṇḍinya and his twelve hundred followers, as well as bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who had resolved upon the paths of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha. Each of them thought to themselves:
"Now, for what reason does the World-Honored One so earnestly praise skillful means and speak thus:
'The Dharma attained by the Buddha is extremely profound and difficult to understand; its underlying intent is difficult to discern, and it is beyond the reach of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas'?"
“The Buddha has taught the meaning of a single liberation; we too have attained this Dharma and reached Nirvana, yet now we do not know where this meaning leads.
At that time, Śāriputra, knowing the doubts in the minds of the fourfold assembly and being himself also not yet fully certain, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
For what cause and by what condition do you so earnestly praise the Buddhas' foremost skillful means—the profound, subtle, and difficult-to-understand Dharma?
Since the past, I have never heard such a teaching from the Buddha;
now the fourfold assembly all harbor doubts.
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound upon this matter.
For what reason does the World-Honored One so earnestly praise this profound, subtle, and difficult-to-understand Dharma?
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“The Great Holy Honored One, the Sun of Wisdom, has at last proclaimed this Dharma;
he himself declares that he has attained such inconceivable dharmas as the powers,
the fearlessnesses, the samādhis, the meditative concentrations, and the liberations.”
Regarding the Dharma attained at the site of enlightenment, there is no one able to pose a question;
my intent is difficult to fathom, and likewise, there is no one able to ask.
Without being questioned, I shall speak of my own accord, praising the path I have traveled.
This wisdom is most subtle, that which all Buddhas have attained.
Now even the outflow-free arhats and those seeking nirvana have all fallen into a web of doubt: for what reason has the Buddha spoken this?
Those seeking the state of a Pratyekabuddha— monks and nuns,
devas, nāgas, and spirits, as well as gandharvas and others—
looked at one another with hesitation and gazed up in reverence at the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings.
What is the meaning of this matter? I pray that the Buddha will explain it for me.
Among the assembly of śrāvakas, the Buddha declared me to be foremost;
yet now, regarding my own wisdom, I am beset by doubt and cannot comprehend it.
Is this the ultimate Dharma?
Is this the path to be traversed?
The sons born from the Buddha’s own mouth join their palms, gazing up at him in expectation.
I pray that you will emit a subtle and wondrous sound, and at this time speak according to reality.
The devas, nāgas, and spirits, numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges,
and the bodhisattvas who seek the Buddha, numbering eighty thousand in great measure— [all wait for your teaching].
Furthermore, from the many billions of lands, the wheel-turning sage-kings arrived;
with palms joined in a reverent heart, they desired to hear the complete path.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
"Stop, stop! There is no need to speak further.
If this matter were to be spoken, all the devas and humans in the entire world would be struck with alarm and doubt."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One, we pray that you will speak of this; we pray that you will speak of this! Why is this so?

In this assembly are countless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya sentient beings who have previously seen various Buddhas; their faculties are sharp and keen, and their wisdom is clear and lucid, such that upon hearing what the Buddha speaks, they are able to respond with reverence and faith.
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Dharma King, the Unsurpassed Honored One, Please speak; pray do not hesitate."
"In this assembly there are immeasurable multitudes, some of whom are capable of reverent faith.
The Buddha again restrained Śāriputra, saying:
"If you were to speak of these matters, all the worlds—including devas, humans, and asuras—would be struck with alarm and doubt; monks of overweening pride would fall into a great abyss."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Cease, cease; there is no need to speak, For my Dharma is subtle and inconceivable.
Those with overweening pride, Upon hearing it, will certainly not show respect or faith."
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We only pray that you will speak of this; we only pray that you will speak of this!”
In this assembly now, there are hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of beings like ourselves who, life after life, have already received transformation through the Buddha.
People such as these will certainly be able to respect and believe [the teaching], remaining peaceful and secure throughout the long night, and bringing great benefit to many.
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"O Unsurpassed One, Honored among Two-legged Beings, I pray you, preach the foremost Dharma.
As I am the Buddha’s eldest son, I entreat you to explain it in detail."
This assembly consists of immeasurable multitudes who are able to revere and believe in this Dharma;
the Buddha has already, throughout successive lifetimes, taught and transformed such as these.
All now join their palms with single-minded devotion, desiring to hear and receive the Buddha’s words.
"We, the twelve hundred, and the others who seek Buddhahood,
pray that for the sake of this assembly you will deign to explain it in detail.
When these people hear this Dharma, they will give rise to great joy."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
"Since you have earnestly requested this three times, how could I not speak?
Listen now with focused attention and reflect well upon it; I shall analyze and explain it for you."
When these words were spoken, five thousand members of the assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—immediately rose from their seats, paid homage to the Buddha, and withdrew.

Why is this so? Because these individuals have deeply rooted and heavy karmic offenses, as well as overweening pride; they claim to have attained what they have not attained and claim to have realized what they have not realized. Possessing such faults, they do not abide [in the Dharma].
The World-Honored One remained silent and did not stop him.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
“In this assembly of mine now, there are no longer any branches or leaves; it consists purely of the solid core.”
Śāriputra! For such people of overweening pride, it would be better even if they were to regress.
Listen well now; I shall speak for you.
Śāriputra said:
“So be it, World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it.”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Such a sublime Dharma as this is preached by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, only from time to time; it appears but once in a long while, like the udumbara flower."
Śāriputra! You all should believe what the Buddha has spoken; his words are not false. Śāriputra!
The Buddhas teach the Dharma according to what is appropriate; their underlying intentions are difficult to understand. Why is this?
By means of countless skillful expedients, various causes and conditions, parables, and modes of expression, I have expounded all dharmas.
This Dharma cannot be understood through deliberation or discrimination; only the Buddhas are able to know it.
Why is this? It is because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely for the sake of the one great causal matter.
Śāriputra! Why is it said that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely for the sake of one great causal matter?
It is because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, wish to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and to bring them to purity; for this reason, they appear in the world.
He appears in the world because he wishes to reveal to sentient beings the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
he appears in the world because he wishes to cause sentient beings to awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
he appears in the world because he wishes to cause sentient beings to enter the path of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
"Śāriputra!
It is for the sake of this one great causal matter that all Buddhas appear in the world.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, teach and transform only bodhisattvas; whatever they do is always for a single purpose: solely to manifest and awaken sentient beings to the knowledge and vision of the Buddha."
Śāriputra! The Tathāgata teaches the Dharma for sentient beings solely by means of the Single Buddha Vehicle; there is no other vehicle, whether a second or a third.
"Śāriputra! The Dharma of all Buddhas in the ten directions is likewise thus. Śāriputra!"

The Buddhas of the past, by means of immeasurable and innumerable skillful expedients, various causes and conditions, parables, and modes of expression, have expounded all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings; these dharmas are all for the purpose of the Single Buddha Vehicle.
These sentient beings, having heard the Dharma from the Buddhas, will ultimately all attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). "Śāriputra!

Future Buddhas who shall appear in the world will likewise, through immeasurable and innumerable skillful means, by means of various causes, conditions, parables, and expressions, expound the various Dharmas for the sake of sentient beings; these Dharmas are all for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle."
These sentient beings, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, will ultimately all attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). "Śāriputra!

In the present, throughout the immeasurable hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, and millions of buddha-fields in the ten directions, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, bring great benefit and peace and happiness to sentient beings. These Buddhas also, by means of immeasurable and innumerable skillful expedients (*upāya*), through various causes, conditions, parables, and expressions, expound the various dharmas for the sake of sentient beings; yet these dharmas are all for the purpose of the Single Buddha Vehicle."
These sentient beings, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, will ultimately all attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). "Śāriputra!

These Buddhas teach and transform only bodhisattvas because they wish to reveal the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to sentient beings, because they wish to awaken sentient beings through the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and because they wish to cause sentient beings to enter into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision."

“Śāriputra! I am now likewise in this way: knowing that sentient beings have various desires and deep-seated attachments, I preach the Dharma for them through the power of skillful means, using various causes and conditions, parables, and expressions, in accordance with their fundamental natures.”
Śāriputra! All this is for the sake of attaining the single Buddha-vehicle and all-knowledge. Śāriputra!
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is not even the vehicle of the two vehicles, let alone the three.

Śāriputra, the Buddhas appear in the world of the five turbidities: namely, the turbidity of the eon, the turbidity of afflictions, the turbidity of sentient beings, the turbidity of views, and the turbidity of lifespan.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

During the period of the turbidity of the kalpa, when sentient beings are heavily defiled and possess stinginess, greed, and jealousy, and because they have brought to fruition various unwholesome roots, the Buddhas, through the power of skillful means, distinguish and teach three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle.

Śāriputra! If any of my disciples claim to be Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas, yet do not hear of nor know that all Buddhas and Tathāgatas teach and transform only Bodhisattvas, these are not disciples of the Buddha, nor Arhats, nor Pratyekabuddhas.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

These bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, claiming for themselves that they have already attained arhatship, that this is their final body, and that they have reached ultimate nirvāṇa, no longer aspire toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; you should know that such people are all those with overweening pride."
Why is this? If there were a bhikṣu who had truly attained arhatship and yet did not believe in this Dharma, such a thing would be impossible—
except after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when the Buddha is no longer present before them.
Why is this? After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain the meaning of such sutras as these will be difficult to find.
If they encounter other Buddhas, they will then attain definitive understanding within this Dharma.
Śāriputra! You all should with one mind believe, understand, accept, and uphold the Buddha’s words.
The words of the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are not false; there is no other vehicle, but only the Single Buddha Vehicle.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs who harbor overweening pride,
upāsakas with arrogance, and upāsikās lacking faith— ”
Such as these were the fourfold assembly, numbering five thousand;
they did not perceive their own faults, had deficiencies and omissions in their precepts,
and cherished their own blemishes.
The chaff and dregs among the assembly have departed due to the Buddha’s majestic power;
such people lack merit and are unable to receive this Dharma.
This assembly is now free of branches and leaves, consisting only of the pure and substantial.
Śāriputra, listen well!
The Dharma attained by all Buddhas, through the power of immeasurable skillful means, is taught for the sake of sentient beings.
According to what is contemplated in the minds of sentient beings, and according to the various paths they practice—
The various dispositions toward sensual desires and the wholesome or unwholesome karma of past lives—
the Buddha knows them all. Through the power of skillful means, employing various causes, analogies, and modes of expression, he causes all beings to rejoice.
Some speak of the sūtras, gāthās, itivṛttakas,
jātakas, and adbhutadharmas; they also speak of nidānas,
avadānas, and geyas, as well as upadeśa sūtras.
For those of dull faculties who delight in inferior teachings, who are greedily attached to birth and death,
who fail to practice the profound and wondrous path under the countless Buddhas,
and who are distressed and distracted by manifold sufferings— for their sake, I preach Nirvana.
I have established these skillful means to enable you to enter the Buddha’s wisdom;
I have never said to you that you shall attain the path of Buddhahood.
The reason I have not said so is that the time for such a teaching has not yet arrived.
Now is precisely the time to definitively expound the Mahāyāna.
These ninefold teachings of mine were spoken in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings;
since they take entry into the Mahāyāna as their foundation, I have therefore preached this sūtra.
There are sons of the Buddha whose minds are pure, Who are gentle and of sharp faculties;
In the presence of immeasurable Buddhas, They practice the profound and wondrous Way.
For these sons of the Buddha, I preach this Mahāyāna sūtra.
I have made this prediction for such people: that in a future life they shall attain the Buddha-way, because they have recited the Buddha’s name with a profound mind and cultivated the pure precepts.
Upon hearing that they shall attain Buddhahood, great joy pervades their entire bodies.
The Buddha, knowing their mental dispositions and conduct, therefore expounds the Mahāyāna for them.
Whether they be śrāvakas or bodhisattvas, upon hearing the Dharma I preach—
even if only a single verse— they shall all undoubtedly attain Buddhahood.
Throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the One Vehicle Dharma;
there is neither a second nor a third,
except for the expedient teachings spoken by the Buddhas.
It is only by means of provisional names that the Buddhas appear in the world to guide sentient beings and preach the wisdom of the Buddha.
This alone is the one true reality; the other two are not real.
He never uses the Lesser Vehicle to deliver sentient beings.
The Buddha himself abides in the Great Vehicle; according to the Dharma he has attained, adorned with the power of concentration and wisdom, he delivers sentient beings by means of this.
I have realized for myself the unsurpassed path, the Dharma of equality of the Mahāyāna;
if I were to transform even a single person by means of the Hīnayāna,
I would fall into stinginess and greed— this would be unacceptable.
If a person places faith and takes refuge in the Buddha, The Tathāgata does not deceive or mislead, Nor does he harbor thoughts of greed or envy; He has severed all evils within the realm of dharmas.
Therefore, throughout the ten directions, The Buddha alone is free from fear.
Adorned with the marks upon my body, My radiance illuminates the world;
Honored by immeasurable multitudes, I shall preach the Seal of the True Reality.
Śāriputra, you should know: In the past, I established this vow:
I desire that all sentient beings be no different from me.
As I vowed in the past, it is now fulfilled:
I shall transform all living beings and cause them all to enter the Buddha-way.
If I encounter sentient beings, I teach them all the Buddha-way;
yet those without wisdom are confused and, being deluded, do not accept the teaching.
I know these sentient beings have never cultivated the roots of goodness.
Firmly attached to the five desires, they give rise to affliction through delusion and craving.
Due to the causes and conditions of these desires, they fall into the three evil realms;
wandering through the six destinies, they undergo all manner of bitter suffering.
The subtle form of the conceived embryo grows ever more through successive lifetimes.
Those of meager virtue and little merit are oppressed by manifold sufferings;
they enter the dense forest of false views, such as those of "existence" or "non-existence."
Relying upon these various views, they are fully possessed of the sixty-two [wrong views];
deeply attached to false dharmas, they stubbornly cling to them and refuse to relinquish them;
with self-conceit and arrogance, their minds are crooked and insincere.
For thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, they have not heard the name of the Buddha, nor have they heard the True Dharma;
such people are difficult to deliver. Therefore, Śāriputra!
I employ skillful means to teach the various paths for the exhaustion of suffering and point them toward nirvana.
Although I speak of nirvana, it is not ultimate extinction;
all phenomena, from their very origin, are by nature eternally in a state of quiescent extinction.
When the sons of the Buddha have practiced the Way, they shall become Buddhas in future lives.
Possessing the power of skillful means, I reveal and teach the Dharma of the three vehicles.
Yet all the World-Honored Ones preach only the path of the One Vehicle.
Now, this great assembly, you should all eliminate your doubts and delusions;
the words of all Buddhas do not differ, for there is only the One Vehicle and no second.
Throughout incalculable kalpas of the past, there have been immeasurable Buddhas who have entered parinirvāṇa.
Of hundreds, thousands, millions, and billions of kinds, their number is immeasurable.
Such World-Honored Ones, through various causes, conditions, and parables,
and by the power of countless skillful means, expound the characteristics of all phenomena.
All these World-Honored Ones preach the Dharma of the One Vehicle,
transforming immeasurable sentient beings and causing them to enter the Buddha-way.
Furthermore, these Great Holy Lords know all worlds.
For the sake of the gods and all classes of beings, according to what their deep hearts desire,
I employ further diverse skillful means to assist in revealing the ultimate truth.
If there are any among the classes of sentient beings who have encountered the Buddhas of the past,
Whether they heard the Dharma and practiced giving, or observed the precepts, practiced patience,
diligence, meditation, and wisdom— those who cultivated various forms of merit and insight—
all such persons have already attained the Way of the Buddha.
After the various Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa, those beings who possess a virtuous and gentle mind—
all such sentient beings have already attained the Buddha-way.
After the various Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa, those who make offerings to their relics...
They erected billions of kinds of stupas, adorned with gold, silver, and crystal;
with musaragalva and agate; with rose-colored gems and lapis lazuli beads—pure, vast, and magnificently decorated, they embellished all the stupas.
Some may erect stone temples, made of sandalwood or aloeswood,
of tagara or other timbers, or of brick, tile, clay, and earth. Or,
in the midst of a wilderness, they may heap up earth to create a temple for the Buddha.
Even those who, in play as children, gathered sand to make stūpas for the Buddha—
all such persons have already attained the path of Buddhahood.
If anyone, for the sake of the Buddha, establishes various images,
Those who have carved and fashioned various images, all have already attained the path of Buddhahood.
Whether made of the seven treasures, or of brass, red or white copper,
tin, lead, and pewter, or of iron, wood, and clay—
Or those who used glue, lacquer, and cloth to solemnly adorn and fashion images of the Buddha—
all such persons as these have already attained the Way of the Buddha.
Or those who painted images of the Buddha with its marks adorned by a hundred blessings.
Whether they made them themselves or had others make them, all have already attained the Buddha-way.
Even children’s playthings, or images drawn with grass, wood, or brushes,
or even those traced with fingernails— these too constitute the making of Buddha-images.
These various people, gradually accumulating merit and endowed with a heart of great compassion,
have all already attained the path of Buddhahood.
They merely transform bodhisattvas and deliver immeasurable multitudes.
If a person, with a reverent mind, makes offerings of flowers, incense, banners, and canopies to stupas and temples, to precious images, or to painted images;
or if they cause others to perform music, beating drums and blowing horns and conchs—
Flutes, pipes, lutes, and harps; lutes, gongs, and cymbals—such various wondrous sounds as these, all held up as offerings.
Or, with a heart of joy, one may sing hymns in praise of the Buddha’s virtues.
Even those who have uttered but a single small sound have all already attained the Buddha-way.
If a person, with a distracted mind, offers even a single flower as an offering to a painted image,
they will gradually come to see countless Buddhas.
If there are those who prostrate, or even merely join their palms,
or raise a single hand, or even slightly bow their heads—
by making such offerings to the images, they will gradually come to see immeasurable Buddhas.
Having spontaneously attained the unsurpassed path, he extensively delivered countless multitudes;
entering nirvana without remainder, like a fire extinguished when the fuel is exhausted.
If a person with a distracted mind enters a stupa or temple, [they shall likewise attain merit].
Those who have once uttered "Namo Buddha" have all already attained the path of Buddhahood.
Regarding the Buddhas of the past, whether they were still in the world or had entered parinirvāṇa,
if there were any who heard this Dharma, they have all already attained the path of Buddhahood.
The future World-Honored Ones, Their number being immeasurable—
All these Tathāgatas likewise Teach the Dharma through skillful means.
All Tathāgatas, by means of Immeasurable skillful means,
To deliver all sentient beings and lead them into the Buddha’s untainted wisdom—should there be anyone who hears this Dharma, not one among them shall fail to become a Buddha.
This is the fundamental vow of all Buddhas: "The path of Buddhahood which I have practiced..."
Universally desiring that all sentient beings May likewise attain this path,
The Buddhas of future ages, Though they preach hundreds of thousands of billions Of countless Dharma-gates, Their reality is but the One Vehicle.
The Buddhas, the Honored Ones among bipeds, know that all phenomena are eternally without intrinsic nature;
yet the lineage of the Buddhas arises from conditions, and for this reason they teach the One Vehicle.
This Dharma abides in its own place, and the characteristics of the world are eternally constant.
Having realized this at the site of enlightenment, the Teacher speaks through skillful means.
Honored by devas and humans, the Buddhas currently present in the ten directions are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; they have appeared in the world.
For the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings, he likewise preaches such a Dharma.
Knowing the supreme tranquility, yet through the power of skillful means,
although he displays various paths, they are in reality for the Buddha Vehicle alone.
Knowing the various conducts of sentient beings, their deep-seated thoughts and inclinations,
the karmic actions practiced in the past, their desires, natures, and powers of diligence,
as well as the sharpness or dullness of their faculties— through these various causes and conditions—
Parables and words are likewise spoken as skillful means according to what is appropriate.
Now I am also like this; for the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings, I proclaim the Buddha-way through various gateways of the Dharma.
By the power of my wisdom, I know the dispositions and desires of sentient beings;
through skillful means I preach all dharmas, causing them all to attain joy.
Śāriputra, you should know this!
Seeing the sentient beings of the six realms, Poor and lacking in merit and wisdom,
entering the perilous path of birth and death, Their succession of suffering uninterrupted,
deeply attached to the five desires, Like a yak that loves its tail.
Shrouded by craving and attachment, they are blind and see nothing.
They do not seek the Buddha of Great Power, nor the Dharma that severs suffering;
they plunge deeply into various false views, seeking to abandon suffering through further suffering.
For the sake of these sentient beings, I have given rise to a heart of great compassion.
Since I first sat at the site of enlightenment, observing the tree and walking in meditation,
for the space of twenty-one days, I contemplated such matters as these.
The wisdom I have attained is subtle, profound, and supreme.
Yet the faculties of sentient beings are dull; blinded by attachment to pleasure and delusion, how can such as these be delivered?
At that time, the Brahma kings, as well as Śakra, Lord of the Devas,
the four World-protecting Heavenly Kings, and Maheśvara,
together with the rest of the host of devas and their retinues numbering hundreds of thousands of millions, [all assembled].
With reverent palms joined in salutation, they entreated me to turn the wheel of Dharma.
I then reflected within myself:
"If I were to praise only the Buddha Vehicle, sentient beings submerged in suffering would be unable to believe this teaching."
Because they destroy the Dharma and lack faith, they shall fall into the three evil realms.
I would rather not preach the Dharma and quickly enter nirvana;
yet I reflect upon the past Buddhas and the power of the skillful means they employed.
"The path I have now attained, I should likewise proclaim as the Three Vehicles.
While he was reflecting thus, the Buddhas of the ten directions all appeared and comforted him with Brahma-sounds:
“Excellent, Śākyamuni!
Supreme Guide, you have attained this unsurpassed Dharma;
following all Buddhas, you employ the power of skillful means.”
We too have all attained the most wondrous and supreme Dharma;
for the sake of all classes of sentient beings, we distinguish and preach the three vehicles.
Those of little wisdom who delight in inferior dharmas do not believe that they themselves can become Buddhas.
"Therefore, by means of skillful expedients, I distinguish and speak of various fruits.
Although I teach the three vehicles, it is solely for the purpose of instructing bodhisattvas.
Śāriputra, you should know this!
Hearing the holy lion’s voice, profound, pure, and subtle, I joyfully acclaim: "Namo Buddha!
Furthermore, I form this thought:
"I have appeared in this world of turbid evil; as all Buddhas have taught, I too shall practice in accordance with their words."
Having reflected upon these matters, he immediately proceeded to Vārāṇasī.
The mark of the cessation of all dharmas cannot be expressed in words;
yet, by the power of skillful means, he preached it for the sake of the five bhikṣus.
This is called the turning of the wheel of Dharma;
Thereupon arise the sounds of Nirvana, As well as the designations "Arhat," And the distinct names of the Dharma and the Sangha.
From kalpas long ago, The Dharma of Nirvana has been praised and revealed.
"The suffering of birth and death is forever ended; this is what I have always taught.
Śāriputra, you should know that those who aspire to seek the Buddha-way are immeasurable, numbering in the thousands, tens of millions, and billions."
With hearts full of reverence, they all came to where the Buddha was;
they had previously heard from various Buddhas the teachings spoken through skillful means.
I then had this thought:
"The reason the Tathāgata has appeared is to expound the Buddha-wisdom; now is precisely the time for this.
Śāriputra, you should know!
Those of dull faculties and small wisdom, who are attached to signs and full of pride, cannot believe in this Dharma.
Now, joyful and fearless, among these bodhisattvas,
I directly set aside expedient means and preach only the unsurpassed Way.
When the Bodhisattvas heard this Dharma, their nets of doubt were entirely removed;
the twelve hundred Arhats shall all likewise become Buddhas,
following the ritual for preaching the Dharma as practiced by the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
I am now likewise thus, preaching the Dharma free from conceptual discrimination.
The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is remote and difficult to encounter;
even if they do appear in the world, it is further difficult for them to preach this Dharma.
Throughout immeasurable and incalculable kalpas, it is difficult to hear this Dharma;
likewise, those who are able to listen to this Dharma are also rare.
Just as the udumbara flower is loved and cherished by all, so too is this Dharma.
Rare among gods and humans, appearing only once in a great while,
those who hear the Dharma with joy and praise— even uttering but a single word—
have thereby made offerings to all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Such a person is most rare, surpassing even the udumbara flower.
You all should have no doubt; I am the King of All Dharmas.
I proclaim to the great assembly: I teach only the path of the One Vehicle.
He transforms and instructs the various bodhisattvas, and has no śrāvaka disciples.
You, Śāriputra— both śrāvakas and bodhisattvas—
should know that this wondrous Dharma is the secret essence of all Buddhas.
In this world of the five turbidities, beings take pleasure only in various desires;
such sentient beings will never seek the Buddha-way.
In future ages, wicked people, upon hearing the Buddha preach the One Vehicle, will reject it.
Those who are deluded and do not believe or accept [the teaching] will destroy the Dharma and fall into evil paths.
For those who possess shame and remorse, who are pure, and who aspire to seek the Buddha-way,
one should extensively praise the path of the One Vehicle for their sake.
Śāriputra, you should know!
Through ten thousand koṭis of skillful means, I preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate;
those who have not practiced and studied cannot understand this.
Since you have now understood that the Buddhas, the teachers of the world,
employ various skillful means according to what is appropriate, you should no longer harbor any doubts.
With hearts filled with great joy, know for yourselves that you shall become Buddhas.
The Lotus Sutra, Fascicle One;
The Lotus Sutra, Fascicle Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master from Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Translated by Kumārajīva by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Three: Similes At that time, Śāriputra was filled with exultation and joy; he immediately rose, joined his palms, gazed up at the Honored Countenance, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Now, having heard this sound of the Dharma from the World-Honored One, my heart leaps with courage and joy, attaining what I have never experienced before.”

Why is this? In the past, I heard such a teaching from the Buddha, seeing various bodhisattvas receive the prediction of their future buddhahood, yet we ourselves were not included in this matter; we felt deeply grieved, feeling as though we had lost the Tathāgata’s immeasurable knowledge and vision.
“World-Honored One!
When I dwell alone in mountain forests or beneath trees, whether sitting or walking, I constantly reflect:
‘We have all entered the same Dharma-nature; why does the Tathāgata deliver us by means of the Hīnayāna teachings?’”
"This is our own fault, not that of the World-Honored One. Why is this?
Had we waited for the causes and conditions for the realization of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi to be explained, we would surely have attained liberation through the Mahāyāna."

"However, we did not understand that these were teachings spoken through skillful means according to what was appropriate; upon first hearing the Buddha's Dharma, we immediately believed, accepted, contemplated, and realized it.
"World-Honored One! [They said.]

"From the past until now, throughout day and night, I have constantly reproached myself; yet today, having heard from the Buddha this unprecedented Dharma never heard before, all my doubts and regrets are severed. My body and mind are at ease, and I have attained swift peace and security."
"Today I finally know that I am truly a son of the Buddha, born from the Buddha’s mouth, transformed by birth from the Dharma, and having obtained a portion of the Buddha-Dharma.
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Hearing this sound of the Dharma, I have attained what I never had before."
My heart is filled with great joy, and the net of doubt has been entirely removed.
Having long since received the Buddha’s teaching, I have not lost the Mahāyāna.
The Buddha’s voice is most rare and marvelous; it can eliminate the afflictions of sentient beings.
I have attained the destruction of the outflows; hearing this also removes my grief and distress.
Dwelling in mountain valleys or beneath the trees of the forest, whether sitting or walking in meditation, I constantly contemplate this matter.
Alas, I reproach myself deeply: how have I deceived myself?
We too are sons of the Buddha, having equally entered the dharma free from outflows;
yet we are unable, in the future, to expound the unsurpassed path.
The golden hue and the thirty-two marks, the ten powers and the various liberations—
though all these are within the same single Dharma, they do not attain this state;
nor the eighty minor marks of excellence, nor the eighteen unique qualities.
Such virtues as these, I have entirely lost.
When I was walking alone, I saw the Buddha amidst the great assembly;
his fame filled the ten directions, and he brought vast benefit to all sentient beings.
Reflecting that I have lost this benefit, I have been deceiving myself.
Day and night, I constantly contemplate this matter, wishing to ask the World-Honored One: "Have I lost it, or have I not?"
I have often seen the World-Honored One praise the various bodhisattvas;
for this reason, day and night, I have contemplated such matters.
Now I hear the Buddha’s voice preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate.
The untainted is inconceivable, leading all beings to the site of enlightenment.
Originally I was attached to false views and served as a teacher to the brahmins;
the World-Honored One, knowing my mind, uprooted my errors and preached nirvana.
I have completely eliminated all wrong views and attained realization of the dharma of emptiness;
at that time, my mind thought to itself, "I have reached nirvana.
Yet now I realize for myself that this was not true nirvana.
When I attain Buddhahood, endowed with the thirty-two marks,
revered by the multitudes of devas, humans, yakṣas, nāgas, and spirits—
only at that time may it be said that [suffering] is forever extinguished without remainder.
The Buddha, amidst the great assembly, declared, "I shall become a Buddha.
Hearing such a sound of the Dharma, all my doubts and regrets were entirely removed.
When I first heard what the Buddha spoke, my heart was greatly struck with alarm and doubt.
"Could it be that a Māra has manifested as a Buddha to disturb my mind?
Yet the Buddha, through various causes and conditions and skillful metaphors, has spoken with eloquence;
my mind is now as calm as the ocean, and upon hearing this, the net of my doubts is severed."
The Buddha has said that in past ages, immeasurable Buddhas who have entered parinirvāṇa,
abiding in skillful means, have all likewise preached this Dharma.
As for the Buddhas of the present and the future, their number is likewise immeasurable.
Likewise, through various skillful means, he expounds such a Dharma.
Just as the World-Honored One of the present— from his birth and renunciation,
to his attainment of the Way and turning of the wheel of Dharma— has likewise taught by means of skillful means.
The World-Honored One teaches the true path, whereas Pāpīyān has no such thing;
therefore I know with certainty that this is not Māra acting as a Buddha.
Because I had fallen into the net of doubt, I thought this was the work of Māra.
Hearing the Buddha’s gentle voice— profound, far-reaching, and most subtle—
as he expounds the pure Dharma,
my heart is filled with great joy; doubt and regret are forever exhausted, and I abide securely within true wisdom.
"I shall certainly become a Buddha, revered by devas and humans;
I shall turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma and teach and transform all bodhisattvas.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:

"I now declare among this great assembly of devas, humans, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas: in the past, at the abodes of twenty thousand koṭis of Buddhas, for the sake of the unsurpassed path, I have constantly instructed and transformed you; you, too, throughout the long night, followed me to receive my teachings."
It was because I used skillful means to guide you that you were born into my Dharma. Śāriputra!
In the past, I taught you to set your aspirations on the Buddha-way, yet now you have completely forgotten this and instead claim that you have already attained nirvāṇa.

Now, because I wish to cause you to remember the path you have practiced according to your original vow, I shall preach this Mahāyāna sūtra for the sake of all śrāvakas; it is titled *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the teaching of the Bodhisattvas, which is protected by the mindfulness of the Buddhas.

“Śāriputra! In a future age, after immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable kalpas have passed, you shall make offerings to many hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, uphold the True Dharma, and fulfill the path practiced by Bodhisattvas; you shall then attain Buddhahood, with the title Flower Radiance Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.”
The land is named Vimalā; its terrain is level and even, pure and magnificently adorned, peaceful, secure, and prosperous, with a vast multitude of devas and humans.
Its ground is made of lapis lazuli, featuring eight intersecting roads, with golden cords marking their boundaries.
Beside each [tree] were rows of trees made of the seven treasures, always bearing flowers and fruit.
The Tathāgata Puṣpārāma also taught and transformed sentient beings by means of the three vehicles. “Śāriputra!
When that Buddha appeared, although it was not an age of evil, he preached the Dharma of the Three Vehicles by virtue of his original vows.
That kalpa was named Mahāratnavyūha.
For what reason was it called Mahāratnavyūha?

Because Bodhisattvas are regarded as the great jewels within that land, those Bodhisattvas are immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and beyond the reach of calculation or analogy; none can know them except through the power of a Buddha’s wisdom.
When they wish to walk, precious flowers receive their feet.

These bodhisattvas have not merely set their minds on enlightenment for the first time; they have all long planted the roots of virtue, having purified their Brahma-conduct in the presence of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of buddhas, and are constantly praised by all the buddhas.

Constantly cultivating the Buddha-wisdom and possessing great supernormal powers, they are well-versed in the gateways of all dharmas; upright and without guile, their resolve and mindfulness are firm and steadfast.
Such bodhisattvas fill that land.
“Śāriputra! The lifespan of the Buddha Puṣpārāma will be twelve minor kalpas, excluding the time when he was a prince and had not yet attained Buddhahood.
The people of that land will have a lifespan of eight minor kalpas.”
After twelve intermediate kalpas had passed, the Tathāgata Padmaprabha bestowed upon the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhavati the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"This Bodhisattva Dṛḍhavati shall next become a Buddha, named Padmapādasthita-gati Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyak-saṃbuddha; the Buddha-land of that Buddha shall likewise be such as this."

"Śāriputra! After the parinirvāṇa of that Buddha Puṣpārāma, the True Dharma shall remain in the world for thirty-two intermediate kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma shall likewise remain in the world for thirty-two intermediate kalpas."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse: “In a future age,
Śāriputra shall become a Buddha, a Honored One of Universal Wisdom,
Named Flower Light (Puṣyarāja), who shall deliver immeasurable multitudes.”
Having made offerings to countless Buddhas and fully perfected the bodhisattva practices,
he realized the unsurpassed path through merits such as the ten powers.
After immeasurable kalpas had passed, there was a kalpa named Mahāratnavyūha.
