The world is named Vimalā, pure and free from all defilement.
Its ground is made of lapis lazuli, its paths demarcated by golden cords,
and it is filled with trees of various colors made of the seven jewels, always bearing flowers and fruit.
The bodhisattvas of that land are always firm in their resolve and mindfulness;
they have all fully perfected the supernatural powers and the pāramitās.
Having studied the bodhisattva path well under countless buddhas, they have mastered it thoroughly.
Such great beings as these were transformed by the Buddha Flower-Light.
When that Buddha was a prince, he abandoned his kingdom and renounced worldly glory;
in his very last body, he left the home life and attained the Way of the Buddha.
The Buddha Flower-Light shall dwell in the world for a lifespan of twelve minor kalpas;
the people of that land shall have a lifespan of eight minor kalpas.
After the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain in the world.
For thirty-two minor kalpas, he extensively delivers all sentient beings.
When the True Dharma has been extinguished, the Semblance Dharma shall last for thirty-two [kalpas];
his relics will be widely disseminated, and gods and humans will universally make offerings to them.
The deeds performed by the Buddha Padmaprabha were all exactly like this;
that Honored One among bipeds was most supreme and without peer.
He is none other than your own self—you should truly rejoice in this.

At that time, the fourfold assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—as well as the great multitude of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others, seeing Śāriputra receive the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* from the Buddha, were filled with great joy and leaped for immeasurable delight. Each of them removed the upper garment they were wearing to offer it as an act of worship to the Buddha.

Śakra Devānām-Indra, Brahmā Sahāmpati, and countless sons of gods likewise made offerings to the Buddha with celestial fine garments, celestial *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, and so forth. The celestial garments they scattered remained suspended in mid-air, revolving of their own accord;
hundreds of thousands of millions of kinds of celestial music played simultaneously in the sky, and a rain of various celestial flowers fell. They then spoke these words:
"In the past, the Buddha first turned the wheel of Dharma at Vārāṇasī; now he has once again turned the unsurpassed, greatest wheel of Dharma."
At that time, the sons of the gods, wishing to reiterate this meaning,
spoke these verses: "In the past, at Vārāṇasī, You turned the wheel of the Four Noble Truths,
Discriminatingly explaining all phenomena, The arising and ceasing of the five aggregates."
Now you again turn the most wondrous, supreme, and great wheel of Dharma;
this teaching is exceedingly profound and subtle, and few are able to believe it.
Since time immemorial, we have repeatedly heard the World-Honored One’s preaching.
Never before have we heard such a profound and sublime supreme Dharma.
Since the World-Honored One has preached this Dharma, we all rejoice.
The one of great wisdom, Śāriputra, has now received the World-Honored One’s prediction of enlightenment.
We, too, shall be just like this; we shall certainly attain Buddhahood.
Among all worlds, there is none more honored or supreme.
The Buddha-way is inconceivable; it is taught through skillful means according to what is appropriate.
"Whatever meritorious deeds I have performed, whether in this life or in past lives,
as well as the merit from beholding the Buddha— may it all be dedicated toward the path of Buddhahood.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I now have no further doubt or regret, having personally received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* before the Buddha.
As for these twelve hundred who have attained mastery over their minds, they formerly dwelt in the stage of training (*śaikṣa-bhūmi*), and the Buddha constantly instructed and exhorted them, saying:”
"Our Dharma can bring about liberation from birth, old age, sickness, and death, culminating in ultimate Nirvana.

Those who were still in training and those beyond training likewise each considered themselves to have attained Nirvana by being free from the view of a self and the views of existence and non-existence;
yet now, having heard before the World-Honored One what they had never heard before, they all fall into doubt and confusion.
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will explain the causes and conditions for the sake of the fourfold assembly, so that they may be freed from doubt and regret.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
“Did I not say before:
‘The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, employ various causes and conditions, parables, and skillful means in their verbal teachings of the Dharma, all for the sake of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi’?”
"All that has been said was for the purpose of transforming bodhisattvas.
However, Śāriputra,
I shall now further clarify this meaning through a parable, for those who possess wisdom attain understanding by means of parables."
“Śāriputra! Suppose there is a great elder in a kingdom, city, or village who is advanced in years, possesses immeasurable wealth, and owns many fields, houses, and servants.”
His house was vast and had but a single door; many people—perhaps a hundred, two hundred, or even five hundred—dwelt within it.

The halls and pavilions were dilapidated and old; the walls and partitions had collapsed, the bases of the pillars were rotten, and the beams and rafters were tilted and precarious. Suddenly, fires broke out all around simultaneously, burning down the house and its dwellings.
The elder’s sons—whether ten, twenty, or as many as thirty—were within this house.
When the elder saw this great fire breaking out from all four sides, he was seized with great alarm and fear, and thought to himself:

"Although I am able to escape safely through this gate that is being consumed by flames, my sons are delighting in play within the burning house; they do not perceive or understand, nor are they startled or terrified. As the fire approaches their bodies, its pain cuts to the very core, yet their hearts feel no aversion or distress, and they have no intention of seeking escape."
"Śāriputra! This elder thought to himself:
'My hands and body possess great strength; I shall carry him out of the house using my lap or a small table.'"
He further reflected:
"This house has but a single door, and it is moreover narrow and small.
My children are young and lack discernment; they are attached to their playthings and might fall down and be burned by the fire."
"I shall speak to you of matters that cause fear: this house is already burning; you should quickly exit at once, lest you be harmed and consumed by the fire.
Having formed this thought, he informed his sons in full according to what he had considered: "All of you, come out swiftly!"
Although the father felt compassion for them and sought to entice them with kind words, the sons were so attached to their play that they refused to believe or accept his advice;
they were neither startled nor afraid, having no intention at all of escaping, and they did not even know what fire was.
"What constitutes 'home,' and what constitutes 'loss'?
He merely runs about here and there playing, looking only at his father."
At that time, the elder thought to himself:
"This house has already been consumed by a great fire; if I and my children do not exit at once, we shall surely be burned to death."
"I shall now employ skillful means to enable my sons to escape this calamity.
The father, knowing that each of his sons had previously cherished various preferences for diverse rare treasures and extraordinary objects to which they were surely attached, addressed them, saying:
"The playthings you delight in are rare and difficult to obtain; if you do not take them now, you will surely feel regret later."
"Such various sheep-carts, deer-carts, and ox-carts are now outside the gate for you to play with.
You should all come out quickly from this burning house; whatever you desire, I shall give it all to you."

At that time, having heard their father speak of the rare and precious playthings, the sons—because these suited their desires—each felt courageous and spirited; they pushed and shoved one another, racing together in competition to be the first to flee from the burning house.

At that time, the elder saw that his sons had all emerged safely; they were sitting on the open ground at the crossroads, free from all obstructions, their minds at ease, and leaping for joy with great delight.
Then each of the sons addressed their father, saying:
"Father, we pray that you will grant us at once the playthings you previously promised—the goat-carts, the deer-carts, and the ox-carts."

"Śāriputra! At that time, the elder bestowed upon each of his sons an identical great carriage. These carriages were high and broad, adorned with various jewels, surrounded by railings, and hung with bells on all four sides.

Furthermore, canopies were spread over them, likewise embellished with rare and diverse precious gems; they were bound with jeweled cords, draped with flower tassels, layered with fine rugs, and fitted with crimson pillows."
He was drawn by white oxen, whose coats were pure and clean, whose forms were beautiful, and who possessed great strength; their gait was level and steady, and they moved as swiftly as the wind;
moreover, he was attended by a large retinue of servants and guards.
Why is this? Because this great householder possesses immeasurable wealth, and his various treasuries are all overflowing; he thinks to himself:
"My wealth and goods are infinite; I ought not to give inferior, small carts to my sons."
"These young children here are all my sons; my love for them is without partiality.
I possess such great treasure-carts of the seven jewels, in numberless quantity, which I ought to bestow upon each with an equal mind; it is not fitting to treat them differently."
"Why is this? Because with these goods of mine, I could provide for an entire kingdom without exhaustion, let alone for my sons!
At that time, the sons each mounted a great carriage; they experienced what they had never known before, far exceeding their original expectations.
“Śāriputra, what do you think?
Would this elder be guilty of any falsehood in giving these precious great chariots to his sons?
Śāriputra replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
That elder merely enabled his children to escape the disaster of fire and preserve their lives;
it was not a falsehood. Why is this so?

If one were to preserve their entire life and limb, that would already constitute the acquisition of a cherished possession; how much more so, World-Honored One, to employ skillful means to rescue them from that burning house!
Even if the elder did not give so much as a single small chariot, he would still not have been guilty of falsehood. Why is this?
Because the elder had previously formed this intention:
"I used skillful means to enable my sons to escape.
For this reason, there is no falsehood in my words.
How much more so when the elder, knowing for himself that his wealth is immeasurable, desires to benefit his sons by giving them all equally great chariots?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“Excellent, excellent!
It is just as you have said.”
Śāriputra! The Tathāgata is also like this; he is the father of all the world.

Having forever exhausted, without remainder, all fears, decays, afflictions, anxieties, and the darkness of ignorance, he has fully accomplished immeasurable knowledge and vision, powers, and fearlessnesses. Possessing great supernormal power and the power of wisdom, and being endowed with the perfection of skillful means and wisdom, as well as great kindness and great compassion, he is ever without weariness and constantly seeks what is wholesome to benefit all beings. Thus he enters the dilapidated and decaying fire-houses of the triple world to deliver sentient beings from the fires of birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, affliction, folly, darkness, and the three poisons, teaching and transforming them so that they may attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

He saw that all sentient beings were being scorched and boiled by birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction; furthermore, for the sake of the five desires and material gain, they underwent various kinds of suffering.

Moreover, because of their greedy attachment and pursuit, they experienced manifold sufferings in the present life, and in the future, they would undergo the sufferings of the hells, animals, and hungry ghosts.

Even if born in the heavens or among humans, they would face such various sufferings as poverty and hardship, the suffering of separation from loved ones, and the suffering of encountering those one hates.

Sentient beings are submerged within it, playing with joy; they neither perceive nor know [their plight], they are neither startled nor terrified, nor do they give rise to weariness [with saṃsāra], nor seek liberation.
Within this burning house of the triple world, they run hither and thither; though they encounter great suffering, they do not regard it as a calamity.
"Śāriputra! Having seen this, the Buddha then thought to himself:"

"I am the father of all sentient beings; I ought to uproot their suffering and distress, bestow upon them the immeasurable and boundless joy of the Buddha’s wisdom, and cause them to sport therein. "Śāriputra!..."
The Tathāgata further reflects:

"If I were to rely solely on the power of my supernatural faculties and the power of my wisdom, setting aside skillful means, and were to praise for the sake of all sentient beings the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, his powers, and his fearlessnesses, sentient beings would not be able to attain liberation through these."

Why is this? Because these sentient beings have not yet escaped birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction, and are being scorched by the burning house of the triple world;
how then could they understand the Buddha’s wisdom?

“Śāriputra! Just as that elder, although possessing strength in his body and arms yet not using it, instead employed diligent skillful means to rescue his children from the peril of the burning house, and subsequently gave each of them a precious great chariot.”

The Tathāgata is also like this: although he possesses powers and fearlessness, he does not employ them; rather, by means of wisdom and skillful means, he rescues sentient beings from the burning house of the triple world, preaching the three vehicles—the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, and the buddha-vehicle—and speaks these words:
"Do not take pleasure in dwelling within the burning house of the triple world; do not crave coarse and inferior forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles."
If you give rise to craving through attachment, you will be consumed by it.
You must quickly escape the three realms; you shall then attain one of the three vehicles—the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, or the buddha-vehicle.
"I now guarantee this matter for you; it shall never prove false.
You should simply cultivate yourselves with diligent vigor.
By such skillful means, the Tathāgata entices and encourages sentient beings, further speaking these words:
"You should know that these three vehicles of the Dharma are all praised by the noble ones; they are sovereign and unconditioned, requiring no further seeking or reliance.

By mounting these three vehicles, one enjoys oneself through the untainted faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, path, meditative concentrations, liberations, and samādhis, thereby attaining immeasurable peace and happiness."

“Śāriputra! If there are sentient beings who possess an internal nature of wisdom, who hear the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and accept it with faith; who are diligent and energetic, desiring to quickly escape the triple world and seeking nirvāṇa for themselves—this is called the Śrāvaka Vehicle, like those sons who left the burning house seeking the goat carts.

If there are sentient beings who hear the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and accept it with faith; who are diligent and energetic, seeking spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*), delighting in solitary tranquility, and deeply understanding the causes and conditions of all phenomena—this is called the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, like those sons who left the burning house seeking the deer carts.”

If there are sentient beings who, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, receive it with faith and practice it with diligent effort, seeking all-knowledge, Buddha-knowledge, self-arising knowledge, teacherless knowledge, the Tathāgata’s insight, powers, and fearlessness; and who, out of compassion, bring peace and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, benefit devas and humans, and deliver all—this is called the Mahāyāna. Because Bodhisattvas seek this vehicle, they are called Mahāsattvas, just as those sons sought ox-carts and emerged from the burning house.

“Śāriputra! Just as that elder, seeing his children safely emerge from the burning house and reach a place of fearlessness, reflects upon his own immeasurable wealth and bestows great chariots equally upon all his children.”

The Tathāgata is likewise so; he is the father of all sentient beings. If he sees immeasurable billions of sentient beings who, through the gateway of the Buddha's teaching, emerge from the suffering of the triple world and the perilous paths of fear, attaining the bliss of nirvāṇa.
At that time, the Tathāgata thought to himself:

"I possess an immeasurable and boundless treasury of the Buddha-dharma, including wisdom, powers, and fearlessnesses. All these sentient beings are my children; I shall bestow the Mahāyāna equally upon them, so that no one shall attain parinirvāṇa alone, but rather all shall be brought to parinirvāṇa through the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata."

"Those sentient beings who have been liberated from the three realms are all provided with the various implements for enjoyment, such as the meditative concentrations and liberations of the Buddhas; these are all of one characteristic and one kind, praised by the sages, and capable of producing the supreme, pure, and wondrous bliss."
“Śāriputra! Just as that elder first used three vehicles to entice his children and later gave them only great vehicles, adorned with precious objects and supreme in security;
yet that elder was not guilty of falsehood.
The Tathāgata is likewise thus: being free from falsehood, he first teaches the three vehicles to guide sentient beings, and subsequently delivers them by means of the Great Vehicle alone.

Why is this? Because the Tathāgata possesses an immeasurable treasury of dharmas—wisdom, powers, and fearlessnesses—and is able to bestow the Mahāyāna Dharma upon all sentient beings; however, they are not all able to receive it in its entirety.

“Śāriputra! By these causes and conditions, you should know that it is through the power of the skillful means of the Buddhas that they distinguish and teach three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle.
Wishing to restate this meaning, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"It is, for example, like an elder who has a large house; this house is long-standing and has become utterly dilapidated.
The halls and chambers are high and perilous; the bases of the pillars are decayed and rotten;
the beams and rafters are leaning; the foundations and steps have collapsed; and the walls are crumbling and split apart."
The plastered coating has flaked away, the thatched roof lies in disarray and falls down, the rafters and eaves are askew and detached,
the surrounding walls are bent and warped, and all is filled with various impurities.
Five hundred people dwell within it.
Vipers, snakes, vipers, and scorpions; centipedes and millipedes;
lizards, many-legged insects, wildcats, and field mice—these various species of evil creatures run about, darting hither and thither.
A place foul with excrement and urine, where impurities overflow; dung beetles and various insects swarm upon it.
Foxes, wolves, and jackals chew and trample upon it, gnawing at corpses until bones and flesh lie scattered in disarray.
Because of this, a pack of dogs vied with one another to seize and pounce; emaciated by hunger and filled with terror, they sought food everywhere.
They fought and clawed at each other, snarling and barking; the house was thus filled with such terrifying transformations.
Everywhere there were *chī-mèi* and *wǎng-liǎng* spirits, yakṣas, and malevolent ghosts who devoured human flesh;
various species of venomous insects and all manner of wicked birds and beasts were breeding, nursing their young, and giving birth, each guarding its own offspring.
The yakṣas vied with one another to come and scramble for their food;
having eaten their fill, their evil intentions grew even more intense, and the sounds of their quarreling were truly terrifying.
The kumbhāṇḍa spirits crouch upon earthen mounds;
sometimes they rise a foot or two off the ground, moving back and forth with unrestrained playfulness.
They seize dogs by their two hind legs, throw them down until they cry out, and press their feet against their necks.
Fearing dogs, they take pleasure in themselves;
naked, black, and emaciated, they constantly dwell therein, emitting great evil sounds,
crying out and seeking food.
Furthermore, there are various ghosts whose throats are like needles.
There are also various ghosts with heads like those of oxen; some eat human flesh, while others devour dogs.
Their hair is disheveled and matted, and they are cruel, harmful, and terrifying.
Driven by hunger and thirst, they cry out and run about.
Yakṣas, hungry ghosts, and various evil birds and beasts, frantic with hunger, look in from all four directions through the windows and doors.
Such are these perils, with immeasurable terrors.
This dilapidated old house belongs to a single person.
Later, in that dwelling, a fire suddenly breaks out, all at once on all four sides.
The flames blazed together;
the beams, rafters, pillars, and columns burst with a thunderous crack, breaking and falling, while the walls collapsed.
The various ghosts and spirits raised their voices in loud cries;
the vultures, eagles, and other birds, as well as the kumbhāṇḍas and others, were distraught and terrified, unable to escape.
Fierce beasts and venomous insects hide within their burrows;
due to their meager merit, they are driven by the fire, where they mutually slaughter one another,
drinking blood and devouring flesh.
Various great and evil beasts vied with one another to come and devour them; foul-smelling smoke billowed forth, filling all four directions.
Scorched by the fire, they struggled to run out of their burrows, along with the kumbhāṇḍa ghosts.
They seize whatever they can find and eat it.
Furthermore, those hungry ghosts have flames burning upon their heads; tormented by hunger, thirst, and heat, they run about in frantic agitation.
That house was thus, utterly terrifying, with poisonous harms and fires, and manifold perils beyond count.
At that time, the master of the house stood outside the gate and heard someone say:
"Your sons, having previously been playing, have entered this house."
"Immature and ignorant, they take delight in and cling to these pleasures.
Having heard this, the elder was startled and entered the burning house; it was only right that he provide rescue and relief, so that none should suffer the harm of being burned.
He exhorted his sons, speaking of their many afflictions and perils:
the malevolent spirits and venomous insects, the spreading conflagration, and the succession of manifold sufferings that continue without end.
Venomous snakes, vipers, and adders, as well as various yakṣas and kumbhāṇḍa spirits;
jackals, foxes, dogs, eagles, vultures, crows, and owls;
and the class of centipedes—afflicted by hunger and thirst, they are most terrifying.
In this place of suffering and hardship, how much more so with the great fire!
Though the children are ignorant and have heard their father’s instruction, they still delight in their attachments and do not cease their play.
At that time, the elder had this thought:
"My sons being thus, they increase my grief and distress.
Now, in this house, there is not a single thing to be enjoyed, yet my sons—"
"Addicted to play and sport, they do not accept my teaching and will surely be harmed by fire.
He then reflected and devised various expedient means, saying to his sons:
"I have all kinds of precious playthings and magnificent, fine chariots."
"The sheep-drawn carts, the deer-drawn carts, and the great ox-drawn carts are now outside the gate.
Come forth, all of you! I have prepared these carts for you;
as you please, you may play and enjoy yourselves therein."
These various chariots, at that very moment, raced and vied with one another,
galloping forth until they reached an open space, far removed from all suffering and hardship.
The elder, seeing his children have emerged from the burning house and standing at the crossroads,
sat upon a lion throne and said to himself in celebration:
"I am now happy!"
These sons of mine were with great difficulty conceived and raised; yet, being foolish, small, and ignorant, they entered a perilous house.
Within it are many venomous insects and terrifying goblins, while fierce, blazing fires break out on all four sides.
Yet these sons were greedily attached to their play;
I have already rescued them and enabled them to escape this peril.
Therefore, O people, I am now joyful.
At that time, the sons, knowing their father was sitting at ease, all went to where he was and said to him:
"We pray you grant us these three kinds of precious chariots."
As previously promised:
"Come forth, my children; I shall provide you with three chariots according to your desires.
Now is precisely the time; please deign to bestow them upon us.
With gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musāragalva, and agate— using these various precious substances— they fashioned great chariots.
They were adorned and magnificently decorated, with railings encircling them on all sides, bells suspended from the four corners, and golden cords interlacing them.
Spread over it were golden flowers and various necklaces hanging down everywhere;
adorned with a variety of colorful fabrics, they surrounded it on all sides, while soft silks and cotton served as cushions and bedding.
Exquisite, fine cotton cloth, worth ten billion in value, fresh white and pure clean, covers it from above.
There is a great white ox, fat, strong, and powerful, with a beautiful form, yoked to the precious chariot.
With many attendants to serve and guard him,
he gives these wondrous chariots equally to all his sons.
Riding upon these precious chariots, they travel through the four quarters, sporting and enjoying themselves in happiness.
With sovereign mastery and unimpededness, he addressed Śāriputra:
"I am likewise so: the most honored among all sages, the father of the world."
All sentient beings are my children; deeply attached to worldly pleasures, they lack the heart of wisdom.
There is no peace in the three realms, which are like a burning house, filled with manifold sufferings and most terrifying.
There are always the anxieties and afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, and death; such fires burn fiercely and without ceasing.
The Tathāgata has already departed from this burning house of the triple world; he dwells in tranquil seclusion, peacefully settled in the forests and wilds.
Now these three realms are all mine; the sentient beings therein are all my children.
Yet in this place there are many afflictions and perils, and I alone am able to provide rescue and protection.
Although they were thus instructed and exhorted, they did not believe or accept it, because their greed and attachment to the defilements of desire were so deep.
By these skillful means, he taught the Three Vehicles for them, causing all sentient beings to know the suffering of the three realms,
and he revealed and expounded upon the supramundane path.
These sons, if their minds are resolute, will be endowed with the three types of supernormal knowledge and the six supernatural powers;
some will attain the state of a pratyekabuddha, while others will become non-retrogressive bodhisattvas.
"You, Śāriputra!
For the sake of sentient beings, I have used this parable to preach the Single Buddha Vehicle.
If you all can believe and accept these words, then all of you shall surely attain the path to Buddhahood."
Supremely pure, unsurpassed among all worlds,
and approved by the Buddha;
he is one whom all sentient beings should praise, make offerings to, and pay homage.
With immeasurable billions of powers, liberations, meditative concentrations, and wisdoms, as well as the other qualities of a Buddha, they attain such a vehicle.
Causing all these sons to constantly enjoy play day and night for kalpas,
together with the bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas, they shall ride upon this precious vehicle straight to the site of enlightenment.
"For this reason, if one seeks truthfully throughout the ten directions, there is no other vehicle to be found, except for the Buddha’s skillful means.
He addressed Śāriputra:
"All of you, my followers, are my children, and I am your father."
Throughout many kalpas, you have been scorched by manifold sufferings;
I have rescued you all and caused you to emerge from the triple world.
Although I previously said:
"You have attained extinction," they say, yet it is merely the exhaustion of birth and death; in truth, there is no extinction.
What you must now accomplish is solely the wisdom of a Buddha.
If there are bodhisattvas within this assembly who can listen with a single-minded focus to the true Dharma of all Buddhas—
though the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, employ skillful means—
the sentient beings thus transformed are all bodhisattvas.
For those of small wisdom who are deeply attached to craving and desire, it is for their sake that the Truth of Suffering is taught.
Sentient beings rejoice, attaining what they have never known before; the Buddha’s teaching on the Truth of Suffering is true and without deviation.
If there are sentient beings who do not know the root of suffering, who are deeply attached to the causes of suffering, and cannot relinquish them even for a moment—
for their sake, I preach the Way through skillful means.
Craving is the root; if craving is extinguished, there is no further basis for existence.
With the total cessation of all suffering, this is called the Third Truth.
For the sake of the Truth of Cessation, one practices the Path; being freed from all bonds of suffering, this is called attaining liberation.
From what does such a person attain liberation?
To merely be free from delusion is called "liberation," yet in reality,
one has not attained all-encompassing liberation.
The Buddha says that such a person has not truly entered parinirvāṇa.
Because these people have not yet attained the unsurpassed Way, it is not my intention that they should reach final nirvana.
As the Dharma King, I possess mastery over the Dharma; I appear in the world to bring peace and security to all sentient beings.
O Śāriputra! Desiring to benefit the world, you have spoken this; wherever you travel, do not propagate it recklessly.
If there are those who hear it, rejoice in it, and receive it upon their heads, you should know that such persons are *avaivartika*.
As for this Dharma of the sutra, these persons have already in the past seen the Buddhas of the past,
paid them respect and made offerings, and have also heard this Dharma.
If you believe what you have said, then you shall see me, and you shall also see you yourself,
as well as the community of bhikṣus and all the bodhisattvas.
This Lotus Sūtra is taught for those of profound wisdom; those of shallow understanding, upon hearing it, will be confused and fail to comprehend it.
All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are beyond the reach of its power within this sūtra.
"Śāriputra! You yourself can yet enter this sutra through faith;
how much more so the other śrāvakas!"
The other śrāvakas, because they place faith in the Buddha’s words, follow this sutra; it is not within the scope of their own wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Do not preach this sutra to those who are arrogant and indolent, or to those who harbor views of a self.
Do not preach it to ordinary people of shallow understanding who are deeply attached to the five desires; they will not understand it even if they hear it.
If a person does not believe and slanders this sutra, they sever all seeds of the Buddha in the world.
Or if they frown and harbor doubts, you should listen as I describe the retribution for such a person's sins.
Should there be those who slander such a sutra as this, or who, upon seeing one who reads,
recites, copies, or upholds it, treat them with contempt and disdain, harboring hatred and resentment.
Listen now further to the retribution for this person's offenses:
when his life ends, he enters the Avīci Hell, remaining there for a full kalpa; when the kalpa is exhausted, he is born once more.
Thus passing from one state to another, through countless kalpas, they emerge from the hells only to fall among the animals.
Whether as dogs or jackals, their forms are emaciated and withered; they are dark-complexioned and afflicted with scabies and leprosy, tormented by the touch of others.
Despised and held in contempt by all, they are constantly tormented by hunger and thirst;
their flesh and bones wither away as they endure agonizing suffering while alive, and are struck by shards and stones when dead.
Because they have severed the seed of the Buddha, they undergo this retribution for their sins:
their bodies are constantly burdened with heavy loads and subjected to the blows of canes and whips;
they think only of water and grass, knowing nothing else.
Because of slandering this sutra, one incurs such transgressions as these:
one becomes a jackal that enters villages, with a body covered in scabies and sores,
and missing one eye.
Beaten and pelted by various youths, they undergo all manner of agonies, sometimes even meeting death.
Having died there, they further receive the body of a python.
Deaf and witless, with no feet, they crawl belly-first, being devoured by various small insects;
day and night they suffer, without any rest.
Because they slander this sutra, they incur such offenses as these.
Even if they should obtain human form, their faculties will be dull and dark; they will be short and deformed, withered and crippled, blind, deaf, and hunchbacked.
Whatever they may say, people do not believe or accept; their breath is constantly foul, and they are possessed by malevolent spirits.
Poor and lowly, they are driven about by others; plagued by many ailments and emaciated, they have no one to rely upon.
Though they may become close to others, those people do not hold them in high regard; whatever they may have gained, they soon forget and lose it again.
If they practice the way of medicine, treating illness according to the prescriptions, they instead increase the other's ailments or even cause death.
If one is personally afflicted by illness and has no one to provide medical treatment, even if they take excellent medicine, the condition will only worsen.
If others commit acts of rebellion, plunder, or theft, such transgressions will cause them to suffer calamity through no fault of their own.
Such a person of sin shall never behold the Buddha, the King of all Sages, preaching the Dharma to transform and instruct beings.
Such a person of sin shall always be born in difficult circumstances; mad, deaf, and with a distracted mind, they shall never hear the Dharma.
For incalculable kalpas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they were born deaf and mute, their faculties incomplete.
They constantly dwelt in hell as if wandering through pleasure gardens;
they remained in other evil realms as if in their own homes, with camels, donkeys, pigs, and dogs as their places of activity.
Because they slander this sutra, they incur such transgressions as these.
Even if they should obtain human form, they will be deaf, blind, mute, and dumb; poverty and all manner of misfortunes will serve as their own adornment.
With dropsy, consumption, scabies, leprosy, carbuncles, and abscesses— such diseases as these serving as their clothing;
deeply attached to the view of self, increasing their hatred, and with lust blazing fiercely.
"Without distinguishing between birds and beasts,
because they slander this sutra, they incur such offenses.
Thus he addressed Śāriputra:
"If one were to describe the sins of those who slander this sutra, they would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon.
For this reason, I tell you:
do not preach this sutra among those who lack wisdom."
One who possesses clear wisdom, is widely learned, and has a powerful memory—
such a person who seeks the Buddha-way is one to whom this may be taught.
Those who have planted all roots of goodness under hundreds of thousands of millions of buddhas, whose deep resolve is firm and steadfast—
only for such persons as these may you preach this teaching.
If there are people who are diligent and constantly cultivate a mind of loving-kindness, who do not begrudge their own bodies or lives— only for them may you preach this.
If there are people who are reverent, free from distracted thoughts, who have distanced themselves from the vulgar and foolish,
and dwell alone in the mountains and marshes— for such people as these, you may preach it.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If you see someone who has abandoned evil associates and draws near to virtuous friends, such a person is one for whom you may preach this.
If you see a son of the Buddha, pure in the observance of the precepts like a bright,
clear pearl, who seeks the Mahāyāna sūtras— only to such a person as this may you preach.
If a person is free from anger, upright and gentle, always compassionate toward all beings,
and reveres the Buddhas— only for such a person may you preach this.
Furthermore, there are sons of the Buddha who, amidst the great assembly, with a pure mind,
use various causes and conditions, parables, and modes of speech to expound the Dharma without hindrance;
to such persons as these, you may indeed speak this.
For one who seeks the Dharma in all four directions for the sake of omniscience, who receives it upon the crown of their head with palms joined,
and delights solely in upholding the Mahāyāna sūtras—
such that they would not accept even a single verse from any other scripture— it is to such a person as this that you may preach.
Just as a person with a sincere heart seeks the relics of the Buddha, so too does one seek this sutra;
having obtained it, they receive it upon the crown of their head.
Such a person no longer aspires to seek other sutras, nor do they ever think of the scriptures of the non-Buddhists. Such a person—
"Only then may one explain it to them. He addressed Śāriputra:
"If I were to describe these characteristics for those who seek the Buddha-way, I would not reach the end even after an entire kalpa."
"Such persons as these will be able to believe and understand; you should preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for them.

Chapter Four: The Chapter on Faith and Understanding (*Adhimukti-parivarta*) At that time, the Venerable Subhūti, Mahākātyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, and Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having heard from the Buddha this unprecedented Dharma and the World-Honored One’s bestowal of the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon Śāriputra, gave rise to a rare and marvelous mind. Overjoyed and leaping for joy, they immediately rose from their seats, adjusted their robes, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, joined their palms with single-minded devotion, bowed in reverence, and gazing up at the Honored One’s countenance, addressed the Buddha, saying:

"We occupy the foremost positions among the Sangha; our years are advanced and we are decrepit. We believed that we had already attained Nirvana and were incapable of further effort, no longer seeking Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi."

World-Honored One, in the past when the Dharma had been taught for a long time, I was seated in the assembly; my body grew weary and exhausted, and I thought only of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. Regarding the Bodhisattva teachings—such as sporting with supernatural powers, purifying Buddha-lands, and bringing sentient beings to maturity—my heart found no joy in them.
Why is this? World-Honored One, you have caused us to emerge from the triple world and attain the realization of nirvana.

Furthermore, we are now advanced in years; regarding the Buddha’s teaching and transformation toward the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of the bodhisattvas, we do not give rise to even a single thought of joyful aspiration.

"We have now, before the Buddha, heard the bestowal of the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi upon the śrāvakas; our hearts are filled with great joy, having attained what we have never experienced before."

I did not expect that, all of a sudden, I would now hear this rare Dharma; I am deeply grateful and fortunate to have obtained such great and wholesome benefit—immeasurable treasures acquired without seeking them.
“World-Honored One!
We now wish to employ a parable to clarify this meaning.

Suppose there is a man who, while still young, abandoned his father and fled, dwelling in another land for a long time—perhaps ten, twenty, or even fifty years. As he grew older and became increasingly impoverished, he wandered in all directions in search of food and clothing.”
Traveling by degrees, he eventually encountered his own country.
His father had previously come seeking his son but had not found him, so he settled in a certain city.
His family was immensely wealthy, possessing immeasurable treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, crystal, pearls, and the like—and all their granaries and treasuries were overflowing.
He has many servants, ministers, officials, and subjects;
his elephants, horses, carriages, oxen, and sheep are beyond counting. His income and interest extend throughout other countries, and his merchants and traders are likewise exceedingly numerous.
At that time, the impoverished son wandered through various villages and passed through kingdoms and cities until he eventually reached the city where his father resided.

For more than fifty years since their separation, the father had constantly thought of his son, yet he never spoke of this matter to anyone; he merely pondered it within himself, harboring regret and remorse. He thought to himself: "I am now old and decrepit, yet I possess vast wealth—gold, silver, rare jewels, and granaries overflowing with grain.
I have no offspring; were I to pass away one day, my property would be lost and scattered, as there would be no one to whom I could entrust it."
Therefore, I constantly and earnestly remember my son, and again I think to myself:
"If I were to obtain my son and entrust him with my wealth and property, I would be at ease and happy, free from further anxiety."
“World-Honored One!
At that time, the impoverished son, wandering about in search of employment, happened upon his father’s house and stood by the side of the gate.

From afar he saw his father seated upon a lion throne with a precious footstool supporting his feet, surrounded with respectful devotion by Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and householders; his body was adorned with pearl necklaces worth ten million pieces of gold.”
Officials, commoners, servants, and attendants stood in attendance on his left and right, each holding a white whisk.

A precious canopy was spread above him, with various flowered banners hanging down; fragrant water was sprinkled upon the ground, and many kinds of famous flowers were scattered about. Precious objects were arranged in rows, and as they were brought out, put away, or exchanged, there were all manner of such elaborate adornments, making his majestic virtue exceptionally sublime.
Seeing that his father possessed great power and influence, the impoverished son was immediately seized with terror and regretted having come here.
He thought to himself in secret:
"This man must be either a king or someone equal to a king; this is no place for me to earn wealth through hired labor."
"It would be better to go to a poor neighborhood where there is ample ground for exertion and food and clothing are easily obtained.
If I remain here long, I may be coerced and forced into labor."
Having had this thought, he ran away quickly.
At that time, the wealthy elder, seeing his son upon the lion throne, recognized him immediately; his heart was filled with great joy, and he thought to himself:

He saw the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, seated upon a lion throne, surrounded by gods, nāga kings, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans who paid him reverent homage; he also saw the sixteen princes entreating the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma.

Then the Brahma Kings prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, and immediately scattered celestial flowers over the Buddha—flowers as vast as Mount Sumeru—and simultaneously offered them to the Buddha’s Bodhi tree.
Having made offerings of flowers, each offered their own palace to that Buddha and spoke these words:
"We pray only that you look upon us with compassion and bring us benefit."
"We offer these palaces; we pray that you will graciously accept them.
At that time, the Brahma kings, before the Buddha, with single-minded devotion and in unison, spoke in verse:
"The World-Honored One is most difficult to behold, He who has destroyed all afflictions."
After more than one hundred and thirty kalpas, I have now finally seen you once.
You who satisfy all hungry and thirsty sentient beings with the rain of Dharma—
such a person of immeasurable wisdom has never been seen before.
Like the udumbara flower, which we encounter today for the first time;
our various palaces have been adorned by the power of this light.
O World-Honored One of great compassion, we pray only that you will graciously accept them.
At that time, after the Brahma Kings had praised the Buddha with verses, each of them spoke these words:

"We only pray that the World-Honored One will turn the Wheel of Dharma, so that all the devas, Māras, Brahmas, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas in the entire world may attain peace and security and achieve liberation."
Then the Brahma Kings, with one mind and in unison, spoke in verse:
"We pray only that the Honored One of Gods and Men Will turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma;
Beat the great drum of the Dharma And blow the great conch of the Dharma."
"May you universally rain down the great Dharma rain, To deliver immeasurable sentient beings.
We all humbly entreat you: Please manifest your profound and far-reaching voice.
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently granted his consent.
The same was true for the southwest and even down to the nadir.

At that time, the Great Brahma Kings of five million billion lands in the zenith all beheld the radiance and majestic brilliance of their respective palaces, such as they had never seen before. Overjoyed and leaping with delight, they conceived a sense of wonder and immediately went to one another to discuss this matter:
"By what cause and condition do our palaces possess such radiance?"
At that time, there was among that assembly a Great Brahmā King named Śikhin, who spoke these verses for the sake of the host of Brahmās:
"For what cause and condition now Are all our palaces Radiant with majestic virtue and light,
Adorned in a manner never seen before?"
Such wondrous signs as these have never before been heard or seen;
are they produced by the birth of a Great Virtuous One,
or is it because a Buddha has appeared in the world?

“At that time, five million billion Brahma kings, together with their palaces, each took celestial flowers in the folds of their robes and went collectively to the lower direction to investigate the meaning of these signs.”

He saw the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, seated upon a lion throne, surrounded with reverence by devas, nāga kings, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others; and he also saw the sixteen princes entreating the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma.

Then the Brahma kings prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet and circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times. They immediately scattered celestial flowers over the Buddha—flowers as vast as Mount Sumeru—and simultaneously made offerings to the Buddha’s Bodhi tree.
Having made offerings of flowers, each offered their own palace to that Buddha and spoke these words:
"We pray only that you look upon us with compassion and bring us benefit."
"We offer these palaces; we pray that you will graciously accept them.
Then the Brahma Kings, before the Buddha, with single-mindedness and in unison, spoke in verse:
"How excellent it is to behold the Buddhas, The Holy Honored Ones who save the world!"
Able to urge all sentient beings out from the prison of the triple world;
the Honored One among gods and men, possessed of universal wisdom, takes pity on the various classes of living beings,
able to open the gate of ambrosia and extensively deliver all.
In the past, throughout immeasurable kalpas, time passed in vain without a Buddha;
when the World-Honored One had not yet appeared, the ten directions were perpetually shrouded in darkness,
the three evil realms increased, and the asuras also flourished.
The hosts of devas steadily diminish, and many who die fall into the evil realms.
Failing to hear the Dharma from the Buddha, they constantly engage in unwholesome deeds;
thus their physical form, strength, and wisdom—all these decrease.
Due to the causes and conditions of sinful karma, they lose both happiness and the perception of happiness;
abiding in the teachings of false views, they do not recognize virtuous conduct and fail to receive the Buddha’s transformation,
thus constantly falling into the evil realms.
The Buddha is the eye of the world; appearing only after a vast expanse of time, he manifests in the world out of compassion for all sentient beings.
Having transcended and attained perfect enlightenment, we rejoice most greatly.
Together with all other assemblies, they joyfully marveled at this unprecedented event:
"Our various palaces have been magnificently adorned by virtue of this light;
we now offer them to the World-Honored One—please deign to accept them out of compassion."
"By this merit, may it extend universally to all;
may we and all sentient beings together attain the path of Buddhahood.
At that time, after the five million billion Brahma kings had praised the Buddha with these verses, they each addressed the Buddha, saying:
“May the World-Honored One turn the wheel of Dharma, bringing peace and security to many, and liberating many.
Then the Brahma Kings spoke in verse:
“The World-Honored One turns the wheel of Dharma, Beating the drum of the Dharma of Ambrosia.”
To deliver sentient beings from suffering and distress, you reveal the path to Nirvana.
We pray that you will accept our invitation and, out of compassion,
expound with your great and subtle voice the Dharma practiced throughout immeasurable eons.

At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū accepted the invitation of the Brahmā kings of the ten directions and the sixteen princes, and immediately turned the Wheel of Dharma in its twelve aspects through three revolutions—a wheel which no śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or any other being in the world could turn—namely: "This is suffering; this is the origin of suffering; this is the cessation of suffering; this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.

He also extensively expounded the Dharma of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination: ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions becoming; becoming conditions birth; and birth conditions old age, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and despair.

With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; and with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair cease.

When the Buddha preached this Dharma amidst the great assembly of devas and humans, six hundred *koṭi-nayuta* of people—by not grasping at any phenomena—attained liberation of the mind from all outflows (*āsrava*), and all attained profound and wondrous meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), the three knowledges (*vidyā*), the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*).

During the second, third, and fourth preachings of the Dharma, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *nāyuta* of sentient beings, equal in number to the sands of the Ganges River, likewise attained liberation of the mind from all outflows (*āsrava*) by not grasping at any phenomena.
From that time forward, the assembly of śrāvakas became immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable.

At that time, the sixteen princes—all of whom had left home as youths to become śrāmaṇeras, possessed keen faculties, were clear in wisdom, had already made offerings to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of buddhas, had purely cultivated the brahma-faring, and sought anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—unitedly addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
All these immeasurable thousands of myriads of kotis of great virtuous śrāvakas have already achieved this.
May the World-Honored One also preach for us the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; having heard it, we shall all together practice and study it.
“World-Honored One!
Our aspirations are for the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision; what our deep minds contemplate, the Buddha himself knows and witnesses.
At that time, among the multitude led by the Wheel-Turning Sage King, eighty trillion people, seeing that the sixteen princes had left the household life, also sought to leave the household life.
The King immediately granted his permission.

At that time, having accepted the śrāmaṇera’s invitation, after twenty thousand kalpas had passed, that Buddha preached this Mahāyāna sūtra titled “The Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma” (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka) amidst the fourfold assembly—a teaching for bodhisattvas, which is protected and remembered by the Buddhas.
When this sutra had been spoken, the sixteen śrāmaṇeras, for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, all together received, upheld, recited, and mastered it.
When this sutra was being preached, the sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras all believed and accepted it;
among the assembly of śrāvakas, there were also those who believed and understood;
yet the remaining beings, numbering in the thousands of myriads of koṭis, all gave rise to doubt and confusion.
The Buddha preached this sutra for eight thousand kalpas without ceasing or resting.
Having finished preaching this sutra, he immediately entered a quiet chamber and dwelt in meditative concentration for eighty-four thousand kalpas.

At that time, the sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras, knowing that the Buddha had entered his room and was in silent meditative concentration, each ascended a Dharma seat and, for eighty-four thousand kalpas, extensively expounded and analyzed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for the fourfold assembly.

Each one delivered six million billion nayutas of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River; they instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened them, causing them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

After eighty-four thousand kalpas had passed, the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū arose from his samādhi, proceeded to the Dharma-seat, and sat down with serene composure. He then addressed the great assembly:

"These sixteen śrāmaṇera bodhisattvas are truly rare; their faculties are sharp and penetrating, their wisdom is clear and lucid, and they have already made offerings to immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas."
In the presence of all Buddhas, they constantly cultivate the pure conduct, receive and uphold the Buddha’s wisdom, and reveal it to sentient beings, causing them to enter therein.
You all should repeatedly draw near to them and make offerings to them.

Why is this? If śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas can believe in the sūtra teachings spoken by these sixteen bodhisattvas, and receive, uphold, and do not disparage them, such persons shall all attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“These sixteen bodhisattvas constantly delight in preaching this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.

Each of these bodhisattvas has converted six million billion nayutas of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River; in every lifetime they have been born with these bodhisattvas, and having heard the Dharma from them, they have all attained faith and understanding. By virtue of these causes and conditions, they have encountered four million billion Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and even now, they are not yet exhausted.”
“O bhikṣus! I now tell you:

‘Those sixteen śrāmaṇeras who were disciples of that Buddha have all now attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; they currently reside in buddha-fields throughout the ten directions preaching the Dharma, with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas as their retinues.’”
Those two śrāmaṇeras will become Buddhas in the eastern direction: one named Akṣobhya, residing in the Land of Joy, and the second named Sumerukūṭa;
in the southeastern direction there are two Buddhas, one named Siṃhanāda and the second named Siṃhavikrīḍita;
in the southern direction there are two Buddhas, one named Gaganasthita and the second named Nityopaśānta.
In the southwest are two buddhas: the first is named Tejodhipati, and the second is named Brahmajāla;
in the west are two buddhas: the first is named Amitābha, and the second is named Sarvalokadhātūpadravodvegapratyuttīrṇa;
in the northwest are two buddhas: the first is named Tamālapatracandanagandhābhijña, and the second is named Merudhvaja.
In the north are two Buddhas: the first is named Cloud Sovereign (*Megheśvara*), and the second is named Cloud Sovereign King (*Megheśvararāja*).

In the northeast is a Buddha named Destroyer of All Worldly Fears (*Sarvalokabhayavighātin*). As for the sixteenth, I, Śākyamuni Buddha, have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in the Sahā world-system.

"O Bhikṣus! When we were śrāmaṇeras, each of us individually taught and transformed immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, who heard the Dharma from us and [set their minds] upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Among these sentient beings, there are those who currently abide on the stage of the śrāvaka; I constantly teach and transform them toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
These individuals should gradually enter the Buddha-way by means of this Dharma.
Why is this? Because the wisdom of the Tathāgata is difficult to believe and difficult to understand.

Those immeasurable beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who were transformed by me at that time are none other than you, monks, and my śrāvaka disciples in future ages after my parinirvāṇa.

After my parinirvāṇa, there will again be disciples who have not heard this sutra; unaware and unperceiving of the conduct of bodhisattvas, they will conceive the notion of having attained parinirvāṇa based on the merits they themselves have acquired, thinking, "I shall enter nirvana."
In other lands I shall become a Buddha under different names.

Although these people have conceived the thought of extinction and entered *nirvāṇa*, they will seek the wisdom of a Buddha in those lands; there they will hear this sutra and attain extinction solely through the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*), for there is no other vehicle, except for the skillful means (*upāya*) by which the Tathāgatas preach the Dharma.

“O bhikṣus! When the Tathāgata knows for himself that the time for his parinirvāṇa has arrived, and when the assembly is pure, their faith and understanding firm, they have thoroughly realized the dharma of emptiness, and have deeply entered meditative concentration, he then gathers the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas and preaches this sūtra for them.”
In this world, there are no two vehicles by which one attains extinction; it is only through the Single Buddha Vehicle that one attains extinction.
Bhikṣus, you should know!

Through the skillful means of the Tathāgata, he has deeply entered the nature of sentient beings; knowing that they delight in inferior teachings and are deeply attached to the five desires, he preaches nirvāṇa for their sake.
If such a person hears this, they will immediately believe and accept it.
"It is like a perilous and evil road five hundred yojanas long, desolate and devoid of people, a place of terror."
Suppose there is a large multitude who wish to travel this path to reach a place of precious treasures.

There is a guide, wise and discerning, who thoroughly understands the characteristics of the dangers and the passages and blockages of the perilous road; he leads the multitude, intending to get them across this difficulty.
The multitude they were leading grew weary and despondent along the way, and addressed the guide, saying:
"We are utterly exhausted and filled with fear; we can no longer proceed.
The road ahead is still long, and we now wish to turn back."
The guide, possessing many skillful means, thought to himself:
"These people are to be pitied; why do they wish to turn back after having abandoned such great treasures?
Having had this thought, by the power of his skillful means, he created an illusory city three hundred yojanas into the perilous path and addressed the multitude, saying:
"Do not fear, and do not turn back.
You may dwell within this great city and do as you please.
If you enter this city, you will find swift peace and security."
"If you can reach the place of treasure ahead, you may also go.
At that time, the exhausted multitude was filled with great joy and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence, exclaiming:
"We have now escaped this evil path; we have swiftly attained peace and security."
Thereupon, the multitude entered the conjured city, conceiving the thought that they had already reached their destination and feeling a sense of security.
At that time, the guide knew that these people had found rest and were no longer weary.
He immediately extinguished the conjured city and said to the multitude:
"Come, you all; the place of treasure is near.
That great city we saw earlier was a creation of mine, made merely for the sake of providing rest."
"O bhikṣus! The Tathāgata is likewise so;
he now acts as your great guide, knowing that the various births and deaths, afflictions, evil paths, perils, and long distances must be departed from and crossed over."
If sentient beings were to hear only the Single Buddha Vehicle, they would not wish to see the Buddha nor wish to draw near to him, and would instead think:
"The path of the Buddha is long and distant; it can only be accomplished after enduring diligent suffering for a long time."
The Buddha, knowing that their minds were timid, weak, and inferior, employed skillful means to provide them with rest along the way and spoke of two types of nirvāṇa.
When sentient beings abide in these two stages, the Tathāgata then says to them:

"What you have accomplished is not yet complete; the stage upon which you abide is close to the wisdom of the Buddha. You should observe and deliberate that the nirvāṇa you have attained is not the ultimate reality."
"However, by the power of the Tathāgata’s skillful means, he distinguishes and teaches three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle.
It is like that guide who, for the sake of providing rest, conjures a great city.
Once they knew their breathing had ceased, he told them:
"The place of treasure is near; this city is not real; I have conjured it by transformation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas;
yet the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him, and he could not attain the path of Buddhahood.
The various devas, nāga kings, and the hosts of asuras—”
Constantly raining celestial flowers as an offering to that Buddha;
the devas beat celestial drums and perform various musical arts;
fragrant winds blow away the withered blossoms and rain down fresh and beautiful ones once more.
After ten intermediate kalpas had passed, he finally attained the path of Buddhahood;
all the devas and people of the world felt their hearts leap with joy.
That Buddha’s sixteen sons, together with their retinues, [all followed him].
Surrounded by hundreds of thousands of millions, they all proceeded together to the place where the Buddha was;
prostrating their heads at the Buddha’s feet, they requested him to turn the wheel of Dharma:
"O Holy Lion, let the rain of Dharma fill us and all beings."
The World-Honored One is most difficult to encounter;
appearing but once in the course of a vast eon, he awakens all living beings and causes all things to tremble.
Throughout the worlds of the eastern direction, across five hundred trillion lands—
The light of the Brahma palaces shone forth, such as had never been seen before.
When the various Brahmas beheld this omen, they immediately came to where the Buddha was;
scattering flowers as an offering, they also presented their palaces.
He entreated the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma, praising him with verses.
Knowing that the time had not yet come, the Buddha accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
It was likewise so for the three directions, the four intermediate points, and the zenith and nadir.
Scattering flowers as an offering to the palace, they entreated the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma:
"The World-Honored One is most difficult to encounter;
we pray that with great compassion you will widely open the gate of ambrosia and turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma."
The World-Honored One of Immeasurable Wisdom, having accepted the invitation of those people,
proclaimed for them various teachings:
"The Four Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination— from ignorance to old age and death— all exist conditioned by birth."
Such are the many faults and afflictions; you all should understand them.
When this Dharma was proclaimed, six hundred trillion nayutas attained the end of all suffering and all became arhats.
During the second preaching of the Dharma, A multitude as numerous as the sands of ten million Ganges Rivers Did not grasp at any phenomena And likewise attained arhatship.
From that time onward, those who attained the Way Were beyond measure in number.
Even through the calculation of billions of kalpas, one could not reach its limit.
At that time, the sixteen princes left the household life as śrāmaṇeras and together requested that Buddha to expound the Mahāyāna Dharma:
"We, along with our retinues, shall all attain the Way of the Buddha;
may we obtain, like the World-Honored One, the foremost purity of the eye of wisdom.
The Buddha, knowing the minds of the youths and their practices in past lives, [spoke thus].
Through immeasurable causes and conditions, and by means of various parables,
he expounds the six pāramitās as well as the matters of the supernormal powers.
He analyzes the true Dharma, the path traversed by bodhisattvas.
He preached this Lotus Sutra in verses as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
After that Buddha had finished preaching the sutra, he entered meditative concentration in a quiet chamber,
sitting with single-minded focus in one place for eighty-four thousand kalpas.
These śrāmaṇeras, knowing that the Buddha had not yet emerged from meditation,
preached the unsurpassed wisdom of the Buddha for the sake of immeasurable billions of beings.
Each sat upon a Dharma-seat and expounded this Mahāyāna sūtra.
After the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, they proclaimed and assisted in the transformation through the Dharma.
Each of those śrāmaṇeras saved six million billion sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
After that Buddha has passed into extinction, these who have heard the Dharma will always be born together with their teacher in every Buddha-land.
These sixteen śrāmaṇeras will fully practice the path of the Buddhas.
Now, throughout the ten directions, they have each attained perfect enlightenment.
Those who heard the Dharma at that time are now each in the presence of various Buddhas;
those who abide as śrāvakas are gradually taught the Buddha-way.
In the sixteen kalpas, I have already spoken to you;
therefore, by means of skillful expedients, I lead you toward the Buddha’s wisdom.
For these fundamental causes and conditions, I now preach the Lotus Sutra.
I shall cause you to enter the Buddha-way; be careful not to harbor fear or dread.
It is like a perilous and evil road, remote and desolate, abounding in venomous beasts, and furthermore lacking water and grass—a place that strikes terror into all people.
Countless tens of millions of beings wish to traverse this perilous path;
it is exceedingly vast and remote, extending for five hundred yojanas.
At that time, there was a guide who possessed powerful memory and wisdom.
With a mind of clear understanding and resolve, he rescues the multitude from their perils.
When all the people were weary and exhausted, they said to the Guide:
"We are now utterly spent; we wish to turn back here."
The Guide thought to himself:
"How pitiable are these people! How can they wish to turn back and lose such great treasures?"
Immediately he contemplated a skillful means,
intending to employ his supernormal powers to manifest a great city and walled capital, with its houses and dwellings magnificently adorned,
surrounded by gardens and groves, canals, streams, and bathing pools.
With heavy gates and lofty towers, it was filled with men and women.
Having performed this transformation, he comforted the multitude, saying: "Do not fear!
You may enter this city and each enjoy whatever you desire."
Once the people had entered the city, their hearts were all filled with great joy;
they conceived thoughts of security and each thought themselves already delivered.
Knowing that they had rested, the Guide gathered the assembly and addressed them, saying:
"You all should press forward; this is merely a conjured city.
Seeing that you were utterly exhausted and wished to turn back midway, I used the power of skillful means to temporarily manifest this city."
"You all must apply yourselves with diligent vigor; together you shall reach the place of treasure.
I, likewise, am the guide for all;
seeing those who seek the Way faltering and becoming weary on the path, I say:
Unable to cross over birth and death, And the various perilous paths of affliction,
He therefore employs the power of skillful means To preach nirvana for their relief,
saying:
"Your suffering is extinguished; that which was to be done has all been accomplished.
Since you have realized Nirvana and all attained Arhatship, you may now assemble the great multitude and preach the True Dharma for them."
Through the power of skillful means, the Buddhas distinguish and teach the three vehicles;
yet there is only the single Buddha-vehicle, and the two were taught for the sake of providing rest.
Now I shall speak the truth to you: that which you have attained is not final extinction.
For the sake of the Buddha’s omniscience, you should arouse great diligence.
When you realize omniscience, possessing the ten powers and other Buddha-qualities along with the thirty-two marks, that is indeed true cessation.
The Teachers of all Buddhas preach nirvana in order to bring about rest;
once they know that [the beings] have found rest, they lead them into the Buddha-wisdom.
— *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Scroll Three.
The Lotus Sutra, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty, by Imperial Decree.

Chapter Eight: The Prophecy for the Five Hundred Disciples At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, having heard from the Buddha this teaching of wisdom and skillful means according to what was appropriate, and having further heard the bestowal of the prophecy of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon the great disciples, and having heard the matters concerning their past causes and conditions, and having heard that all Buddhas possess the power of great sovereign spiritual transformations, attained what he had never experienced before; his heart was purified and he leaped with joy.

He immediately rose from his seat, went before the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. Gazing up at the Honored One’s countenance without averting his eyes for even a moment, he thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One is most extraordinary; what he does is rare and marvelous!"
In accordance with the various dispositions of the world, we preach the Dharma through skillful means and insight, drawing sentient beings out from their attachments everywhere.
Regarding the Buddha’s merits, our words cannot fully express them; only the World-Honored Buddha can know the deep-seated intentions and original vows within our hearts.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do you see this Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra?

I have always declared him to be the foremost among those who preach the Dharma, and I have also constantly praised his various merits. He has diligently protected and assisted in proclaiming my Dharma; he is able to instruct, benefit, and gladden the fourfold assembly, fully expounding the Buddha’s true Dharma, and greatly benefiting his fellow practitioners of the Brahma-faring life."
Aside from the Tathāgata himself, none are able to exhaust the eloquence of his discourse.

You should not think that Pūrṇa is merely able to protect and assist in proclaiming my Dharma; he has also, in the presence of ninety billion Buddhas of the past, protected and assisted in proclaiming the true Dharma of those Buddhas, and among those who preached the Dharma, he was likewise the foremost.

Furthermore, regarding the Dharma of emptiness taught by all Buddhas, they have clearly understood and thoroughly penetrated it, attaining the four types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*). They are always able to expound the Dharma with meticulous discernment and purity, free from any doubt, and are fully endowed with the supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) of a bodhisattva.
Throughout his entire lifespan, he constantly practiced the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*); all the people of that Buddha-world regarded him as being truly a *śrāvaka*.

Yet, through this skillful means, Pūrṇa benefited immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings and further transformed immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* persons, causing them to establish themselves in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"For the sake of purifying Buddha-fields, he constantly performs the work of a Buddha, teaching and transforming sentient beings. 'O Bhikṣus!

Pūrṇa was foremost among those who expounded the Dharma under the seven Buddhas; now, among those who expound the Dharma under me, he is likewise foremost. Furthermore, among those who expound the Dharma under all future Buddhas of this Bhadrakalpa, he shall again be foremost, always protecting, upholding, and assisting in the proclamation of the Buddha-dharma.'"

Furthermore, in the future, they shall protect, uphold, and propagate the immeasurable and boundless teachings of all Buddhas, teaching and benefiting immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to be established in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For the sake of purifying a Buddha-field, he constantly exerts himself with diligence to transform sentient beings, gradually fulfilling the path of a bodhisattva.

After the passing of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in this land, and his name shall be Dharmaprabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat.

That Buddha takes as many trichiliocosms as there are sands in the Ganges River to constitute a single buddha-field. Its ground is composed of the seven treasures and is as level as the palm of a hand, without mountains, hills, valleys, gullies, or ravines. Within it, towers and pavilions made of the seven treasures fill the space, while the palaces of the devas hover nearby in the void; thus humans and devas interact, each able to see the other.
There are no evil realms, nor are there women; all sentient beings are born by transformation and are free from lustful desire.

They have attained great supernormal powers, their bodies emit radiance, and they travel through the air with ease. Their resolve and mindfulness are firm, and they possess diligence and wisdom. All are universally golden in color, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
The sentient beings of that land always subsist on two kinds of food:
first, the food of the joy of the Dharma; second, the food of the bliss of dhyāna.

There are immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya, thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of bodhisattvas who have attained great supernormal powers and the four unhindered wisdoms, and who are skillfully able to transform and guide all classes of sentient beings.
The assembly of his śrāvakas is beyond the reach of calculation or reckoning; they have all fully attained the six supernormal powers, the three clarities, and the eight liberations.
Such immeasurable meritorious adornments as these are perfected in that Buddha-land.
The kalpa was named Jewel Radiance, and the land was named Virtuous Purity.
That Buddha’s lifespan lasted for immeasurable asankhyeya kalpas, and the Dharma remained for a very long time.
After the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, stupas made of the seven treasures were erected, filling the entire land.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Listen attentively, O bhikṣus!
The path traveled by the sons of the Buddha, because they have skillfully studied expedient means, is inconceivable."
