Knowing that the multitude delights in inferior teachings and fears great wisdom,
the Bodhisattvas therefore manifest as Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas,
employing countless skillful means to transform all classes of sentient beings.
Though they claim to be śrāvakas and remain far from the Buddha-way,
they deliver immeasurable multitudes, all of whom attain full accomplishment;
even if their aspirations are small and they are indolent, they shall gradually be made into Buddhas.
Secretly practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva within, while outwardly appearing as a śrāvaka;
having few desires and weary of birth and death, they in truth purify their own buddha-field.
They manifest the presence of the three poisons to the multitude, and further display the marks of false views.
My disciples are like this, delivering sentient beings through skillful means.
If I were to describe in full detail all the various manifestations of my transformations,
sentient beings who heard them would harbor doubts and confusion in their hearts.
Now this Pūrṇa, under thousands of billions of Buddhas in the past,
diligently cultivated the path he was to travel and proclaimed and protected the teachings of all those Buddhas.
Seeking supreme wisdom, he did so in the presence of all those Buddhas.
He currently dwells as the foremost among the disciples;
Possessing great learning and wisdom, his speech is fearless.
He is able to bring joy to the multitude, Never experiencing weariness, as he assists in the Buddha’s work.
Having already attained great supernormal powers and being endowed with the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge,
he knows the sharpness or dullness of all faculties and constantly preaches the pure Dharma.
Expounding such meanings, he instructs billions of beings.
Causing them to abide in the Mahāyāna Dharma, they purify their own Buddha-fields.
In the future as well, they will make offerings to immeasurable and innumerable Buddhas,
protecting and assisting in the proclamation of the True Dharma, and likewise purifying their own Buddha-fields.
Constantly employing various skillful means, he preached the Dharma with fearlessness,
delivering countless multitudes and accomplishing all-encompassing wisdom.
He made offerings to all Tathāgatas and protected and upheld the treasury of the Dharma-jewel.
Thereafter he attained Buddhahood, named Dharmaprabha.
His land was called Supariśuddha, composed of the seven treasures,
and the eon was named Ratnaprabha.
Their number is immeasurable in the hundreds of millions;
all have attained great supernormal powers, fully endowed with majestic virtue and strength, filling his land.
His śrāvakas are likewise countless, possessing the three insights and the eight liberations.
Having attained the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, they constitute the Saṃgha through such qualities.
All sentient beings in that land have completely severed lustful desire;
they are born solely by transformation, their bodies adorned with the primary marks.
Feeding on the joy of the Dharma and the delight of dhyāna, they have no further thought of other food.
There are no women there, nor are there any evil realms.
The bhikṣu Pūrṇa has fully perfected all his meritorious virtues.
"When this pure land is attained, the assembly of worthy sages will be exceedingly vast.
Such immeasurable matters as these, I have now explained only in brief.
At that time, the twelve hundred arhats who had attained mastery over their minds thought to themselves:
“We are filled with joy at having attained what we have never experienced before.
If the World-Honored One would likewise bestow a prediction of enlightenment upon each of us, as he has done for the other great disciples, would that not be most wonderful!”
The Buddha, knowing the thoughts in their minds, addressed Mahākāśyapa:
"These twelve hundred arhats, I shall now, in their very presence, grant them the prediction of unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) in successive order."

Within this assembly, my great disciple, the bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya, shall make offerings to sixty-two thousand billion buddhas; thereafter, he will attain buddhahood, known by the name Samantaprabha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.

As for those five hundred arhats—Uruvilvākāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, Nadīkāśyapa, Kālodāyin, Udāyin, Aniruddha, Revata, Kapphiṇa, Bakula, Cunda, and Śāgata—they shall all attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and they shall all share the same name: Samantaprabhāsa (Universal Radiance).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“The bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya Shall see immeasurable buddhas;
After incalculable kalpas have passed, He shall then achieve equal and perfect enlightenment.”
Constantly emitting great radiance, Fully endowed with all supernormal powers,
His fame pervades the ten directions, And he is revered by all;
He constantly proclaims the unsurpassed path, And is therefore named Samantaprabha.
That land is pure and serene; all bodhisattvas are courageous and valiant.
They ascend together into exquisite pavilions and travel through the lands of the ten directions, offering unsurpassed articles of worship to all the Buddhas.
Having made these offerings, his heart filled with great joy, he returned to his own country in an instant; such was his supernatural power.
The Buddha’s lifespan was sixty thousand kalpas, and the True Dharma remained for twice that duration.
The period of the Semblance Dharma shall be twice as long again; when the Dharma perishes, devas and humans will grieve.
Those five hundred bhikṣus shall successively become buddhas, all sharing the same name, Samantaprabha, as they receive their predictions in succession.
After my parinirvāṇa, such-and-such a person shall become a Buddha;
the world they transform shall be just like mine today.
As for the majesty and purity of their land, as well as their various supernormal powers—
The assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, the duration of the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma,
and the number of kalpas of their lifespans— all are as previously described.
Kāśyapa, you already know that there are five hundred masters of self-mastery.
"The other śrāvakas shall likewise be so.
For those who are not present in this assembly, you should proclaim [the teaching] for them.

At that time, the five hundred arhats, having received their predictions from the Buddha, were filled with joy and exultation. They immediately rose from their seats, went before the Buddha, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and repented, reproaching themselves:
“World-Honored One!
We have always harbored this thought, believing ourselves to have already attained ultimate nirvāṇa; only now do we realize that we were like those lacking wisdom.”
Why is this? We ought to attain the wisdom of the Tathāgata, yet we have instead become content with our own meager wisdom.
"World-Honored One! [they said.]
For example, suppose there is a man who goes to the house of a close friend and falls asleep after drinking wine.
At that time, the friend has business to attend to at the government office; he ties a priceless jewel into the lining of the man's garment, gives it to him, and departs.
That person, having fallen asleep drunk, was entirely unaware of it.
Once he had risen, he wandered about and arrived in another country.
For the sake of food and clothing, he sought them with diligent effort, undergoing great hardship.
If one has attained only a little and considers that sufficient,
later a friend may encounter him and say: "Alas, O man!..."
Why do you concern yourself with food and clothing to such an extent?

In the past, wishing to bring you peace and happiness and to allow you to indulge freely in the five desires, I tied a priceless jewel inside your garment on such and such a day of such and such a month in a certain year.
"It is actually present here now, yet you do not know it.
To toil and suffer in grief and anxiety in order to sustain yourself is truly foolish.
You may now trade this treasure for whatever you require; it shall always fulfill your wishes, and you will never lack for anything."
"The Buddha is likewise; when he was a bodhisattva, he taught and transformed us, causing us to resolve upon the mind of omniscience.
Yet we soon forgot it, neither knowing nor perceiving it."
Having attained the path of Arhatship, they considered themselves to have reached final nirvana;
yet, as their livelihood remained difficult and they were content with little, their aspiration for omniscience still persisted without being lost.
Now the World-Honored One has awakened us by speaking these words:
"O bhikṣus! That which you have attained is not ultimate cessation."

"For a long time I have caused you all to plant the roots of goodness for Buddhahood; by means of skillful expedients, I have manifested the appearance of nirvana, yet you each thought that you had truly attained extinction.
"World-Honored One! [the disciples said.]
"I now know for certain that I am indeed a bodhisattva who has received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For this reason, I am filled with great joy, having attained what I never had before."
At that time, Ājñātakauṇḍinya and the others, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"We have heard the unsurpassed, The voice of the bestowal of the prophecy of peace;
With unprecedented joy, We pay homage to the Buddha of Immeasurable Wisdom."
Now, before the World-Honored One, I repent of all my transgressions;
having obtained but a small portion of nirvana from the immeasurable Jewel of the Buddhas,
I was like an ignorant fool who considered myself sufficient.
For example, it is like a poor man who goes to the house of a kinsman;
that household is exceedingly wealthy and has prepared all manner of delicacies.
[The kinsman] ties an invaluable jewel within the lining of his inner garment.
He silently accepted it and departed, while at that time [the owner] lay down and remained unaware.
Once this man had risen, he traveled on to another country, seeking food and clothing to sustain himself; his livelihood was exceedingly difficult.
Having obtained a little, he considers it sufficient and no longer aspires for anything better.
Unaware that within his inner garment there is a priceless jewel,
a kinsman who possesses that jewel later encounters this poor man.
Having rebuked him with harsh words, he showed him the jewel that had been tied [to his garment].
When the poor man saw this jewel, his heart was filled with great joy;
possessing all manner of wealth, he indulged himself in the five desires.
We, too, are just like this; throughout the long night, the World-Honored One has constantly looked upon us with compassion and taught us, causing us to plant the unsurpassed aspiration.
Because we lacked wisdom, we neither perceived nor understood.
Having attained a small portion of nirvāṇa, I was self-satisfied and sought nothing more.
Now the Buddha has awakened me, saying that this is not true extinction;
only upon attaining the unsurpassed wisdom of a Buddha does one achieve true extinction.
"Now that I have heard from the Buddha The prophecy concerning these matters of adornment, And the successive conferral of predictions, My body and mind are filled with universal joy.
Chapter Nine: The Prophecy for Those in Training and Those Beyond Training. At that time, Ānanda and Rāhula had this thought:
"Each of us has constantly reflected:
'If we were to receive a prediction of enlightenment, would it not be most joyful?
" Thereupon, they rose from their seats, went before the Buddha, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and together addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We too should have a share in this; only the Tathāgata is our refuge.
Furthermore, we are known and recognized by all the world—its devas, humans, and asuras: Ānanda constantly serves as your attendant, upholding the treasury of the Dharma.”
Rāhula is the son of the Buddha—if the Buddha were to grant him the prophecy of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, my own vow would be fulfilled and the hopes of the multitude would be satisfied.

At that time, two thousand disciples—both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)—all rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, and approached the Buddha. With single-minded palms joined, they gazed up at the World-Honored One and stood to one side, just as Ānanda and Rāhula had wished.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda:

"In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Śāgarabuddhi-vaiśāradya-vaśavarti-rāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat."
After making offerings to sixty-two billion buddhas and upholding the treasury of the Dharma, you shall then attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
You shall teach and transform twenty thousand koṭis of bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, causing them to achieve Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The land is named Constantly Erected Victorious Banner; its soil is pure, with lapis lazuli for its ground.
The eon is named Pervasive Wondrous Sound.

The lifespan of that Buddha is immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya kalpas; even if one were to calculate and reckon for thousands of myriads of koṭis of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, one could not know it.
The True Dharma shall remain in the world for twice as long as his lifespan, and the Semblance Dharma shall remain in the world for twice as long as the True Dharma. Ānanda!

This Buddha, King of Sovereign Supernatural Powers of Mountain-like Ocean Wisdom, is praised together by immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions, who extol his merits.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"I now declare within this assembly: Ānanda, the upholder of the Dharma, shall make offerings to all Buddhas, and thereafter attain perfect enlightenment."
He is titled the Buddha Sovereign of the Unhindered Penetrations of Mountain and Sea Wisdom.
His pure land is named Constantly Erected Exalted Banner.
He transforms and guides bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The Buddha possesses great majestic virtue, and his fame fills the ten directions.
His lifespan is immeasurable; out of compassion for all sentient beings, he remains.
The True Dharma shall last twice the length of his lifespan, and the Semblance Dharma shall last twice that again.
Like the sands of the Ganges, countless sentient beings shall,
within this Buddha-dharma, plant the causal conditions for the path to Buddhahood.
At that time, eight thousand bodhisattvas who had newly resolved their minds within the assembly all had this thought:
"We have not even heard of the great bodhisattvas receiving such a prediction; for what cause and condition do these śrāvakas receive such a definitive assurance?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas, addressed them, saying:
"O sons of good family!
I and Ānanda and the others simultaneously gave rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in the presence of the Buddha Śūnyarāja."

"Ānanda has always delighted in extensive learning, while I have always been diligent and energetic; therefore, I have already attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Ānanda shall protect and uphold my Dharma, and likewise protect the Dharma-treasuries of all future Buddhas, teaching and bringing to maturity the assembly of Bodhisattvas. Since his original vow was such, he has received this prediction."

In the presence of the Buddha, Ānanda personally heard his own prediction of enlightenment and the splendor of his buddha-field; his aspirations being fully realized, his heart was filled with great joy at having attained what he had never experienced before.

Immediately, he recollected the Dharma-treasuries of immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of past Buddhas, attaining unimpeded mastery as if hearing them for the first time, and he also recognized his own original vows.
At that time, Ānanda spoke these verses:
“The World-Honored One is most rare and extraordinary, Causing me to recollect the teachings of immeasurable Buddhas of the past, Just as I have heard them this very day.”
"I now have no further doubt; I abide securely in the Buddha-way.
Acting as an attendant through skillful means, I shall protect and uphold all the Buddhas' teachings.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Rāhula:

"In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Ratnapadmacaraṇa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
He shall make offerings to as many Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as there are atoms in ten worlds, constantly serving as their eldest son, just as he does now.

As for this Buddha Padmaprabha (Flower-Treading Seven-Jewels), his land’s adornments, the duration of his lifespan in kalpas, the disciples he transforms, and his True Dharma and Semblance Dharma will be no different from those of the Tathāgata Sāgaradharabuddhivikrīḍitābhijña (King of Ocean-like Wisdom and Sovereign Supernatural Powers); he shall likewise serve as the eldest son of this Buddha.
"After this has passed, you shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"When I was a prince, Rāhula was my eldest son;
Now that I have attained the path of Buddhahood, you shall receive the Dharma as my Dharma-son.
In future ages, you shall behold immeasurable billions of Buddhas and serve as their eldest son, single-mindedly seeking the path of Buddhahood.
Rāhula’s secret practice is known only to me;
though he now appears as my eldest son, it is to demonstrate this to all sentient beings.
His immeasurable billions of merits are beyond counting.
"Abiding securely in the Buddha-dharma, they seek the unsurpassed path.

At that time, the World-Honored One saw that the two thousand disciples, both those in training and those beyond training, were of supple mind, tranquil and pure, with single-minded devotion gazing upon the Buddha.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Do you see these two thousand persons, those in training and those beyond training?
"Indeed, I see them."
“Ānanda! These people shall make offerings to as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in fifty worlds, honoring, respecting, and upholding their treasury of Dharma.”

At the end, they shall simultaneously attain Buddhahood in various lands throughout the ten directions; all shall bear the same title: Ratnaketu Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
"Their lifespan shall be one kalpa;
the adornments of their lands, as well as their śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and both the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma, shall all be identical.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"These two thousand śrāvakas, who now stand before me,
have all been granted the prediction that they shall attain Buddhahood in the future.
The number of Buddhas they have made offerings to is as vast as the atoms described above."
Protecting and upholding this treasury of the Dharma, they shall later attain perfect enlightenment.
Each in the lands of the ten directions, they shall all share one and the same name;
simultaneously sitting at the site of enlightenment, they shall realize unsurpassed wisdom.
All are named Ratnalakṣaṇa;
their lands and disciples, as well as the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma, are all equal and without distinction.
All, by means of various supernormal powers, deliver sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
"His fame shall spread everywhere, and he will gradually enter nirvana.
At that time, two thousand disciples, both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), hearing the Buddha’s bestowal of the prophecy, leaped for joy and spoke these verses:
"The World-Honored One, lamp of wisdom, we have heard the sound of the prophecy;”
Their hearts were filled with joy, as if they had been sprinkled with ambrosia.

Chapter Ten: The Dharma-Preacher The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Ten: The Dharma-Preacher At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, addressed eighty thousand great beings:
“Bhaiṣajyarāja!

“Do you see these in the great assembly—the immeasurable devas, nāga kings, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, as well as bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—those who seek the path of śrāvakas, those who seek the path of pratyekabuddhas, and those who seek the Buddha-way? To all such beings as these, who before the Buddha hear even a single verse or a single line of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, or even for a single moment rejoice in it, I bestow the prediction that they shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
The Buddha told Bhaiṣajyarāja:

"Furthermore, after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, if there should be anyone who hears even a single verse or a single phrase of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and rejoices in it for even a single thought-moment, I shall likewise bestow upon them the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

Furthermore, if there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, or transcribe even a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and who regard this scripture with reverence as they would the Buddha, making various offerings—of flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, ointment incense, burning incense, silk canopies, banners, pennants, robes, and music, and even joining their palms in respectful salutation.
Bhaiṣajyarāja!

You should know that these people have already made offerings to ten trillion buddhas; having fulfilled their great vows in the presence of those buddhas, they have been born into this human world out of compassion for sentient beings.
“Bhaiṣajyarāja!
If someone should ask:
‘Which sentient beings will attain Buddhahood in a future age?’”
One should show them:
"These people will surely attain Buddhahood in a future age. Why is this?

If any good man or good woman, regarding even a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, upholds, recites, explains, or transcribes it, and makes various offerings to the scripture—such as flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, ointment incense, burning incense, silk canopies, banners, flags, robes, and music—and pays homage with palms joined;
such a person should be venerated by all the world and should be honored with the same offerings one would offer to a Tathāgata.

You should know that this person is a great bodhisattva who has accomplished *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; out of compassion for sentient beings, he has made a vow to be born here to extensively expound and analyze the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
How much more so for those who are able to fully receive, uphold, and offer various kinds of worship?
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja!

You should know that such a person, having personally relinquished their own pure karmic retribution, will, out of compassion for sentient beings after my parinirvāṇa, be born into an evil world to extensively expound this sutra."
If there are good sons or good daughters who, after my parinirvāṇa, are able to secretly preach even a single verse of the Lotus Sūtra for the sake of a single person,
you should know that such a person is an emissary of the Tathāgata, one sent by the Tathāgata, performing the work of the Tathāgata.
How much more so if one were to preach it extensively for others amidst a great assembly?
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja!

If there were an evil person who, with an unwholesome mind, stood before a Buddha for an entire kalpa constantly reviling and abusing him, their transgression would still be light; [but this is not so for one who slanders this sutra]."
If a person, with even a single evil word, reviles those—whether lay or ordained—who read and recite the Lotus Sūtra, their sin is exceedingly grave.
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja!
Those who read and recite the Lotus Sutra should be known as persons adorned with the adornments of the Buddha; they are carried upon the shoulders of the Tathāgata.

In whichever direction he may go, one should face him and prostrate; with a single-minded focus, join the palms in homage, and pay respectful offerings, honoring and praising him with flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, unguents, burning incense, silk canopies, banners and streamers, robes, and delicacies, performing various musical performances as the supreme offerings among humans. One should hold celestial jewels and scatter them, and present the gathered treasures of the heavens as offerings.
Why is this? Because this person joyfully expounds the Dharma, and upon hearing it for even a brief moment, one immediately attains ultimate *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If one wishes to abide in the Buddha-way And achieve spontaneous wisdom,
One should always diligently make offerings To those who receive and uphold the Lotus Sutra."
Those who wish to quickly attain all-encompassing wisdom should receive and uphold this sutra,
as well as make offerings to those who uphold it. If there are those capable of receiving and upholding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, [they shall achieve their goal].
You should know that these are the messengers sent by the Buddha, who take pity upon all sentient beings.
Those who are able to receive and uphold this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* have left the pure lands and been born here out of compassion for the multitude.
You should know that such a person, possessing mastery over their place of rebirth,
will be able to extensively proclaim the unsurpassed Dharma in this degenerate age.
One should honor them with celestial flowers and incense, as well as celestial jewels and garments.
With a collection of exquisite jewels from the heavens, one should make offerings to the teacher of the Dharma.
In the evil world after my parinirvāṇa, those who are able to uphold this sutra should be saluted with palms joined in reverence,
just as one would make offerings to the World-Honored One.
With the finest delicacies and various sweet foods, as well as diverse garments,
they made offerings to these sons of the Buddha, hoping to hear [the teaching] for even a brief moment. If, in future ages,
there are those who can receive and uphold this sutra, [they shall likewise attain such merit].
I have dispatched them among human beings to perform the deeds of a Tathāgata.
If, for the duration of a single kalpa, one should constantly harbor an unwholesome mind and,
with a wrathful countenance, revile the Buddha, they shall incur immeasurable and grave offenses.
If there are those who read, recite, and uphold this Lotus Sūtra,
yet for even a moment address them with evil words, their sin shall exceed that of the former.
Suppose there is someone seeking the Buddha-way who, throughout an entire eon, [practices...]
Joining their palms before me, they praised me with countless verses.
Because of this praise of the Buddha, they attained immeasurable merit;
yet the merit of one who extols those who uphold this sutra exceeds that even further.
For eighty billion kalpas, one may offer the most exquisite forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes,
and tactile objects to those who uphold this sutra. Having made such offerings,
if one should hear it for even a brief moment, [the merit is far greater].
Then you should rejoice within yourself: "I have now attained a great benefit.
O Bhaiṣajyarāja, I now tell you:
among all the sūtras I have preached, the Lotus Sūtra is the foremost.
At that time, the Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja:

“Of the immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of sūtras that I have spoken—those already spoken, those being spoken now, and those yet to be spoken—among them all, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the most difficult to believe and the most difficult to understand.”
“Bhaiṣajyarāja!
This sutra is the secret treasury of all Buddhas; it must not be distributed or recklessly bestowed upon others.
It is guarded by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and has never been openly proclaimed since time immemorial.”
"Furthermore, while the Tathāgata is still present, this sutra already encounters much resentment and jealousy; how much more so after his parinirvāṇa?
'O Bhaiṣajyarāja!

You should know that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, those who are able to write, uphold, read, recite, make offerings to, and explain it to others will be covered by the Tathāgata’s robe, and they will also be protected and remembered by the Buddhas currently residing in other directions.'"
This person possesses the power of great faith, the power of aspiration, and the power of all roots of goodness.
You should know that such a person dwells together with the Tathāgata, and it is as if the Tathāgata were to stroke their head with his own hand.
“Bhaiṣajyarāja!

Wherever this sutra is preached, read, recited, or written, or wherever the scroll containing it may reside, one should erect a stupa made of the seven treasures, making it as high, broad, and magnificently adorned as possible; there is no need to enshrine relics therein.”
Why is this? Because within it already resides the entire body of the Tathāgata.
This stūpa should be honored, revered, respected, and praised with all kinds of flowers, incense, necklaces, silk canopies, banners, streamers, music, and songs.
If there are those who see this stūpa, pay homage to it, and make offerings to it, you should know that all such persons draw near to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Bhaiṣajyarāja!

There are many people, whether householders or those who have left the home life, who practice the bodhisattva path; yet if they are unable to see, hear, read, recite, copy, uphold, or make offerings to this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, you should know that these persons have not yet skillfully practiced the bodhisattva path.
If there are those who do hear this sūtra, only then can they skillfully practice the bodhisattva path.”

If there are sentient beings who seek the Buddha-way and either see or hear this Lotus Sūtra, and having heard it, believe, understand, accept, and uphold it, you should know that such persons have drawn near to Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Bhaiṣajyarāja!
It is as if there were a person, parched with thirst and in need of water, who dug for it on a high plateau. Seeing only dry earth, he knew the water was still far off;
yet, not ceasing his efforts, he saw moist soil appear, and eventually reached mud. His mind became certain that the water must be near.”

It is the same for a bodhisattva: if they have not yet heard, understood, or been able to practice this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, one should know that such a person is still far from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
if, however, they do hear and understand it, contemplate it, and practice it, one must know that they are certainly drawing near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why is this? Because the Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi of all Bodhisattvas belongs entirely to this sutra—this sutra opens the gate of skillful means and reveals the mark of reality.
"This treasury of the Lotus Sūtra is profound, solid, remote, and deep; no one can reach it. Now, the Buddha teaches and transforms bodhisattvas to reveal and explain it.
O Bhaiṣajyarāja!"
If there are bodhisattvas who, upon hearing this Lotus Sutra, are startled, doubtful, or terrified, you should know that they are bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds.
If śrāvakas hear this sutra and are startled, doubtful, or terrified, you should know that they are those of overweening pride.
“Bhaiṣajyarāja!
If there are good men or good women who, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, wish to preach this Lotus Sūtra for the fourfold assembly, how should they preach it?”

These sons and daughters of good family, having entered the Tathāgata’s chamber, donned the Tathāgata’s robe, and sat upon the Tathāgata’s seat, should then extensively expound this sutra for the fourfold assembly.
The chamber of the Tathāgata is the mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings;
the robe of the Tathāgata is the mind of gentleness and patience;
the seat of the Tathāgata is the emptiness of all phenomena.
Abiding therein, you should then, with a mind free from indolence, extensively expound this Lotus Sūtra for the sake of the bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly.
"Bhaiṣajyarāja!

In other lands, I shall dispatch emanated persons to assemble for him a congregation to hear the Dharma, and I shall also dispatch emanated bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās to listen to his preaching of the Dharma.
These emanated beings hear the Dharma and receive it with faith, following it in accordance and not opposing it.
If the teacher of the Dharma is in a secluded place, I shall at that time dispatch many devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and so forth, to listen to their preaching of the Dharma.
Although I am in another land, I shall from time to time cause those who preach this Dharma to behold my body.
If they should forget or lose any phrases or clauses of this sutra, I will recite them for them once more, so that they may attain completeness.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If you wish to abandon all indolence, You should listen to this sutra.
This sutra is difficult to hear, And those who believe and accept it are likewise rare."
Just as a person who thirsts for water, Digs into a high plateau,
And seeing only dry earth, Knows that water is still far away;
But gradually seeing moist soil and mud, They know with certainty that water is near.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know this:
if one has not heard the Lotus Sūtra, one remains very far from the Buddha’s wisdom;
yet if one hears this profound sūtra, one will definitively understand the Dharma of the śrāvakas.
This is the king of all sutras; having heard it, one should contemplate it with careful attention.
Know that such persons as these are close to the Buddha’s wisdom.
If anyone speaks this sutra, they should enter the Tathāgata’s chamber.
Clad in the robes of the Tathāgata, Seated upon the throne of the Tathāgata, He dwells among the assembly without fear, Expounding and analyzing the Dharma extensively.
Great compassion is his chamber; Gentleness and forbearance are his robe.
Taking the emptiness of all phenomena as one's seat, one dwells therein to preach the Dharma.
When preaching this sutra, if someone should revile you with harsh words or strike you with knives,
staves, tiles, or stones, you should endure it by recollecting the Buddha.
In thousands of myriads of kotis of lands, I manifest a pure and solid body,
preaching the Dharma for sentient beings throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas.
If, after my parinirvāṇa, there should be those who can preach this sutra, [they shall be my true disciples].
I dispatch four groups of emanations— monks and nuns,
as well as laymen and laywomen— to make offerings to the Dharma Master,
to guide all sentient beings, and to assemble them so that they may hear the Dharma.
If someone intends to inflict harm with swords, staves, tiles, or stones,
I shall dispatch emanated beings to provide them with protection.
If a person who preaches the Dharma is alone in a secluded place, [I shall likewise protect them].
In a place of solitude where no human voice is heard, when one recites this sutra,
I shall then manifest for them a body of pure radiance.
If they should forget or lose any passages, I will explain them so that they may master them thoroughly.
If a person possesses these virtues, whether they preach for the fourfold assembly,
recite the sutras in a secluded place, or do so anywhere else, they shall all behold my body.
If a person dwells in a quiet retreat, I shall dispatch the celestial kings and dragon kings [to protect them].
Yakṣas, spirits, and other such beings serve as the assembly for listening to the Dharma.
This person delights in preaching the Dharma, analyzing it without obstruction;
because they are protected and remembered by all Buddhas, they are able to bring joy to the great assembly.
If one draws near to a Dharma Master, One will swiftly attain the Bodhisattva path;
By following and learning from such a teacher, One shall behold Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Chapter Eleven: The Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa *The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Eleven: The Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa At that time, before the Buddha, there appeared a stupa made of the seven treasures. It was five hundred *yojanas* in height and two hundred and fifty *yojanas* in length and breadth. It emerged from the earth and remained suspended in mid-air, adorned with various kinds of precious objects.
There were five thousand railings and ten million grottoes; it was adorned with countless banners and streamers, and billions of precious necklaces and jeweled bells hung from above.
From all four directions, the fragrance of tamāla-pattra sandalwood issued forth, pervading the entire world.

Those various banners and canopies were composed of the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, pearl, and ruby—and reached as high as the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings.
The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven rained down māndārava flowers as an offering to the jeweled stūpa.

Furthermore, many hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of other devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, with all kinds of flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, canopies, and musical instruments, made offerings to the jeweled stūpa, honoring, respecting, and praising it.
At that time, a great voice issued forth from within the precious stupa,
exclaiming in praise: "Excellent, excellent,
World-Honored One Śākyamuni!"

He was able, by means of his great wisdom of equanimity, to preach for the great assembly the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—the Dharma for instructing bodhisattvas and that which is protected by the Buddhas. It is so, it is so!
“Śākyamuni World-Honored One!
All that has been spoken is indeed true.

At that time, the fourfold assembly, seeing the great jeweled stupa abiding in mid-air and hearing the sounds issuing from within it, all attained the joy of the Dharma. Astonished by this unprecedented occurrence, they rose from their seats, joined their palms in reverence, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Mahāpratibhāna, who, knowing the doubts in the minds of all the devas, humans, asuras, and others in the world, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"For what cause and condition has this jeweled stūpa emerged from the earth, and why does it emit such a sound from within?
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāratnakūṭa:

"Within this jeweled stūpa is the entire body of a Tathāgata. In the past, in the east, beyond immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya worlds, there was a land named Ratnaviśuddha. Therein dwelt a Buddha named Prabhūtaratna."
When that Buddha was practicing the bodhisattva path, he made this great vow:

"If, after I have attained Buddhahood and entered parinirvāṇa, there should be places in the lands of the ten directions where the Lotus Sūtra is being preached, may my stūpas appear before them by leaping forth for the sake of hearing this sūtra, acting as witnesses and praising it, saying, 'Excellent!'"
"After that Buddha had attained enlightenment, as he approached the time of his parinirvāṇa, he addressed the bhikṣus amidst the great assembly of devas and humans:
'After my parinirvāṇa, those who wish to make offerings to my entire body should erect a single great stūpa.'"

"By the power of that Buddha's supernormal faculties and vows, wherever in any place throughout the worlds of the ten directions there may be one who preaches the Lotus Sutra, that jeweled stupa will emerge before them; with his entire body within the stupa, he will praise them, saying:
'Excellent, excellent!'"
“Mahāpratibhāna! Now, because they have heard the preaching of the Lotus Sūtra, the stupa of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna has emerged from the earth and uttered these words of praise:
‘Excellent, excellent!’”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsukhavighuṣṭa, through the supernatural power of the Tathāgata, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We wish to behold this body of the Buddha.”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Pramuditanirdeśa:
“This Buddha Prabhūtaratna has made a profound and solemn vow:

‘If my jeweled stupa emerges before the Buddhas for the sake of hearing the Lotus Sutra, and anyone wishes to manifest my body to the fourfold assembly, then all those emanations of that Buddha who are currently preaching the Dharma throughout the worlds of the ten directions must gather together at one place; only then shall my body appear.’”
“Mahāpratibhāna! Those transformation Buddhas of mine who are currently preaching the Dharma in the worlds of the ten directions should now assemble.
Mahāpratibhāna addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We also wish to see the Buddhas who are emanations of the World-Honored One, so that we may pay them homage and make offerings.

At that time, the Buddha emitted a single ray of light from the tuft of white hair between his brows, and immediately the Buddhas of five million *koṭi-nayuta* Ganges-sands of lands in the eastern direction became visible. In those lands, the ground was all made of crystal, adorned with jeweled trees and jeweled garments; countless thousands of millions of *koṭis* of bodhisattvas filled them, with jeweled canopies spread everywhere and jeweled nets draped above.

In those lands, the various Buddhas preach all dharmas with great and wondrous voices; furthermore, one sees immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattvas filling all those lands, preaching the Dharma for the sake of the multitudes.
In the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below, wherever the light from the mark of the white tuft of hair shines, it is likewise so.
At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions each addressed their respective assemblies of bodhisattvas, saying:
"O sons of good family!
"I should now go to the Sahā world to the presence of Śākyamuni Buddha, and also pay homage to the precious stūpa of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna.

At that moment, the Sahā world was instantly transformed into purity: its ground became made of lapis lazuli, adorned with jeweled trees, and demarcated by golden cords along the eightfold paths; it was devoid of all villages, hamlets, towns, cities, great oceans, rivers, mountains, valleys, forests, and marshes.
Great precious incense was burned, and *mandārava* flowers were strewn across the ground; it was covered above with jeweled nets and canopies, and precious bells were suspended from them.
Only the assembly of this gathering was left behind, while all the devas and humans were moved to other lands.
At that time, each of the Buddhas took a great bodhisattva as his attendant and arrived at the Sahā world, each reaching the foot of a precious tree.

Each precious tree was five hundred yojanas high, adorned in succession with branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits. Beneath each precious tree there was a lion throne five yojanas high, likewise embellished with great jewels.
At that time, each of the Buddhas sat cross-legged upon these seats.
In this manner, they spread out in succession until they filled the trichiliocosm; yet, even within the single direction of Śākyamuni Buddha alone, his emanated bodies were still not yet exhausted.

At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha, wishing to accommodate the Buddhas who had manifested as his emanations, further transformed two million *koṭi-nayuta* lands in each of the eight directions, making them all pure and free from hells, hungry ghosts, animals, and asuras; he also moved the devas and humans from those places and placed them in other lands.

The lands to be converted likewise have lapis lazuli for their ground and are adorned with precious trees. These trees are five hundred yojanas high, their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits arrayed in successive tiers of splendor. Beneath each tree there is a precious lion throne, five yojanas high, embellished with various kinds of jewels.

Furthermore, there were no great oceans, rivers, or any of the kings of mountains—such as Mount Mucilinda, Mount Mahāmucilinda, the Cakravāḍa Mountains, the Mahācakravāḍa Mountains, or Mount Sumeru—all of which together constituted a single buddha-field.
The ground of jewels was level and even, covered everywhere by canopies of interlaced jewels;
banners and parasols were suspended above, great precious incense was burned, and celestial jewel flowers were strewn across the entire surface.

Because Śākyamuni Buddha intended for all the Buddhas to sit there in the future, he further transformed two million billion nayutas of lands in each of the eight directions, making them all pure and free from hells, hungry ghosts, animals, and asuras; furthermore, he moved the devas and humans to other lands.

The lands to be converted shall likewise have ground made of lapis lazuli and be adorned with precious trees. These trees will be five hundred yojanas high, their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits arranged in successive tiers of adornment. Beneath each tree there shall be a precious lion throne five yojanas high, also embellished with great jewels.

Furthermore, there were no great oceans, rivers, or mountain kings such as Mount Mucilinda, Mount Mahāmucilinda, the Cakravāḍa Mountains, the Mahācakravāḍa Mountains, or Mount Sumeru; all were unified into a single buddha-field.
The ground of jewels was level and even, covered everywhere by jeweled latticed canopies;
banners and parasols were suspended, great precious incense was burned, and celestial jewel flowers were strewn across the entire surface.

At that time, the Buddhas who were emanations of Śākyamuni Buddha from the east—in lands as numerous as the sands of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Ganges Rivers—each preaching the Dharma, assembled here;
in this manner, the Buddhas of the ten directions all successively gathered and took their seats in the eight directions.
At that time, in each of the ten directions, there were four million billion nayutas of lands filled with Tathāgatas, Buddhas.

At that moment, each of these Buddhas sat beneath a jeweled tree upon a lion throne and sent their attendants to inquire after the well-being of Śākyamuni Buddha. Each attendant brought a handful of precious flowers and said to them:
"O sons of good family!
Go to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa to where the Buddha Śākyamuni is, and speak these words on my behalf:
"Are you free from illness and affliction? Are you physically strong and at ease? And are the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas all dwelling in peace and security?"
Scattering these precious flowers as an offering to the Buddha, he spoke these words:
"That certain Buddha [named so-and-so] sends his consent to open this jeweled stūpa.
The Buddhas dispatched their messengers in this same manner.

At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha, seeing that the buddhas who had been emanated as his分身 (emanations) had all assembled and were each seated upon lion thrones, and hearing that all those buddhas desired him to open the precious stupa together with them, immediately rose from his seat and stood in mid-air.
The entire fourfold assembly rose, joined their palms, and gazed upon the Buddha with single-minded devotion.

Thereupon, Śākyamuni Buddha opened the door of the seven-jeweled stupa with his right finger, producing a great sound like that of a massive city gate being swung open after its bolts and keys have been removed.

At that moment, the entire assembly saw the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna seated upon a lion throne within the jeweled stupa, his physical body intact and undispersed, as if he had entered into meditative absorption.
Furthermore, he heard these words:
"Excellent, excellent,
Śākyamuni Buddha!"
"Quickly speak this Lotus Sūtra! It is for the sake of hearing this sūtra that I have come here.

At that time, the fourfold assembly, seeing the Buddha who had entered parinirvāṇa immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas ago speaking these words, marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. They scattered heaps of celestial jewel-flowers over the Buddha Prabhūtaratna and Śākyamuni Buddha.
At that time, within the jeweled stupa, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna offered half of his seat to Śākyamuni Buddha and spoke these words: “Śākyamuni Buddha!
"You may take this seat.
Thereupon, Śākyamuni Buddha entered the stūpa and sat upon half of the seat, assuming the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
At that time, the great assembly saw the two Tathāgatas seated in the full lotus posture upon lion thrones within the seven-jeweled stūpa, and each thought to themselves:
"The Buddha’s seat is high and remote; we pray that the Tathāgata, by means of his supernormal powers, will cause us all to dwell together in the void.
Immediately, Śākyamuni Buddha, by means of his supernormal powers, received the great assembly and placed them all in the void, and with a great voice he universally addressed the fourfold assembly:
"Who among you is able to extensively expound the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* in this Sahā world? Now is precisely the right time."
"The Tathāgata will before long enter parinirvāṇa; the Buddha wishes to entrust this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to those who shall uphold it.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Holy Lord, the World-Honored One, though he has long since entered extinction, remains within the jeweled stupa."
He has come for the sake of the Dharma;
why do you all not strive diligently for the sake of the Dharma?
Since the parinirvāṇa of this Buddha, throughout incalculable kalpas, he has listened to the Dharma everywhere.
Because they are difficult to encounter, by virtue of that Buddha’s original vow: "After my parinirvāṇa, wherever I may go, [may you] always listen to the Dharma for me."
Furthermore, my emanations— immeasurable Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges— have come desiring to hear the Dharma.
Having seen the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, they have each relinquished their wondrous lands,
along with their assemblies of disciples, devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits, and all matters of offering.
To cause the Dharma to abide for a long time, I have come here.
For the sake of the seated Buddhas, by means of my supernatural powers, I have moved immeasurable multitudes and purified this land.
Each of the Buddhas individually proceeds beneath the jewel trees,
like a pure pond adorned with lotuses.
The Buddhas sit upon them, their radiance providing magnificent adornment, as if in the midst of the dark night.
He kindles a great torch of fire;
from his body issues a wondrous fragrance that pervades the lands of the ten directions. Sentient beings who are perfumed by it are overcome with joy beyond measure.
It is like a great wind blowing against the branches of small trees;
by this expedient means, he causes the Dharma to endure for a long time.
He addressed the great assembly:
"After my parinirvāṇa, who will be able to protect, uphold, read, and recite this sutra?
Now, before the Buddha, let each of you speak your own vow."
Although that Buddha Prabhūtaratna has long since entered parinirvāṇa, he utters the lion’s roar by virtue of his great vow.
You should know this intention: that of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, of my own person, and of all the emanated Buddhas who have gathered here.
O sons of the Buddhas, whoever among you is able to protect the Dharma should make a great vow so that it may endure for a long time.
Whoever is able to protect this sutra and its Dharma is thereby making an offering to me and to Prabhūtaratna.
This Buddha Prabhūtaratna, dwelling within the jeweled stupa, constantly travels throughout the ten directions.
For the sake of this sutra, he likewise makes offerings to all the manifested Buddhas who come, and to those who adorn and illuminate all the worlds.
If one preaches this sutra, then one sees me, the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna,
and all the manifested Buddhas.
O sons of good family!
Reflect deeply upon this: it is a difficult task, and you should resolve to make a great vow.
Although other sūtras exist in numbers as vast as the sands of the Ganges, even to expound those is not yet considered difficult.
If one were to take up Mount Sumeru and hurl it to other regions across countless Buddha-fields,
that would not yet be difficult.
If one were to move the great trichiliocosm with a single toe and cast it far away to another land, that too would not yet be difficult.
To stand at the Peak of Existence and expound for the multitude immeasurable other sutras is not yet difficult; but if,
after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one is able to preach this sutra amidst an evil age,
that indeed is difficult.
Even if someone were to grasp empty space with their hands and travel about, it would not be difficult;
but after my parinirvāṇa, if one were to write this down oneself or cause another to write it, that indeed would be difficult.
If one were to take the great earth and place it upon the tip of a toenail, then ascend to the Brahma Heaven,
this would not yet be difficult.
But after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, in this degenerate age, to read this sutra even for a moment— this indeed is difficult.
Even if one were to carry dry grass into the conflagration at the end of an eon and not be burned by it, that would not yet be difficult.
But after my parinirvāṇa, if one upholds this sutra and explains it for even a single person—
that indeed will be difficult.
To expound the twelve divisions of the sūtras for others, causing all listeners to attain the six supernormal powers— though one can do this, it is not yet difficult.
After my parinirvāṇa, to hear and receive this sutra, and to inquire into its meaning and intent—
this indeed is difficult. Even if immeasurable and innumerable beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, were to attain arhatship, [it would still be more difficult than this].
To possess the six supernormal powers, though such benefits exist, is not yet difficult. But after my parinirvāṇa,
if one can receive, uphold, and recite a sutra such as this,
that indeed will be difficult.
From the beginning until now, I have extensively expounded various sutras;
among them all, this sutra is the foremost.
If there are those who can uphold it, they shall be upholding the body of the Buddha.
"O sons of good family!
After my parinirvāṇa, who among you is able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra? Now, before the Buddha, speak your own vow."
This sutra is difficult to uphold; if one upholds it even for a moment, I shall rejoice, and all Buddhas likewise.
Such a person is praised by all Buddhas.
This is indeed valor; this is indeed diligence; this is called upholding the precepts.
For one who practices the dhūtas, the unsurpassed path of the Buddha will be swiftly attained.
Those who, in a future age, are able to read and uphold this sutra are true sons of the Buddha,
dwelling on the ground of pure goodness.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who can understand its meaning are the eyes of all devas and humans in the world.
"In this world of fear, those who can preach [this] for even a moment—every deva and human being should offer them worship.
**Chapter Twelve: Devadatta** At that time, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly of devas and humans:
"In the past, throughout immeasurable kalpas, I sought the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* without ever becoming weary."
Throughout many kalpas, he constantly served as a king, making vows to seek unsurpassed bodhi with a mind that never regressed.

Desiring to fulfill the six pāramitās, he diligently practiced giving with a heart free from stinginess, not sparing elephants, horses, the seven treasures, kingdoms, cities, wives, children, slaves, servants, heads, eyes, marrow, brains, bodies, flesh, hands, or feet, nor begrudging his own life.

At that time, the lifespan of the people of the world was immeasurable. For the sake of the Dharma, he renounced his royal throne and entrusted the administration to his crown prince. He beat a drum to proclaim a decree throughout the four quarters, seeking the Dharma:
"Whoever can expound the Mahāyāna for me, I shall serve as their attendant for the rest of my life."
At that time, there was a rishi who came and said to the king:
"I possess a Mahāyāna sūtra called the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
If you do not oppose me, I shall proclaim it for you."

Upon hearing the words of the seer, the king was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he immediately followed the seer, providing all that was required—gathering fruit, drawing water, collecting firewood, and preparing food—even using his own body as a bed and seat—serving him with body and mind untiring.
For a thousand years, for the sake of the Dharma, he served him with diligent effort, ensuring that he lacked nothing.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“I recall a past kalpa, when, for the sake of seeking the Great Dharma,..."
Though he was the king of the world, he did not crave the pleasures of the five desires.
He struck the bell to proclaim to the four quarters: "Who possesses the Great Dharma?
If you can explain it for me, I shall become your servant."
At that time, there was the seer Asita, who came and addressed the Great King:
"I possess a subtle and wondrous Dharma, rare in this world.
If you are able to practice it, I shall explain it for you."
At that time, having heard the words of the seer, the king’s heart was filled with great joy;
he immediately followed the seer and provided all that was required,
gathering firewood and fruits and melons, respectfully offering them according to the season.
Because their hearts are set upon the sublime Dharma, their bodies and minds never know weariness.
For the sake of all sentient beings, they diligently seek the Great Dharma;
nor do they do so for their own sake, nor for the pleasures of the five desires.
"Therefore, having been a great king, I diligently sought and obtained this Dharma;
consequently, I attained Buddhahood, and for that reason, I now preach it to you.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“The king at that time was none other than myself;
the rishi of that time was Devadatta.

It is because of Devadatta as a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) that I have fulfilled the six pāramitās, the [four immeasurables of] loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, the purple-golden hue, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four methods of attraction, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha’s supernatural powers, thereby attaining equal and perfect enlightenment and extensively delivering sentient beings—all this is due to Devadatta as a spiritual friend.”
He addressed the fourfold assembly:

"Devadatta, after the passing of immeasurable kalpas, shall attain Buddhahood, and his name shall be Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, titled 'Devarāja'."
The world was named Celestial Path (*Devamārga*).

At that time, the Buddha Heavenly King (*Devarāja*) remained in the world for twenty intermediate kalpas, extensively preaching the sublime Dharma for the sake of sentient beings. Sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges attained the fruit of Arhatship; immeasurable sentient beings gave rise to the mind of a Pratyekabuddha; and sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges gave rise to the mind of the Unsurpassed Way, attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), and reached the stage of non-retrogression.
After the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha Devendra, the True Dharma remained in the world for twenty intermediate kalpas.

A stūpa made of the seven precious jewels was erected over his entire body relics, sixty yojanas in height and forty yojanas in length and breadth. Immeasurable sentient beings attained the fruit of arhatship; immeasurable sentient beings awakened to the path of pratyekabuddhahood; and inconceivable numbers of sentient beings gave rise to the bodhicitta and reached the stage of non-retrogression.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

They shall be born before the Buddhas of the ten directions, and in every place where they are born, they shall always hear this sutra."
"If you are born among humans or devas, you shall experience supreme and wondrous bliss; if you are before the Buddha, you shall be born by transformation upon a lotus flower.
At that time, the bodhisattva named Zhijī (Jñānakūṭa), who had followed the World-Honored One Prabhūtaratna from the lower regions, addressed the Buddha Prabhūtaratna:

Śākyamuni Buddha said to Jñānakośa:
"Son of good family,

Before he had finished speaking, countless bodhisattvas, seated upon precious lotus flowers, emerged from the sea and ascended to Vulture Peak Mountain, where they remained suspended in mid-air.
These bodhisattvas have all been transformed and delivered by Mañjuśrī; they are fully endowed with the practices of a bodhisattva and together discourse upon the six pāramitās.
These individuals who were originally śrāvakas were teaching the practices of the śrāvakas while in mid-air; now they all practice the meaning of the Great Vehicle’s emptiness.
Mañjuśrī said to Jñatikauṇḍinya:

At that time, the Bodhisattva Jñānakośa praised him with these verses:

"Expounding the meaning of the true reality (*tathatā*), revealing the Dharma of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*),

"This sūtra is extremely profound and subtle, a jewel among all sūtras, rare in the world."
“Are there any sentient beings who, by applying themselves with diligent vigor and practicing this sutra, can quickly attain Buddhahood?

Deeply entering meditative concentration and thoroughly comprehending all phenomena, they give rise to the bodhicitta in a single moment and attain the stage of non-retrogression with unimpeded eloquence.

Cherishing sentient beings with compassion as if they were their own infants, they are fully endowed with merit; what their minds contemplate and their mouths express is subtle, wondrous, and vast. He contemplates the trichiliocosm and sees that there is not even a space as small as a mustard seed where he has not sacrificed his body and life for the sake of sentient beings; only after this does he attain the path of Bodhi.

The subtle and wondrous pure Dharma-body, Endowed with the thirty-two marks And adorned with the eighty secondary characteristics, Thus adorning the Dharma-body.

He replied, "Very quickly.
The woman said:

At that time, the entire assembly saw the dragon girl suddenly transform into a man, fully endowed with the practices of a bodhisattva. She immediately proceeded to the stainless world in the south, where she sat upon a precious lotus flower and attained equal and perfect enlightenment. Adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, she extensively expounded the wondrous Dharma for all sentient beings throughout the ten directions.

At that time, the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings, as well as humans and non-humans in the Sahā world, all saw from afar that the dragon girl had attained Buddhahood and was preaching the Dharma for the sake of the assembly of gods and humans. Immeasurable sentient beings, having heard the Dharma, attained realization and reached the stage of non-retrogression;
immeasurable sentient beings received the prediction of their future enlightenment.
The Stainless World shook in six ways.

In this Sahā world, three thousand sentient beings dwelt on the stage of non-retrogression, and three thousand sentient beings gave rise to the bodhicitta and received their predictions of enlightenment.
The Bodhisattva Jñānakūṭa, Śāriputra, and the entire assembly accepted this with silent faith.

"After the Buddha's parinirvāṇa, we shall uphold, recite, and expound this sutra.

“World-Honored One!

Because in this Sahā world, people are for the most part depraved and evil; they harbor overweening pride, their merit is meager, and their minds are turbid with anger, deceitful, and crooked, lacking sincerity.

Now, if you wish to know your own prediction: in a future age, amidst the teachings of sixty-eight thousand billion Buddhas, you shall become a great Dharma teacher, as shall six thousand bhikṣuṇīs, both those in training and those beyond training."

In this way, you shall gradually fulfill the bodhisattva path and attain buddhahood, with the name Sarvasattvapriyadarśana Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
“Kauṭamī! This Buddha Sarvasattvapriyadarśana and the six thousand bodhisattvas will, in successive order, receive the prediction of their attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā, mother of Rāhula, thought to herself:
"Among those who have received predictions [of enlightenment], the World-Honored One alone has not mentioned my name."
The Buddha told Yaśodharā:

"In future ages, amidst the teachings of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, you shall cultivate the bodhisattva practices, serve as a great Dharma teacher, and gradually perfect the path to Buddhahood."

In the land of Sukhāvatī, you shall attain Buddhahood, receiving the title Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, named Kūṭastha-koṭi-raśmi-lakṣaṇa.
“The lifespan of the Buddha shall be immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī and the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā, together with their retinues, were all filled with great joy at having attained what they had never experienced before. They then spoke these verses before the Buddha:
“O World-Honored One, Guide, Who brings peace and security to devas and humans, We have heard this prophecy;”
"Their minds are fully endowed with peace.
After the bhikṣuṇīs had spoken this verse, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"We, too, are able to widely proclaim this sutra in other lands.
At that time, the World-Honored One gazed upon eight hundred trillion nayutas of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

These bodhisattvas—all of whom were *avaivartika*, had turned the wheel of non-retrogression, and had attained various *dhāraṇīs*—immediately rose from their seats, went before the Buddha, joined their palms with single-minded devotion, and thought to themselves:
"If the World-Honored One commands us to uphold and proclaim this sutra, we shall widely disseminate this Dharma in accordance with the Buddha's teaching."
Again, they thought:
"The Buddha now remains silent and has given no instruction; what should we do?
At that time, the Bodhisattvas, out of reverence for the Buddha’s intention and desiring to fulfill their own original vows, made a lion’s roar before the Buddha and uttered this oath:
“World-Honored One!

After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, we shall travel back and forth throughout the worlds of the ten directions, enabling sentient beings to copy this sutra, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, explain its meaning, practice according to the Dharma, and maintain right mindfulness—all through the majestic power of the Buddha.”
"We only pray that the World-Honored One will behold us from afar in other lands and protect us.
Thereupon, all the bodhisattvas raised their voices in unison and spoke in verse:
"We only pray that you do not worry Regarding the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa."
In this terrifying and evil age, we shall preach extensively.
Should there be those who lack wisdom and revile us with harsh words,
or even attack us with swords and staves, we shall endure it all.
In this degenerate age, there are bhikṣus whose minds are crooked with false wisdom;
claiming what they have not attained as attained, they are filled with the pride of self-conceit.
Some may dwell in forest hermitages, wearing patched robes in secluded places.
Claiming for themselves that they practice the true path, they look down upon those in the human world.
Because of their greed for gain and offerings, they preach the Dharma to laypeople and are venerated by the world as if they were arhats with the six supernormal powers.
This person harbors an evil mind and constantly dwells on worldly matters;
while falsely claiming to be an *āraṇyaka*, he delights in exposing our faults and speaks thus:
"These bhikṣus, for the sake of craving gain and offerings, preach the discourses of external paths;
they compose these sūtras themselves to delude and mislead the people of the world,
and for the sake of seeking fame and renown, they analyze this sūtra."
Constantly amidst the great assemblies, desiring to disparage us,
they speak ill of us to kings, ministers, brahmins, householders, and other groups of monks.
They are people of false views, preaching the discourses of external paths.
Out of reverence for the Buddha, we endure all these evils.
Because of such words of contempt as, "You are all Buddhas," [we remain patient].
Such words of contempt and disdain, one should endure them all.
In this defiled age of evil, there are many terrors;
malevolent spirits enter their bodies and revile, abuse, and insult me.
We revere and have faith in the Buddha;
we shall don the armor of patience, and for the sake of expounding this sutra, endure all these hardships.

may the World-Honored One himself know this.

Chapter Fourteen: On Peaceful Conduct. At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, Prince of the Dharma, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

These bodhisattvas are truly rare and extraordinary; out of reverence and compliance with the Buddha, they have made a great vow to protect, uphold, read, and recite this Lotus Sutra in the evil world of the future.
“World-Honored One!
How can a bodhisattva-mahāsattva preach this sutra in the evil age to come?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to preach this sutra in the future evil age, they should dwell securely in four dharmas.
First, by dwelling securely in the bodhisattva’s sphere of practice and sphere of association, they will be able to expound this sutra for the sake of sentient beings.”
“Mañjuśrī! What is called the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the ground of patience, being gentle, compliant, and harmonious without being abrupt or violent, and his mind is not startled;”

Furthermore, while not engaging with any phenomena, one contemplates all phenomena as they truly are; neither engaging nor discriminating—this is called the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
What is called the "sphere of association" for a bodhisattva mahāsattva?

A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not associate with kings, princes, ministers, or high officials; nor does he associate with various non-Buddhist brahmins, such as the Nirgranthas, nor with those who compose secular literary works, praise foreign scriptures, or follow the Lokāyatas and the Prati-Lokāyatas.
Furthermore, he does not associate with those engaged in violent games, wrestling, boxing, or various types of acrobatic performances such as those of the Nara-dancers.
Furthermore, one should not associate with outcastes (caṇḍāla), nor with those who raise pigs, sheep, chickens, or dogs, nor with hunters, fishermen, or those engaged in other such evil occupations.
If such persons should occasionally come to him, he should preach the Dharma for them without harboring any expectation of reward.
Furthermore, they do not associate with or even inquire after śrāvaka bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās;
nor do they dwell together with them, whether in a cell, on a walking path, or within a lecture hall.
When someone comes at any time, he should preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate, without seeking anything for himself. "Mañjuśrī!
Furthermore, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should not take up the signs of a woman's body that can give rise to thoughts of desire while preaching the Dharma to her, nor should he delight in seeing her."
If one enters the home of another, one should not converse with young girls, virgins, widows, and the like.

Furthermore, one should not associate closely with the five kinds of impotent persons. One should not enter the home of another alone; however, if there is a necessary reason to enter alone, one should simply maintain single-minded mindfulness of the Buddha.
If one preaches the Dharma for a woman, one should not smile showing one's teeth nor reveal one's chest; even for the sake of the Dharma, one should not become intimate, let alone for other matters.
He does not delight in keeping young disciples, śrāmaṇeras, or children, nor does he delight in having the same teacher as them.
He always prefers to practice dhyāna, dwelling in seclusion to cultivate and collect his mind.
"Mañjuśrī! This is called the first stage of close approach.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates all phenomena as empty, according to their true mark—uninverted, immovable, non-retrogressive, and non-revolving—like space, having the nature of non-existence."

All paths of linguistic expression are severed; it is unborn, unemerged, and unarisen; nameless and signless; truly non-existent; immeasurable and boundless; unobstructed and unimpeded. It exists only through causes and conditions, and is spoken of as such because it arises from inversion.
“Constantly observing the characteristics of dharmas in this way is called the second place of intimacy for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“If there is a bodhisattva, In the evil world of the future, Who possesses a heart free from fear...”
One who wishes to expound this sutra should enter into the proper sphere of conduct and the spheres of association.
One should always keep far away from kings, princes, ministers, and high officials;
from those engaged in cruel games, as well as from caṇḍālas and non-Buddhist brahmins.

[one must remain cautious].
The Bodhisattva, with a mind free from fear and harboring no expectations, shall preach the Dharma.

one engages in inverted discrimination regarding the existence or non-existence of all phenomena, whether they are real or unreal, and whether they are produced or unproduced.

he contemplates all phenomena as being utterly non-existent, like empty space,

After my parinirvāṇa, those who enter this sphere of practice and this proximate station will have no fear or weakness when preaching this sutra.
