after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, if one wishes to preach this sutra during the period of the Final Dharma, one should abide in the practice of peaceful dwelling."
Whether preaching orally or reading the scriptures, one should not take pleasure in speaking of the faults of others or of the sūtras.
Furthermore, one should not treat other Dharma masters with contempt, nor speak of the likes and dislikes, or the strengths and weaknesses, of others.

Regarding śrāvakas as well, one does not mention their names to speak of their faults or evils, nor does one mention their names to praise their virtues; furthermore, one does not give rise to thoughts of resentment or aversion.

Because they have skillfully cultivated such a mind of peace and bliss, no listeners will oppose their intentions; when questioned or challenged, they do not answer with the teachings of the Hīnayāna, but explain only through the Mahāyāna, enabling them to attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Bodhisattvas always delight in preaching the Dharma with peace and security;
upon pure ground, they provide seats."
Wearing new, clean robes, pure both within and without, he sits securely upon the Dharma-seat and speaks according to the questions asked.
To the upāsakas and upāsikās, as well as to kings and princes—
To the assembly of ministers, officials, and citizens, he explained the subtle and profound meaning with a serene countenance.
Should there be any questions or inquiries, he answered in accordance with the principles, elaborating and analyzing them through causes, conditions, and parables.
By these skillful means, they cause all to resolve their minds [on enlightenment]; gradually increasing [their merit], they enter the Buddha-way.
They eliminate sloth and indolence, as well as thoughts of laziness; free from all grief and affliction, they preach the Dharma with a compassionate heart.
Day and night he constantly expounds the unsurpassed teaching of the Way;
through various causes and conditions and immeasurable parables, he reveals it to sentient beings, causing them all to rejoice.
Regarding robes, bedding, food, drink, and medical provisions, they harbor no expectations therein.
With single-minded devotion,
they contemplate only the causes and conditions for expounding the Dharma, vowing to attain the Buddha-way and to cause all beings to do likewise.
This is indeed a great benefit and a source of peace and joy for making offerings.
After my parinirvāṇa, if there should be any bhikṣu who is able to expound this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, [he shall receive such rewards].
There are no afflictions or obstacles, nor is there any sorrow; there is no one who reviles,
nor is there any fear of being struck with swords, staves, and the like, nor is there any expulsion,
because they abide securely in patience.
The wise one who thus skillfully cultivates the mind can abide in peace and happiness, as I have explained above.
The merit of such a person could not be fully described even through calculation or analogy throughout ten million billion kalpas.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

When the Dharma is about to perish in the final age at the end of time, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra must not harbor thoughts of jealousy, flattery, or deceit; nor should they disparage or revile those who study the Buddha-way, seeking out their faults."

If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās—whether they seek the path of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, or the bodhisattva—you must not trouble them or cause them doubt and regret by saying to them:
"You are very far from the Way; you will never be able to attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā)."
Why is this? Because you are a person of negligence, being indolent regarding the Path.
Furthermore, you should not engage in frivolous speculation about phenomena or enter into disputes and contention.

One should conceive the thought of great compassion toward all sentient beings, the thought of a loving father toward all Tathāgatas, and the thought of a great teacher toward all Bodhisattvas; one should always, with a profound mind, pay homage and prostrate to the great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions.

To all sentient beings, he teaches the Dharma with equanimity; because it accords with the Dharma, he speaks neither too much nor too little, and even for those who deeply love the Dharma, he does not speak excessively.

“Mañjuśrī! When the Dharma is about to perish in the final age at the end of time, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have accomplished this third practice of peace and happiness will, when preaching this Dharma, be unable to be disturbed or distracted. They will obtain good companions with whom they may together read and recite this sutra; they will also attract great assemblies who come to listen and receive it. Having heard it, they are able to uphold it; having upheld it, they are able to recite it; having recited it, they are able to explain it; and having explained it, they are able to write it down or cause others to write it down, making offerings to the scripture scrolls, and treating them with reverence, respect, and praise.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If one wishes to preach this sutra, One should abandon envy, anger, pride, Flattery, deception,
and a crooked or false mind, And constantly cultivate straightforward conduct."
Do not despise others, nor engage in frivolous discourse about the Dharma;
do not cause others to doubt or regret by saying, "You shall not attain Buddhahood.
Such is the teaching of the Buddha's sons: they are always gentle, flexible, and patient.
Compassionate toward all, they never give rise to a mind of indolence.
The great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions practice the Path out of pity for sentient beings;
one should generate a heart of reverence toward them, for they are my Great Teachers.
Toward all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, one should conceive the thought of them as one’s unsurpassed father;
having destroyed the mind of pride, one preaches the Dharma without obstruction.
This third dharma is thus; the wise should guard it.
With a single mind practicing peaceful conduct, he is revered by immeasurable multitudes.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

When the Dharma is about to perish in the final age at the end of time, there may be those who uphold this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Toward those who are householders or renunciants, they should give rise to a heart of great loving-kindness; toward those who are not bodhisattvas, they should give rise to a heart of great compassion. They should form this thought:
"Such a person has suffered a great loss.

The Tathāgata teaches the Dharma through skillful means according to what is appropriate; yet they have not heard it, do not know it, and are not awakened to it; they have not asked about it, do not believe it, and do not understand it. Although such a person does not ask about, believe in, or understand this sutra, when I attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, wherever they may be, I shall draw them in by the power of my supernormal faculties and wisdom, causing them to dwell within this Dharma."

“Mañjuśrī! After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, any bodhisattva mahāsattva who accomplishes this fourth dharma will be free from fault when preaching this teaching. They shall always be provided with offerings, honored, respected, revered, and praised by bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, kings, princes, ministers, commoners, brahmins, householders, and others.”
The devas of the void also constantly attend upon him for the sake of hearing the Dharma.

Whether he is in a village, a city, or a secluded forest, if there are those who come to pose difficult questions, the devas will constantly protect him day and night for the sake of the Dharma, enabling all listeners to attain joy.
Why is this? Because this sutra is protected by the spiritual power of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present. Mañjuśrī!
"In immeasurable lands, even the name of this Lotus Sūtra cannot be heard, let alone being seen, upheld, read, or recited. "Mañjuśrī!..."

For example, suppose a powerful Wheel-Turning Sage King (cakravartin-rāja) desires to subdue various kingdoms through his majestic power, yet the minor kings do not obey his commands; at that time, the Wheel-Turning King raises various armies and goes forth to punish them.

When the king saw that his soldiers had performed meritorious deeds in battle, he was filled with great joy and bestowed rewards according to their merit: some were granted fields, houses, villages, and towns;
some were given clothing and ornaments for the body;
and some were given various kinds of rare treasures.
Gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, coral, amber, elephants, horses, chariots, servants, and subjects—of all these he gave them away;
yet the bright pearl from within his topknot, he did not give to them.
Why is this? This single jewel is found only upon the crown of the King’s head; if he were to give it to him, the King’s entire retinue would surely be greatly astonished and amazed. "Mañjuśrī!..."

The Tathāgata is also like this: having attained the kingdom of the Dharma through the power of meditative concentration and wisdom, he reigns as king over the three realms, yet the various Māra kings refuse to submit and obey him.

When the Tathāgata and his noble and holy generals engage in battle with them, he rejoices in the hearts of those who have performed meritorious deeds; amidst the fourfold assembly, he preaches various sūtras for them to gladden their minds, bestowing upon them the wealth of dhyāna-concentration, liberation, the untainted faculties and powers, and all dharmas. Furthermore, he grants them the city of nirvāṇa, declaring that they have attained extinction (parinirvāṇa), thereby guiding their minds and causing them all to rejoice—yet he does not preach this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for them.

“Mañjuśrī! It is like a wheel-turning monarch who, seeing among his troops those who have performed great service, feels profound joy and bestows upon them this difficult-to-believe jewel—a jewel he has long kept within his topknot and never carelessly given to others—now granting it to them.”
The Tathāgata is likewise thus: he is the Great Dharma King within the triple world, teaching and transforming all sentient beings through the Dharma.

When he sees the army of noble sages fighting against the Māra of the five aggregates, the Māra of afflictions, and the Māra of death, achieving great meritorious feats—extinguishing the three poisons, escaping the triple world, and shattering the net of Māra—the Tathāgata then experiences great joy as well.
This Lotus Sutra can enable sentient beings to reach all-knowledge; though it is full of enmity and difficult to believe in all the worlds, that which was not previously taught is now being taught.

Mañjuśrī! This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the foremost teaching of all Tathāgatas; among all teachings, it is the most profound. It is bestowed at the very end, just as a powerful king who has long guarded a bright jewel now finally grants it to another.

Mañjuśrī! This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the secret treasury of all the Tathāgatas; it stands supreme among all sūtras. Having guarded it throughout the long night without proclaiming it recklessly, I now, for the first time, expound it to you and others.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Always practicing patience and compassion for all beings, one is then able to expound the sutras praised by the Buddha."
Toward those who have left home from their families, as well as those who are not bodhisattvas, one should give rise to compassion;
for it would be a great loss if such people do not hear this sutra and do not believe in it.
When I attain the Way of the Buddha, I shall, by means of various skillful expedients, preach this Dharma for them,
so that they may abide therein.
Just as those who have merit in battle are rewarded with all manner of goods— elephants, horses, and chariots—
Adornments for the body, as well as fields and houses, villages and cities, or garments,
various kinds of rare treasures, slaves, and wealth—
these he joyfully bestows.
If there is one who is brave and capable of performing difficult deeds, the King unties the bright pearl from within his topknot and bestows it upon him.
As a Dharma King for all, possessing the great power of forbearance and the treasure-trove of wisdom,
he transforms the world through the Dharma with great compassion.
Seeing all people undergoing various sufferings and afflictions, desiring liberation, and battling against the various Māras—
for the sake of these sentient beings, he preaches various dharmas and, through great skillful means, teaches these sūtras.
Having already known the sentient beings and gained their capacity, he finally, at the very end, preaches this Lotus Sūtra;
it is like a king who unties his topknot and gives them the bright pearl.
I have constantly guarded [this teaching] and did not reveal it recklessly; now is the very time to speak it for you all.
Those who desire peace and security should approach [this teaching] as they expound this sutra.
By these four dharmas,
moreover, one will be free from illness, one’s complexion will be bright and pure, and one will not be born into poverty,
lowliness, or ugliness.
Sentient beings delight in seeing him, as if yearning for a sage; the sons of the gods serve as his attendants.
Weapons do not strike him, nor can poisons harm him; if someone reviles him with evil words, that person's mouth shall be closed.
Wandering with fearlessness, like a lion king; with the light of wisdom, like the shining sun.
Even in dreams, they see only auspicious things.
He beholds all the Tathāgatas seated upon lion thrones,
surrounded by assemblies of bhikṣus as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, preaching the Dharma; with palms joined in reverence, he sees his own body [therein].
He then preached the Dharma for them,
emitting immeasurable light that illuminated all things, and expounded all dharmas with the voice of Brahmā.
Seeing himself situated therein, he joined his palms in praise of the Buddha;
hearing the Dharma with joy, he made offerings, attained dhāraṇī, and realized non-retrogressive wisdom.
The Buddha, knowing their minds and that they had deeply entered the path of the Buddhas, immediately bestowed upon them the prediction of their attainment of supreme perfect enlightenment:
"O sons of good family!..."
In a future age, you shall attain immeasurable wisdom and the Great Way of the Buddha;
your land shall be adorned and pure, vast and beyond compare.
There were also the fourfold assembly, with palms joined, listening to the Dharma. Again,
he saw himself in mountain forests, practicing wholesome dharmas, realizing all true marks,
entering deeply into meditative concentration, and beholding the Buddhas of the ten directions.
The bodies of all Buddhas are golden in color, adorned with the marks of a hundred blessings;
hearing the Dharma and preaching it for others, one always has such auspicious dreams.
Furthermore, one dreams of becoming a king, who renounces his palace, harem, and retinue.
Accompanied by the five most sublime sensual pleasures, he proceeded to the site of enlightenment.
Seated upon the lion throne beneath the Bodhi tree,
he sought the Way for seven days and attained the wisdom of all Buddhas.
Having attained the unsurpassed path, he arose and turned the wheel of Dharma,
preaching the Dharma for the fourfold assembly throughout thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas;
he expounded the subtle Dharma free from outflows, delivering immeasurable sentient beings.
In the future, when entering nirvana, like a lamp extinguished when the smoke has ended;
if, in a future evil age, one preaches this foremost Dharma,
that person shall obtain great benefit, possessing all the merits mentioned above.

Chapter Fifteen: The Emergence from the Earth At that time, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had come from other lands, numbering more than the sands of eight Ganges Rivers, rose from their seats within the great assembly, joined their palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

If you would permit us, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, to apply ourselves with diligent vigor in this Sahā world to protect, uphold, recite, copy, and make offerings to this sutra, we shall extensively expound it in this land.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas:
"Cease, sons of good family!
There is no need for you to protect and uphold this sutra."

Why is this? Within my Sahā world, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the sands of sixty thousand Ganges Rivers; each of these bodhisattvas has a retinue as numerous as the sands of sixty thousand Ganges Rivers. These individuals will be able, after my parinirvāṇa, to protect, uphold, recite, and extensively expound this sutra.

When the Buddha had spoken these words, the ground of the three thousandfold great thousandfold world-system of the Sahā universe quaked and split open; from within it, immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas simultaneously leapt forth.
These bodhisattvas all have golden bodies, possess the thirty-two marks, and emit immeasurable light; they previously resided here, beneath this Sahā world, dwelling within the space of this realm.
These bodhisattvas, having heard the voice spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha, came ascending from below.
Each and every one of these bodhisattvas was a leader among the great assemblies, each bringing with them a retinue equal to sixty thousand Ganges-sands;
let alone those who brought retinues equal to fifty thousand, forty thousand, thirty thousand, twenty thousand, or ten thousand Ganges-sands.
How much more so for even one part in a *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [of sands], half a *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*, a quarter, or even one part in ten million billion *nayuta*s;
how much more so for ten million billion *nayuta*s of retinues;
how much more so for hundreds of millions of retinues?
How much more so those with ten million, a million, or even ten thousand;
how much more so those with one thousand, one hundred, or even ten;
and how much more so those who lead only five, four, three, two, or even a single disciple?
How much more so for those who dwell alone and delight in the practice of seclusion!
Such examples are immeasurable and boundless, beyond what can be known through calculation or analogy.
Once these bodhisattvas had emerged from the earth, they each proceeded to the space before the wondrous seven-jeweled stupa containing the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna and Śākyamuni Buddha.

Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the feet of the two World-Honored Ones. He then went before the Buddhas seated upon lion thrones beneath the various jewel trees and likewise paid homage to them all. Circumambulating them three times to the right, he joined his palms in reverence and praised them with the various modes of praise used by bodhisattvas. Standing to one side, he gazed up at the two World-Honored Ones with joyful devotion.

From the moment these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas first leaped forth, they praised the Buddha with various kinds of bodhisattva eulogies; such was the duration of time that passed, fifty intermediate kalpas.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha sat in silence, and the fourfold assembly likewise remained silent for fifty intermediate kalpas;
yet, through the Buddha’s supernatural power, he caused the great multitude to perceive the time as being like half a day.
At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, the fourfold assembly also saw all the bodhisattvas filling the voids of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of lands.
Within this assembly of bodhisattvas were four leaders:
the first was named Superior Conduct, the second Boundless Conduct, the third Pure Conduct, and the fourth Established Conduct.

These four bodhisattvas were the foremost leaders and guides among that assembly; standing before the great multitude, they each joined their palms together, gazed upon Śākyamuni Buddha, and inquired after his well-being, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
Are you free from much illness and affliction? Are you dwelling in peace and happiness?
Is it not difficult for those who are to be delivered to receive your instruction?
And do you not cause the World-Honored One any weariness?
At that time, the four great bodhisattvas spoke in verse:
“World-Honored One, you are at ease, with little illness and little affliction; in teaching and transforming sentient beings, you have attained freedom from weariness.”
"Furthermore, are these sentient beings easy to transform?
Will you not cause the World-Honored One to become weary?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these words amidst the great assembly of bodhisattvas:
“So it is, so it is! O sons of good family,
the Tathāgata is at ease, with little illness and little affliction;”
These sentient beings are easily transformed and delivered, without any weariness.

Why is this? Because throughout successive lifetimes, these sentient beings have constantly received my transformation; they have also made offerings to and honored past Buddhas, planting various roots of goodness.
When these sentient beings first see my body and hear what I preach, they all immediately believe and accept it, entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata—
with the exception of those who have previously practiced and studied the Hīnayāna.
“Such persons as these, I shall now also cause to hear this sutra and enter into the Buddha’s wisdom.
At that time, the great bodhisattvas spoke in verse:
“Excellent, excellent!”
"O Mahāvīra, World-Honored One!
These sentient beings are easily transformed and delivered.
They are able to inquire about the profound wisdom of the Buddhas, and having heard it, they believe and practice it; we rejoice in this."
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the foremost great bodhisattvas:
"Excellent, excellent!
O sons of good family!"
"You all are able to give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy toward the Tathāgata.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva and the assembly of bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of eight thousand Ganges Rivers, all had this thought:

"From the past until now, we have never seen nor heard of such a great multitude of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas suddenly emerging from the earth, standing before the World-Honored One, joining their palms in worship, making offerings, and inquiring after the Tathāgata’s well-being."

At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of eight thousand Ganges Rivers, and wishing to resolve his own doubts as well, joined his palms toward the Buddha and asked in verse: “O World-Honored One of Two Legs,
please explain this for the sake of the immeasurable thousands of myriads of kotis of the great assembly of bodhisattvas, whom none have ever seen before.”
From where have you come, and by what causes and conditions have you gathered here?
With a colossal body and great supernormal powers, your wisdom is inconceivable;
your resolve is firm and steadfast, and you possess the power of great forbearance.
Delightful for all sentient beings to behold, from where have you come?
Each and every one of these bodhisattvas, with the retinues they lead,
is beyond measure, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
There were great bodhisattvas who, together with a great assembly as numerous as sixty thousand Ganges sands,
sought the Buddha-way with a single mind.
These great teachers, numbering sixty thousand Ganges sands, [were all present].
They all came together to make offerings to the Buddha and to protect and uphold this sutra—
fifty thousand as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, with numbers even exceeding that;
forty thousand, thirty thousand, twenty thousand, down to ten thousand.
One thousand one hundred and so forth, up to as many as the sands of a single Ganges River,
or half, or three-quarters, or four-fifths; even a ten-millionth part of a billion,
or a hundred-thousand-nayuta, or ten-thousand-billion disciples.
Up to fifty million, and their number exceeds even that;
from one million down to ten thousand, one thousand and one hundred,
fifty and ten, and even down to three, two, and one.
Those who are alone without retinue, who delight in dwelling in solitude—
all have come to the presence of the Buddha, their number exceeding even that mentioned above.
If one were to count these great assemblies by means of tally sticks, [the total would be beyond measure].
Even throughout kalpas more numerous than the sands of the Ganges, one could not fully know them.
Who was it that preached the Dharma for these hosts of bodhisattvas of great majesty and virtue,
who through their diligence were taught and brought to fulfillment?
From whom did you first resolve to attain enlightenment?
What Buddha-dharma do you extol?
Which sutras do you uphold and practice?
"What Buddha-path have they cultivated?
Thus it was that these bodhisattvas, possessing great supernatural powers and wisdom,
all leaped forth from within as the earth in the four directions split and cracked open.
World-Honored One, since my past arrival, I have never before seen such a thing;
I pray you tell me from where they come and the name of their land.
Though I have constantly traveled through various countries, I have never before seen such an assembly.
Among this assembly, there is not a single person whom I recognize;
suddenly emerging from the earth, I pray you will explain the causes and conditions for this.
In this great assembly today, there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions.
These bodhisattvas all desire to know this matter;
these multitudes of bodhisattvas wish to understand the causal conditions from beginning to end.
World-Honored One of immeasurable virtue, we only pray that you will resolve the doubts of the assembly.

At that time, the emanated Buddhas of Śākyamuni who had come from immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of lands in other directions were seated cross-legged upon lion thrones beneath the various jeweled trees in the eight directions.
The attendants of those Buddhas each saw this great assembly of bodhisattvas emerging from the earth in the four directions of the trichiliocosm and abiding in the void.
Each addressed their respective Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
From where have these immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable multitudes of bodhisattvas come?"
At that time, each of those Buddhas addressed their respective attendants:
"Good sons, wait but a moment!

There is a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Maitreya—prophesied by Śākyamuni Buddha to be the next to attain Buddhahood—who has asked about this matter. The Buddha is now answering it; you yourselves shall hear it through him."
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva:
“Excellent, excellent! Ajita!”

That you are able to ask the Buddha about such a great matter as this—let all of you now be of one mind, don the armor of diligence, and resolve with firm intent; for the Tathāgata now wishes to reveal and proclaim the wisdom of all Buddhas, the sovereign power of supernatural faculties of all Buddhas, the lion-like prowess of all Buddhas, and the fierce, mighty power of all Buddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"You should be diligent and single-minded; I wish to speak of this matter.
Do not harbor doubt or regret, for the Buddha’s wisdom is inconceivable."
Now you must exert the power of faith and abide in the goodness of patience;
the Dharma never heard before, you shall now hear in its entirety.
I now comfort you: do not harbor doubt or fear.
The Buddha never speaks words that are not true; his wisdom is immeasurable.
The supreme Dharma he has attained is profoundly deep and difficult to discern;
I shall now explain it as it is—listen with a single-minded focus.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva:
“I now announce this to you all within this great assembly. Ajita!

These great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, immeasurable, innumerable, and incalculable, who have emerged from the earth and whom you have never seen before—since I attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in this Sahā world, I have taught, instructed, and guided these bodhisattvas, taming their minds and causing them to resolve upon the path to enlightenment.
All these bodhisattvas dwell beneath this Sahā world, in the space of this realm;
they read, recite, and master the various sūtras, reflecting upon them, analyzing them, and maintaining right mindfulness.
Ajita! These sons of good family do not delight in being among the multitude and speaking much;
they always delight in solitary places, practicing with diligent vigor without ever resting.
Nor do they dwell relying upon humans or devas.
They always delight in profound wisdom that is free from obstruction, and they also constantly delight in the teachings of all Buddhas, seeking unsurpassed insight with single-minded diligence.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Ajita, you should know:
For incalculable kalpas past, I have cultivated the Buddha’s wisdom."
All these have been transformed by me, causing them to resolve upon the mind of the Great Way. They are my children;
dwelling in this world, they constantly practice the dhūta austerities, finding their delight in secluded places.
Having abandoned the clamor of the great assembly, they take no pleasure in much speaking.
Such sons as these study my Way and Dharma;
day and night they are always diligent for the sake of seeking the Buddha-way.
In this Sahā world, dwelling in the space below,
his resolve and power are firm; he constantly and diligently seeks wisdom,
preaching various sublime dharmas with a mind free from fear.
In the city of Gayā, sitting beneath the Bodhi tree,
I attained supreme perfect enlightenment and turned the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
Only then did I teach and transform them, causing them to first give rise to the mind of the Way.
Now all abide in non-retrogression, and shall all attain Buddhahood.
I now speak these true words; you should believe them with one mind.
From long ago, I have been teaching and transforming this assembly.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva and countless other bodhisattvas felt doubt and wonder at such an unprecedented occurrence, and they thought to themselves:

"How is it that in such a short interval of time, the World-Honored One has taught and transformed these immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable numbers of great bodhisattvas, causing them to abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
When the Tathāgata was a prince, he departed from the palace of the Śākyas; not far from the city of Gayā, he sat at the site of enlightenment and attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
From that time until now, only a little more than forty years have passed.

World-Honored One, how is it that in such a short time you have performed such great Buddha-work? By means of the Buddha’s power and the Buddha’s merit, you have taught and transformed such an immeasurable multitude of great Bodhisattvas, who shall all attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
“World-Honored One!

If there are those with profound resolve, pure and upright,
who have heard much and are able to maintain it in memory, they will understand the Buddha’s words according to their meaning.
Such people as these have no doubt regarding this. Furthermore, Ajita,

if there are those who hear that the Buddha’s lifespan is long and far-reaching and understand the meaning of these words, the merit they obtain will be limitless, and they will be able to give rise to the unsurpassed wisdom of the Tathāgata.

How much more so for one who extensively hears this sutra, or causes others to hear it; whether they uphold it themselves or cause others to uphold it; whether they write it themselves or cause others to write it; or if they offer worship to the scroll with flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, flags, silk canopies, fragrant oils, and ghee lamps—the merit of such a person is immeasurable and boundless, and it can give rise to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).

“Ajita! If good sons or good daughters, upon hearing me speak of the long duration of my life-span, develop deep faith and understanding in their hearts, they shall see the Buddha always dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain, surrounded by a great assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, preaching the Dharma.”

Furthermore, he saw that this Sahā world had ground of lapis lazuli, level and even; the eight paths were demarcated by Jāmbūnada gold, with rows of jewel trees and all the terraces and towers constructed entirely of jewels, wherein the assembly of bodhisattvas all resided.
If there are those who can contemplate in this manner, you should know that this is the mark of profound faith and understanding.

Furthermore, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, if one hears this sutra and does not disparage it, but instead gives rise to a heart of sympathetic joy, you should know that this already constitutes the mark of profound faith and understanding; how much more so for those who read, recite, receive, and uphold it—such persons shall be as those who carry the Tathāgata upon their heads.
“Ajita! These good sons and good daughters need not further erect stupas and temples for my sake, nor build monasteries, nor provide the four requisites as offerings to the Sangha.”
Why is this? Because those sons and daughters of good family who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra have already erected stupas, constructed monasteries, and made offerings to the Sangha.

This would be equivalent to erecting a stupa of the seven precious jewels for the Buddha’s relics, high and wide, gradually tapering upward until reaching the Brahma-heaven, adorned with hanging banners, canopies, and various jeweled bells; offering flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, ointments, and burning incense; and providing various drums, music, flutes, pipes, lutes, and all manner of dances and performances, singing hymns and praises with exquisite sounds—having performed such offerings for immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas.

“Ajita! If, after my parinirvāṇa, there should be one who hears this sutra and is able to receive and uphold it—whether by writing it themselves or instructing others to write it—they shall have established a monastic dwelling, constructing thirty-two halls of red sandalwood, eight *tāla* trees in height, lofty, spacious, and magnificent. Within them shall dwell hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus; gardens, bathing pools, walking paths, and meditation caves, as well as robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal decoctions—all such articles of pleasure shall be fully provided therein.”

In this way, there were hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions of monasteries, halls, and pavilions, their number being immeasurable; with these, they made offerings before me and the community of bhikṣus.
For this reason, I say:

"After the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, if there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, or explain it to others; or if they write it themselves or instruct others to write it; or if they make offerings to the sutra scrolls—there is no need for them to further erect stupas or temples, nor to construct monasteries or provide offerings to the assembly of monks."

"How much more so for one who can uphold this sutra while simultaneously practicing generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-minded concentration, and wisdom; their merit is most supreme, immeasurable, and boundless."
Just as space is immeasurable and boundless in the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below;
so too are the merits of this person immeasurable and boundless, and they shall swiftly attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).

If there is a person who reads, recites, accepts, and upholds this sutra, explains it for others, or writes it themselves or teaches others to write it; if they further erect stupas, construct monasteries, and make offerings and praise to the assembly of śrāvakas; if they also praise the merits of bodhisattvas with hundreds of thousands of millions of methods of praise; and if they further explain this Lotus Sutra to others through various causes and conditions according to its meaning; furthermore, if they can maintain the precepts purely, dwell together with those who are gentle, practice patience without anger, possess firm resolve and mindfulness, always value sitting in meditation and attain various profound concentrations, exert themselves with vigor to gather all wholesome dharmas, and possess sharp faculties and wisdom to skillfully answer difficult questions—[they shall obtain such merit].

“Ānanda! If, after my parinirvāṇa, there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, and who further possess such virtuous merits as these, you should know that such persons have already set out for the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), are close to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and are seated beneath the tree of enlightenment.”

“Ajita! Wherever these sons and daughters of good family sit, stand, or walk, a stūpa should be erected there; all devas and humans should make offerings to it as they would to a stūpa of the Buddha.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning,
spoke these verses: “If, after my parinirvāṇa, one is able to uphold this sutra,
the merit of such a person shall be immeasurable, as has been described above.”
This constitutes the fulfillment of all offerings:
by erecting a stūpa for the śarīra, adorned with the seven treasures,
its spire exceedingly high and vast, tapering gradually until it reaches the Brahma-heaven.
Thousands of millions of precious bells, stirred by the wind, emit wondrous sounds. Furthermore,
throughout immeasurable kalpas, one makes offerings to this stupa with flowers,
incense, various necklaces, celestial robes, and manifold music.
By burning incense, oil, and ghee lamps, which constantly illuminate all around,
one who is able to uphold this sutra during the evil age of the Dharma’s final period has already performed,
as described above, every form of complete offering.
If one can uphold this sutra, it is as if the Buddha were present;
with gośīrṣa-candana, one should erect monasteries for offerings.
There shall be thirty-two halls, each eight tāla trees in height.
Exquisite food and fine garments, beds and couches all provided in full;
dwellings for hundreds of thousands of beings, gardens and various bathing pools,
places for walking meditation and dhyāna caves— all of these varieties are magnificently adorned.
If there is one with a mind of faith and understanding who receives, upholds, reads, recites, or transcribes [this sutra],
or further teaches others to transcribe it, and makes offerings to the scripture scrolls by scattering flowers,
incense, and powdered incense— such as sumana and campaka—
With *atimuktaka* flowers and perfumed oil, one should constantly maintain the lamps.
One who makes such offerings shall attain immeasurable merit;
as infinite as space, so too shall their blessings be.
How much more so for one who upholds this sutra, while simultaneously practicing generosity and maintaining the precepts,
delighting in patience and meditative concentration, refraining from anger and harsh speech,
showing reverence to stupas and temples, and humbling themselves before the bhikṣus.
Far removed from the mind of self-exaltation, Constantly contemplating wisdom,
Not becoming angry when questioned or challenged, Explaining the teachings in accordance with the truth—
If one can practice such conduct, One’s merit shall be immeasurable.
If one sees this Dharma-master who has accomplished such virtues,
one should scatter celestial flowers upon him and cover his body with celestial robes;
bowing with the head to touch his feet, one should give rise to the thought of regarding him as a Buddha.
Furthermore, one should reflect thus:
"Before long I shall go to the Tree of Enlightenment and attain the untainted and unconditioned state, widely benefiting all humans and devas.
Wherever I may dwell—whether walking, sitting, or lying down—"
Even if one were to recite but a single verse, a stūpa should be erected there,
adorned and made magnificent, with all manner of offerings.
When a Son of the Buddha dwells on this stage, it is then the very enjoyment of the Buddhas.
"Always remaining therein, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.
*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Scroll Five;
*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter 18: Merit of Rejoicing At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there are good sons or good daughters who, upon hearing this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, rejoice in it, how much merit will they obtain?
Then he spoke in verse:
"After the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One,
if there are those who hear this sutra and are able to rejoice in it, how much merit will they obtain?
At that time, the Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:

“Ajita! After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, if bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, as well as other wise ones—whether old or young—having heard this sutra and rejoiced in it, depart from the assembly and go elsewhere; whether they are in a monastery, in a secluded place, or in cities, streets, villages, or fields, they shall expound it according to their ability for their parents, kinsmen, virtuous friends, and acquaintances, in accordance with what they have heard.”
These people, having heard it, rejoiced and further propagated the teaching;
others, having heard it, likewise rejoiced and propagated the teaching.
In this manner, it was passed on successively until it reached the fiftieth person.
“Ajita! As for the merit of the rejoicing of the fiftieth son or daughter of good family, I shall now speak of it; you should listen well.”

Suppose there were beings in four million billion *asaṃkhyeya* worlds—beings of the six destinies and four modes of birth: those born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation; those with form or without form; those with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception; those without feet, with two feet, four feet, or many feet—all such as are reckoned among the class of sentient beings—and suppose someone seeking merit were to provide them with all the articles of enjoyment they might desire.

For each and every sentient being, one would provide gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, coral, amber, and all manner of exquisite rare jewels, as well as elephants, horses, and carriages, and palaces and towers made of the seven precious gems, filling the entirety of Jambudvīpa.
This great donor, having practiced such giving for a full eighty years, thought to himself:

"I have already provided sentient beings with all manner of objects of enjoyment according to their desires; yet these sentient beings are all in decline, being over eighty years of age, with white hair and wrinkled faces, and death will soon come upon them. I should now instruct and guide them with the Buddha-dharma."

He immediately gathered these sentient beings and proclaimed the transformation of the Dharma, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them; at once, they all attained the stage of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, and Arhat, exhausting all outflows (āsrava), attaining mastery in profound meditative concentrations (dhyāna-samādhi), and being endowed with the eight liberations (aṣṭa-vimokṣa).
"What do you think? Is the merit obtained by this great donor much?
Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
The merit of this person is exceedingly great, immeasurable and boundless.
If such a donor were merely to bestow all manner of articles of pleasure upon sentient beings, their merit would be immeasurable;
how much more so when they cause them to attain the fruit of Arhatship!
The Buddha told Maitreya:

"I now speak to you clearly: if a person were to give all manner of articles of pleasure to the sentient beings of the six realms throughout four million *koṭi-nayuta-asamkhyeya* worlds, and furthermore cause them to attain the fruit of Arhatship, the merit they would thereby acquire would not equal that of the fiftieth person who hears even a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and rejoices in it. A hundredth part, a thousandth part, a hundred-thousand-millionth part, or even any calculation or analogy, cannot reach one fraction of it."

“Ajita! Thus, the merit of the fiftieth person who hears the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* through successive transmission and rejoices in it is already immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*); how much more so for those who hear it at the very beginning of the assembly and rejoice—whose merit is even more superior, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable, beyond all comparison.”
"Furthermore, Ajita!

If a person, for the sake of this sutra, goes to a monastery and listens to it for even a brief moment—whether sitting or standing—by virtue of this merit, in their next rebirth they will obtain excellent and sublime elephant carriages, horse-drawn carriages, precious palanquins, and celestial palaces."

Furthermore, if there is a person sitting at a place where the Dharma is being taught, and another person comes and encourages them to sit and listen, or offers them half of their seat to sit upon, the merit of this person will cause them, upon changing bodies, to obtain the seat of Śakra, or the seat of Brahmā, or the seat of a Cakravartin King.
“Ānanda! If there is another person who says to others:
‘There is a sutra named the Lotus of the True Dharma; we should go together to listen to it.’”

Having immediately accepted his instruction, even if one hears it for but a moment, the merit of that person shall be such that, upon changing bodies, they will be born together with Bodhisattvas who possess *dhāraṇīs*. They will have sharp faculties and wisdom; for hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes, they will never be mute or speech-impaired; their breath will not be foul; their tongue will always be free from disease, as will their mouth; their teeth will not be stained black, nor yellow, nor sparse; they will not be missing, nor crooked; they will not be uneven or curved; their lips will not hang down, nor be retracted, nor be coarse and rough, nor have sores or warts, nor be defective or broken, nor be distorted or askew, nor be thick or large, nor be dark and sallow—possessing none of these loathsome qualities.
His nose was neither flat nor crooked; his facial complexion was neither dark nor narrow and long, nor was it sunken or distorted; there was not a single unpleasing feature about him.

His lips, tongue, and teeth were all perfectly adorned; his nose was long, high, and straight; his countenance was full and round; his eyebrows were high and long; his forehead was broad and level; he was endowed with all the marks of a superior person, and in every lifetime where he was born, he saw the Buddhas, heard the Dharma, and faithfully accepted their teachings.
"Ajita! You should observe this:

if the merit of merely exhorting a single person to go and listen to the Dharma is such as this, how much more so for one who listens with a single mind, recites it, explains it in detail for others among the great assembly, and practices according to what has been taught?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse: “If a person,
at a Dharma assembly, Hears this sutra, even as much as a single verse,
And with sympathetic joy explains it to others, ...[they shall attain supreme enlightenment].”
Thus, through successive instruction, reaching the fiftieth person,
the merit obtained by that final individual shall now be analyzed.
Suppose there were a great donor who provided for an immeasurable multitude.
Having reached a full eighty years of age, one may follow whatever the heart desires;
yet seeing that state of decay— hair white, face wrinkled,
teeth sparse, and the form withered— one reflects that death will not be long in coming.
I should now instruct them, so that they may attain the fruits of the Path.
Thereupon, for their sake, I spoke of the expedient means and the true Dharma of Nirvana:
"All things in the world are not solid; they are like foam, bubbles, and flames."
All of you should, with all haste, give rise to a mind of weary detachment.
Having heard this Dharma, all these people attained arhatship,
being fully endowed with the six supernormal powers, the three insights, and the eight liberations.
Finally, the fiftieth person, hearing a single verse and rejoicing in it,
possesses merit far superior to that [of the previous forty-nine], beyond all comparison. Thus,
as the news is passed on from one to another, the merit remains immeasurable.
How much more so for those who, at a Dharma assembly, hear it for the first time and rejoice;
or if one encourages another person, leading them to listen to the Lotus Sūtra, saying:
"This sūtra is profound and wondrous, difficult to encounter even in ten million kalpas."
He immediately accepted the instruction and went to listen;
even hearing it for but a moment, the karmic reward of such a person shall now be explained in detail:
in every lifetime he will be free from ailments of the mouth, and his teeth will not be sparse, yellow, or black.
The lips are neither thick nor upturned nor deficient, lacking any feature that could be loathed;
the tongue is neither dry, black, nor short; the nose is high, long, and straight;
the forehead is broad, level, and symmetrical; and the face and eyes are entirely dignified and majestic.
They will be pleasing to behold by others, and their breath will be free from foul odors;
the fragrance of the *utpala* lotus will constantly issue from their mouths.
If they intentionally go to a monastery wishing to hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*,
Hearing this for a brief moment brings joy; now I shall describe its merit.
In future lives among gods and humans, one will obtain exquisite elephants, horses, and chariots, as well as precious palanquins and carriages, and ride within celestial palaces.
If, at a place where the Dharma is being preached, one encourages others to sit and listen to the sutras,
through the causal conditions of this merit, one shall obtain the seats of Śakra, Brahmā, and the Cakravartin king;
how much more so for one who listens with a single-minded focus and explains its underlying meaning and intent?
"Practicing according to what has been taught, its merit is immeasurable.

Chapter Nineteen: The Merits of the Dharma-Master *The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Nineteen: The Merits of the Dharma-Master At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Constant Diligence:

"If a good man or a good woman receives, maintains, reads, recites, explains, or copies this *Lotus Sūtra*, that person shall obtain eight hundred merits of the eye, twelve hundred merits of the ear, eight hundred merits of the nose, twelve hundred merits of the tongue, eight hundred merits of the body, and twelve hundred merits of the mind. By means of these merits, they will adorn the six sense faculties, making them all pure."

These sons and daughters of good family, with the pure physical eyes born of their parents, see all the mountains, forests, rivers, and seas within and without the trichiliocosm; from below as far as the Avīci Hell, and above as far as the Peak of Existence, they also see all sentient beings therein, as well as their karmic causes and conditions and the places where they are reborn through the ripening of their fruits—all these they see and know completely.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses: “If,
in the midst of the great assembly, one preaches this Lotus Sūtra with a mind free from fear, listen now to its merits.”
This person attains eight hundred eyes of supreme merit;
because they are thus adorned, their vision is exceedingly pure.
With the eyes born of their parents, they see the entirety of the three thousandfold world system.
The inner and outer Mālu mountains, Sumeru and the Iron Ring Mountains,
along with all other mountain ranges and forests, the great oceans, rivers, and streams,
reaching down to the Avīci Hell and up to the Peak of Existence—
Within it, all sentient beings are seen by everyone;
though they have not yet attained the divine eye, the power of their physical eyes is such as this.
"Furthermore, Constantly Diligent One!
If good sons or good daughters receive and uphold this sutra—whether by reading it, reciting it, explaining it, or copying it—they will attain the twelve hundred merits of the ear.

With this purified ear, one hears all the various internal and external sounds within the trichiliocosm—from the Avīci Hell below up to the Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra) above—including the voices of elephants, horses, oxen, and chariots;
the sounds of weeping, lamentation, and sighing; and the sound of conch shells.
the sound of drums, the sound of bells, the sound of gongs; the sound of laughter, the sound of speech;
the voices of men, the voices of women, the voices of boys, the voices of girls; the sound of the Dharma, the sound of what is not the Dharma;
the sound of suffering, the sound of pleasure; the voices of ordinary persons, the voices of noble ones; the sound of joy, the sound of lack of joy; and the sounds of devas.
...the voices of nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas; the sounds of fire, water, and wind;
the voices of those in the hells, of animals, and of hungry ghosts; the voices of bhikṣus, and...
The voices of śrāmaṇerīs, the voices of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas— in short, all sounds,
both internal and external, existing within the trichiliocosm— he perceives them all with the pure,
natural ear born of his parents, even though he has not yet attained the divine ear.
"By hearing and knowing, one thus discriminates various sounds without impairing the faculty of the ear.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The ears born of one's parents Are pure and free from turbidity and defilement."
With this constant faculty of hearing, one hears the sounds throughout the three thousandfold world system:
the sounds of elephants, horses, chariots, and oxen; the sounds of bells, gongs, conchs, and drums;
the sounds of zithers, lutes, and harps; and the sounds of flutes and pipes.
With pure and beautiful voices, they listen without attachment;
the sounds of countless kinds of people, they hear and can fully comprehend.
Furthermore, they hear the voices of the devas, with their subtle and wondrous songs.
They hear the voices of men and women, and the voices of boys and girls;
in the mountains, rivers, and steep valleys,
they hear the calls of the kalaviṅka birds and all other species such as the jīvajīvaka, perceiving every sound.
The various sounds of agonizing pain from the hells,
And the cries of hungry ghosts oppressed by hunger and thirst as they seek food and drink;
The various asuras dwelling upon the shores of the great ocean—
When they converse with one another, a great sound issues forth.
Such a teacher of the Dharma, dwelling securely in this place,
hears these various sounds from afar without his faculty of hearing being impaired.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, the cries of birds and beasts calling to one another—
all these the person who preaches the Dharma hears here.
Furthermore, from all the Brahma heavens, including the Ābhāsvara and Śubhakṛtsna realms, [he likewise hears them].
Even unto the Peak of Existence, the sounds of speech—
wherever the Dharma Master abides, he hears them all.
All the assemblies of bhikṣus, as well as the bhikṣuṇīs, [he likewise hears].
Whether reciting the scriptures or expounding them for others,
wherever the Dharma Master dwells, they shall all hear them.
Furthermore, there are various bodhisattvas who recite the teachings of the sutras.
If one explains it for others, compiles it, and elucidates its meaning,
all such sounds will be heard. As for the Buddhas,
the Great Holy Honored Ones, who teach and transform sentient beings—
Within all great assemblies, they proclaim the subtle and wondrous Dharma;
those who uphold this Lotus Sutra shall hear them all.
As for all sounds, both internal and external, throughout the trichiliocosm—
From the Avīci Hell below up to the Peak of Existence above,
all hear their voices; yet their faculty of hearing remains unimpaired,
for it is keen and sharp, enabling them to discern and know them all.
One who upholds this Lotus Sutra, though they have not yet attained the divine ear, uses only their natural ears; yet their merit is already such as this.
Furthermore, Constantly Diligent One!
If good sons or good daughters receive and uphold this sutra—whether by reading it, reciting it, explaining it, or copying it—they will achieve eight hundred merits of the nose.

With this purified faculty of the nose, one who upholds this sūtra, while remaining right here, is able to distinguish all the various fragrances throughout the trichiliocosm—above, below, and within and without: the fragrance of *sumanā* flowers, *jāti* flowers, *mallikā* flowers, *campaka* flowers, *pāṭala* flowers; the fragrance of red lotuses, blue lotuses, and white lotuses; the fragrance of flowering trees and fruit-bearing trees; and the fragrances of sandalwood, aloeswood, *tamarapata*, and *tagara*, as well as millions of kinds of blended incenses, whether in powder, pill, or ointment form.

Furthermore, he specifically discerns the scents of sentient beings—the scent of elephants, the scent of horses, the scent of oxen, sheep, and so forth; the scent of men, the scent of women, the scent of boys, and the scent of girls—as well as the scents of grasses, trees, and thickets. Whether near or far, all such scents he perceives and hears without error or confusion.

Those who uphold this sutra, though dwelling here, shall likewise smell the fragrances of the various devas in the heavens—the scents of the pārijātaka and kovidāra trees, as well as the scents of māndārava flowers, mahāmāndārava flowers, mañjūṣaka flowers, mahāmañjūṣaka flowers, sandalwood, aloeswood, and various powdered incenses, along with the scents of diverse blossoms. They shall perceive and know every fragrance produced by such a combination of celestial perfumes.
Furthermore, one smells the bodily fragrances of the various devas—the fragrance when Śakra-devānām-indra is upon his magnificent palace, enjoying and sporting with the five sensual pleasures;
the fragrance when he is in the Hall of the Sublime Dharma, preaching the Dharma for the Trāyastriṃśa devas;
and the fragrance when he is sporting in the various gardens.
They also smell from afar the fragrances of the bodies of other devas, both male and female.

In this manner, the scent reaches as far as the Brahma-world, and they likewise smell the bodily fragrances of all the devas up to the Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra), as well as the incense burned by those devas.
Furthermore, they smell from afar the fragrances of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and the bodies of all Buddhas, and they know their locations.
Although they smell these fragrances, their faculty of the nose is neither impaired nor deluded; if they wish to discern them and explain them to others, their recollection is unerring.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The nose of this person is pure; within this world, whether it be fragrant or foul things, he perceives and knows them all in their various forms."
Sumanas, Jāti, Tamāla, and sandalwood,
Aquilaria and cinnamon fragrance, The scents of various flowers and fruits,
As well as the scents of sentient beings, And the scents of men and women.
When the preacher of the Dharma dwells afar, one knows his location by smelling his fragrance.
As for the powerful universal monarch, the minor wheel-turning kings,
their sons, the ministers, and the palace ladies— one knows their locations by smelling their fragrance.
The precious jewels worn upon the body, And the treasures hidden within the earth,
As well as the precious women of the Wheel-Turning King— By smelling their fragrance, one knows their location.
The various ornaments adorning people’s bodies, Their garments and their necklaces— [All are known by scent.]
By the various scented ointments applied [to their bodies], one knows their forms upon smelling the fragrance.
Whether the devas are walking or sitting, whether they are sporting or manifesting supernatural transformations,
those who uphold this Lotus Sutra can know them all by smelling the fragrance.
The flowers, fruits, and seeds of all trees, as well as the fragrance of ghee and oil—
wherever the upholder of this sutra dwells, he knows them all.
In the deep and perilous places among the mountains, where sandalwood trees are in full bloom, [he likewise knows them].
Those sentient beings dwelling therein, All can be known by smelling their fragrance.
The Iron Ring Mountains and the great oceans, And all the sentient beings within the earth—
The upholder of this sutra, by smelling their fragrance, Knows them all and where they reside.
When the asuras, male and female, along with all their retinues,
engage in combat or sport, he can know it all by smelling their fragrance.
Even in remote wildernesses and perilous narrow passes, he knows of lions, elephants, tigers, and wolves.
Wild oxen, water buffaloes, and the like, their locations are known by the scent.
If there is one who is pregnant, whether male or female is yet undetermined,
or those without sense organs and non-humans— all these can be fully known by smelling their scent.
By the power of smelling fragrances, he knows when one has first conceived,
whether [the pregnancy] will reach fulfillment or not, and whether one will give birth in peace to a blessed child.
By the power of smelling fragrances, he knows the thoughts of both men and women.
He knows those with minds of lust, delusion, and anger, as well as those who cultivate goodness.
Regarding the various hidden treasures beneath the earth— gold, silver,
and all manner of precious gems contained within copper vessels— he is able to know them all by their scent.
Various kinds of necklaces, whose value none can discern,
Are known for their worth, origin, and location by the scent they emit.
The various celestial flowers, such as the Māndārava and Mañjūṣaka—
The pārijātaka tree— by its scent, he knows it all.
The various celestial palaces, with their distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior,
and adorned with flowers of many jewels— by its scent, he knows them all.
In the celestial gardens, excellent palaces, and the sublime Dharma halls of various contemplations, they enjoy themselves;
by smelling their fragrance, [the Bodhisattva] knows them all.
Whether the devas are listening to the Dharma or experiencing the five desires, [he perceives it all].
Whether coming or going, walking, sitting, or lying down, he can know everything by the scent.
The garments worn by the celestial maidens, adorned with exquisite flowers and perfumes—
as they move about and sport, he can know them all by their fragrance.
Thus ascending successively, even unto the Brahma world,
those who enter and emerge from dhyāna— he knows them all by their scent.
From the Ābhāsvara and Śubhakṛtsna heavens, up to the Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra), he likewise perceives them.
Whether beings are first born or passing away, he knows them all by their scent.
The assembly of bhikṣus always exerts themselves with diligence in the Dharma;
whether sitting or walking, or engaged in reading and reciting the sūtras and teachings.
Or perhaps beneath forest trees, they sit in meditation with single-minded focus;
those who uphold the sutras perceive their fragrance and know exactly where they are.
The Bodhisattvas are firm in their resolve, whether sitting in meditation or engaged in recitation.
Or when preaching the Dharma for others, he knows it all by smelling their fragrance.
Wherever the World-Honored One dwells, revered by all,
preaching the Dharma out of compassion for the multitudes— he knows it all by smelling their fragrance.
Sentient beings before the Buddha, Hearing the sutra, all rejoice;
Practicing according to the Dharma, They are able to know everything by smelling the fragrance.
Though they have not yet attained the stage of a Bodhisattva, The faculty of the nose arises through the outflow-free dharmas (anāsrava-dharma).
"Furthermore, those who uphold this sutra will first attain this mark of the nose.
"Moreover, Constantly Diligent!
If a good man or a good woman receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes this sutra, they shall attain twelve hundred merits of the tongue."

Whether good or foul, beautiful or unappealing, or even bitter and astringent things, when they come into contact with his tongue-root, they all transform into the supreme flavor, like celestial ambrosia; there is nothing that is not delicious.

If, with his faculty of the tongue, he should preach among the great assembly, he utters a profound and wondrous sound that can enter their hearts, causing them all to rejoice and be filled with happiness.

Furthermore, the sons of gods, the daughters of gods, Śakra, Brahmā, and all the other devas, hearing this profound and wondrous sound and the orderly sequence of the discourse being expounded, all came to listen.

Furthermore, nāgas and nāga maidens, yakṣas and yakṣī maidens, gandharvas and gandharvī maidens, asuras and asurī maidens, garuḍas and garuḍī maidens, kiṃnaras and kiṃnarī maidens, and mahoragas and mahoragī maidens all came to attend upon, revere, and make offerings to him for the sake of hearing the Dharma.

Furthermore, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas and upāsikās, kings, princes, ministers, and their retinues, as well as minor wheel-turning kings, great wheel-turning kings, and their inner and outer retinues—including the seven treasures and a thousand sons—mounted their palaces and came together to listen to the Dharma, because this bodhisattva was so skilled in preaching the Dharma.
Brahmins, householders, and all the people within the realm shall serve and make offerings to him for as long as they live.
Furthermore, all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas will always delight in seeing him.

In whichever direction this person may be, all Buddhas will turn toward that place to preach the Dharma; they will be able to receive and uphold all Buddha-dharmas, and furthermore, they will be able to produce profound and wondrous sounds of the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The tongue-faculty of this person is pure, And they shall never experience foul flavors;
Whatever they consume and eat Shall all become nectar."
With a profound, pure, and wondrous voice, he preached the Dharma to the great assembly;
using various causes, conditions, and parables, he guided the minds of sentient beings.
All who heard him rejoiced and prepared the most excellent offerings.
The devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and asuras alike,
with hearts full of reverence, all come together to hear the Dharma;
if this speaker of the Dharma wishes to employ a wondrous voice, [he shall attain it].
Pervading the trichiliocosm, he can reach any place at will.
Great and small wheel-turning kings, along with their retinues of a thousand sons,
come constantly with palms joined in a reverent heart to listen to and receive the Dharma.
The devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas,
with hearts full of joy, also constantly delight in coming to make offerings.
The Brahmā King, the Māra King, Īśvara, and Maheśvara—
In this way, the hosts of devas constantly come to his dwelling.
When the Buddhas and their disciples hear the sound of his preaching the Dharma,
they constantly keep him in mind and protect him, and at times manifest themselves before him.
"Furthermore, Constantly Diligent!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, maintains, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes this sutra, they shall obtain eight hundred merits of the body."
He attains a pure body, like clear lapis lazuli, which all sentient beings delight to behold.

Because his body is pure, the birth and death of sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm—their high and low status, their beauty and ugliness, and their rebirth in good or evil realms—all appear within it.
Furthermore, the Cakravāḍa Mountains, the Mahācakravāḍa Mountains, Mount Meru, Mount Mahāmeru, and all other mountains, as well as the sentient beings dwelling therein, all appeared within it.
From the Avīci Hell below to the Peak of Existence above, all things and all sentient beings appear within it.
Whether it be śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or buddhas preaching the Dharma, the physical forms and images of them all appear within his body.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If one upholds the Lotus Sutra, Their body will be exceedingly pure,
Like that of clear lapis lazuli, Such that all sentient beings rejoice to behold it."
Just as a pure, bright mirror Reflects all forms and images,
So the Bodhisattva, within his pure body, Perceives everything that exists in the world;
He alone perceives it with perfect clarity, While others do not see it at all.
Within the three thousandfold world system, all classes of living beings—
gods, humans, asuras, those in the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals—
all such forms and appearances manifest within his body.
The palaces of the various devas, up to the Peak of Existence,
the Iron Ring Mountains and Mount Meru, Mahāmeru,
and all the waters of the great oceans— all these appear within his body.
The Buddhas and their śrāvakas, as well as the Bodhisattvas, sons of the Buddha—
whether alone or in the midst of a multitude— they all manifest when preaching the Dharma.
Although they have not yet attained the stainless, wondrous body of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), [they manifest it].
"By means of the pure, eternal essence, all things manifest therein.
Furthermore, Constant Diligence!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes this sutra, they shall attain twelve hundred merits of the mind."

By means of this purified mental faculty (*manas*), even upon hearing a single verse or a single phrase, one penetrates immeasurable and boundless meanings. Having understood these meanings, one is able to expound upon a single phrase or a single verse for as long as one month, four months, or even a year; all the teachings thus proclaimed accord with their respective significance and never contradict the true nature of reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Whether he speaks of secular scriptures, worldly discourse, or the arts for sustaining life, all are in accord with the True Dharma.
He fully knows the mental activities, the movements of the mind, and the conceptual proliferations of the minds of sentient beings throughout the six realms within the trichiliocosm.
Although they have not yet attained untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), their faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*) is thus purified.
Whatever this person contemplates, deliberates, or speaks is entirely the Buddha-dharma; it is all true and without exception, and is also that which was taught in the sūtras of the former Buddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The mind of this person is pure, Luminous, sharp, and free from defilement.
By means of this wondrous faculty of the mind, He knows the dharmas of superior, middling, and inferior."
Even upon hearing a single verse, they penetrate immeasurable meanings;
explaining them in sequence according to the Dharma, for months, four months, or even years.
To all sentient beings, both within and without this world, [they teach].
Whether they be devas, nāgas, humans, yakṣas, spirits, or others,
whatever various thoughts exist within the six realms of existence—
all these he knows at once as the fruit of upholding the Lotus Sūtra.
The countless Buddhas of the ten directions, Whose marks are adorned with a hundred merits, Preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings; I hear them all and am able to receive and uphold it.
Contemplating immeasurable meanings, They preach the Dharma in immeasurable ways.
From beginning to end they never forget their practice, because they uphold the Lotus Sūtra.
They fully know the characteristics of all dharmas, recognize their sequence according to their meaning, and master names and language; thus they expound what they have realized.
Whatever this person speaks is entirely the Dharma of the former Buddhas;
because they expound this Dharma, they have no fear among the assembly.
One who upholds the Lotus Sutra has the faculty of mind purified in this manner.
Although they have not yet attained the outflows-free state, they already possess such signs.
This person who upholds this sutra abides in a rare stage;
for the sake of all sentient beings, they are joyful and are loved and revered.
"By means of thousands of millions of kinds of skillful speech, they can analyze and preach the Dharma, because they uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. Chapter 20:
The Bodhisattva Sadāparibhūta The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Chapter Twenty: The Bodhisattva Sadāparibhūta At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta:
"You should now know this!

If any bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or upāsikā who upholds the Lotus Sūtra should be subjected to harsh speech, verbal abuse, or slander, they will receive a retribution for great sin as previously described;
yet the merit they shall obtain will be as previously described: their eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind will be purified."
“Mahāsthāmaprāpta!

In the distant past, beyond immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named King of Majestic Sound (*Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja*), a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.”
The kalpa was named Free from Decline, and the land was named Great Achievement.

In that world, the Buddha King of Majestic Voice preached the Dharma for devas, humans, and asuras; for those seeking the vehicle of the śrāvaka, he taught the Dharma corresponding to the Four Noble Truths to deliver them from birth, old age, sickness, and death, culminating in ultimate nirvāṇa;
and for those seeking the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha, he taught the Dharma corresponding to the twelve links of dependent origination.
"For the sake of all bodhisattvas, based upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I shall teach the dharmas corresponding to the six pāramitās, culminating in the wisdom of a Buddha.
Mahāsthāmaprāpta!..."
The lifespan of this Buddha King of Majestic Sound was forty trillion nayutas of kalpas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
the duration that his True Dharma remained in the world was equal to the number of kalpas represented by the dust motes of one Jambudvīpa;
and the duration that his Semblance Dharma remained in the world was equal to the number of dust motes of the four continents.
After that Buddha had extensively benefited sentient beings, he then entered parinirvāṇa.

Following the complete extinction of both the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma, another Buddha appeared in this land, likewise named Vimalacandravikrāntagāmin (King of Majestic Sound) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat.
In this sequence, there were twenty trillion Buddhas, all bearing the same name.

After the original Tathāgata King of Majestic Sound had entered parinirvāṇa and the True Dharma had ceased, during the period of the Semblance Dharma, monks of overweening pride possessed great power.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva bhikṣu named Sadāparibhūta.
Mahāsthāmaprāpta!
For what reason was he named Sadāparibhūta?
Whatever bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās this bhikṣu sees, he bows to and praises them all, saying:
"I deeply respect you all; I do not dare to treat you with contempt."
"Why is this? Because you all practice the bodhisattva path and shall surely attain Buddhahood.

Yet this bhikṣu did not specialize in reading or reciting the sūtras, but practiced only prostrations; even when he saw the fourfold assembly from afar, he would still go toward them to prostrate, praise them, and speak these words:
"I do not dare to look down upon you; you shall all become Buddhas.
Among the fourfold assembly, there were those who gave rise to anger and whose minds were impure, who spoke with foul mouths and reviled him, saying:
"From where has this ignorant bhikṣu come?"
He himself said:
"I do not slight you," and he bestowed upon us the prediction that we shall attain Buddhahood.
"We have no need for such false prophecies.
Thus, for many years, he was constantly reviled, yet he never gave rise to anger and always spoke these words:
"You shall become a Buddha."
When these words were spoken, the crowd struck and pelted him with sticks, clubs, tiles, and stones; yet he retreated to a distance and continued to cry out in a loud voice:
"I do not dare to slight you; you shall all become Buddhas."
Because he constantly spoke these words, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who were arrogant called him "Never-Disparaging."

When this bhikṣu was about to pass away, he heard in the midst of space the twenty thousand koṭis of verses of the Lotus Sūtra previously taught by the Buddha King of Majestic Voice; he was able to receive and uphold them all, and immediately attained the aforementioned purity of the eye faculty, as well as the purity of the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

Having attained this purity of the six sense faculties, his lifespan was further increased by two hundred trillion nayutas of years, during which he extensively preached this Lotus Sūtra for the sake of others.

At that time, the fourfold assembly of those with overweening pride—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—who had looked down upon this person named "Not-Disdainful" (Adīna-mānasa), saw that he had attained the power of great supernormal faculties, the power of eloquence in joyful exposition, and the power of great, sublime tranquility; hearing what he preached, they all believed, submitted, and followed him.
